abstract: I will describe my recent results on the automatic development of fixed(cid:173) width recursive distributed representations of variable-sized hierarchal data structures. One implication of this wolk is that certain types of AI-style data-structures can now be represented in fixed-width analog vectors. Simple inferences can be perfonned using the type of pattern associations that neural networks excel at Another implication arises from noting that these representations become self-similar in the limit Once this door to chaos is opened. many interesting new questions about the representational basis of intelligence emerge, and can (and will) be discussed.

paragraphs: The paper describes automatically developed representations that encode hierarchical data structures in analog vectors of fixed width. The structures being represented can vary in size, while the number of components in their vector representations stays fixed. Their recursive organization allows representations to address data whose parts are themselves structured.

One implication is that certain data structures associated with symbolic artificial intelligence can be expressed in a form suitable for neural-network processing. The author states that simple inferences can then be performed through pattern associations. This links structured information with an operation neural networks handle naturally: learning relationships between distributed patterns.

A second implication concerns the representations' mathematical behavior. The author reports that they become self-similar in the limit, connecting the work to questions about chaos and the representational foundations of intelligence. The contribution thus has both a computational and a conceptual aspect: fixed-width vectors can support some structured reasoning, while their recursive form raises further questions about the geometry and dynamics of representation.
summary.tldr: Recursive distributed representations encode variable-sized hierarchical structures in fixed-width vectors and support simple inference through pattern association.

title: Implications of Recursive Distributed Representations

paragraphs: The paper asks how a grammar can be expressed using connectionist computational principles. Its answer is a Harmonic Grammar: a system of soft constraints evaluated together, with well-formed linguistic structures corresponding to solutions of an optimization problem. This gives grammatical specification a form suited to parallel constraint processing.

The stated contribution is to show that formal languages can also be specified this way. Harmonic Grammars had already been applied to problems concerning natural languages; here the approach extends to formal-language descriptions usually expressed through sequential rewrite rules. The significance is that grammatical structure can be defined through the combined demands of constraints.

The supplied text also connects this framework to a broader account of symbolic computation. A representation can be viewed as distributed neural activity at one level and as a symbolic structure at another. Filler-role bindings describe how constituents occupy structural positions. Within this perspective, Harmonic Grammars provide a route for connecting structured symbolic descriptions to underlying connectionist computation.
summary.tldr: Harmonic Grammars specify formal languages through parallel soft constraints whose optimization identifies well-formed structures.

title: Harmonic Grammars for Formal Languages

abstract: Deciding the appropriate representation to use for modeling human auditory processing is a critical issue in auditory science. While engi(cid:173) neers have successfully performed many single-speaker tasks with LPC and spectrogram methods, more difficult problems will need a richer representation. This paper describes a powerful auditory representation known as the correlogram and shows how this non-linear representation can be converted back into sound, with no loss of perceptually impor(cid:173) tant information. The correlogram is interesting because it is a neuro(cid:173) physiologically plausible representation of sound. This paper shows improved methods for spectrogram inversion (conventional pattern playback), inversion of a cochlear model, and inversion of the correlo(cid:173) gram representation.

paragraphs: The paper asks what representation of sound is suitable for modeling human hearing. It argues that representations successful on many single-speaker engineering tasks may be insufficient for harder auditory problems. Its focus is the correlogram, a nonlinear sound representation that the authors describe as plausible in terms of auditory neurophysiology.

The central contribution is showing how to convert this representation back into sound. This inversion matters because it connects an internal representation to an audible result: the reconstructed sound reveals whether perceptually important information has survived the transformation. The authors report that correlogram inversion preserves such information.

The work also presents improved inversion methods for spectrograms and for a cochlear model. Together, these methods extend pattern playback across several representations used to describe auditory processing. The claim about the correlogram concerns preservation of perceptually important information, rather than an explicitly stated requirement of exact waveform recovery. The paper thus makes a richer auditory representation usable in both directions, from sound into a model and back into sound.
summary.tldr: The paper reconstructs sound from correlograms without losing perceptually important information and improves inversion of other auditory representations.

title: Pattern Playback in the 90s

abstract: Unsupervised learning procedures have been successful at low-level feature extraction and preprocessing of raw sensor data. So far, however, they have had limited success in learning higher-order representations, e.g., of objects in visual images. A promising ap(cid:173) proach is to maximize some measure of agreement between the outputs of two groups of units which receive inputs physically sep(cid:173) arated in space, time or modality, as in (Becker and Hinton, 1992; Becker, 1993; de Sa, 1993). Using the same approach, a much sim(cid:173) pler learning procedure is proposed here which discovers features in a single-layer network consisting of several populations of units, and can be applied to multi-layer networks trained one layer at a time. When trained with this algorithm on image sequences of moving geometric objects a two-layer network can learn to perform accurate position-invariant object classification. 1 LEARNING COHERENT CLASSIFICATIONS A powerful constraint in sensory data is coherence over time, in space, and across different sensory modalities. An unsupervised learning procedure which can capital(cid:173) ize on these constraints may be able to explain much of perceptual self-organization in the mammalian brain. The problem is to derive an appropriate cost function for unsupervised learning which will capture coherence constraints in sensory signals; we would also like it to be applicable to multi-layer nets to train hidden as well as output layers. Our ultimate goal is for the network to discover natural object classes based on these coherence assumptions. 934

paragraphs: The paper tackles unsupervised learning of object-level representations. Its starting point is coherence: related sensory observations can remain consistent across time, space, or different modalities. Encouraging agreement between groups of units receiving separated inputs can turn that consistency into a learning signal, helping a network discover structure beyond low-level features.

The proposed procedure simplifies this agreement-based approach. It learns features in a single-layer network containing several populations of units and can also train multilayer networks one layer at a time. This provides a route for applying the same learning principle to hidden representations as well as final outputs.

When trained on sequences of moving geometric objects, a two-layer network learns accurate object classification that is insensitive to position. The finding shows how temporal coherence can support learning what remains consistent while an object moves. The underlying assumption is that sensory coherence contains useful information about object identity; the demonstrated result uses moving geometric objects to put that principle into practice.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised agreement-based learning procedure uses moving-image coherence to learn position-invariant object classification.

title: JPMAX: Learning to Recognize Moving Objects as a Model-fitting Problem

abstract: In this paper we consider probabilities of different asymptotics of convergent unlearning algorithm for the Hopfield-type neural net(cid:173) work (Plakhov & Semenov, 1994) treating the case of unbiased random patterns. We show also that failed unlearning results in total memory breakdown.
originalAbstract: In this paper we consider probabilities of different asymptotics of convergent unlearning algorithm for the Hopfield-type neural net(cid:173) work (Plakhov & Semenov, 1994) treating the case of unbiased random patterns. We show also that failed unlearning results in total memory breakdown.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes the long-run behavior of a convergent unlearning algorithm for a Hopfield-type neural network. Its focus is probabilistic: the authors consider the chances of different asymptotic outcomes, meaning the behaviors approached as the algorithm continues. The analysis therefore concerns which eventual outcomes occur and how likely they are.

The stated setting uses unbiased random patterns. That assumption defines the pattern population for the analysis and gives the probability questions a specific scope. The paper's subject is the behavior of the unlearning procedure under those conditions, with attention to the possible outcomes rather than only the fact that the algorithm converges.

The central reported result is that failed unlearning leads to total memory breakdown. This makes the failure outcome consequential for the network's memory as a whole. It also shows why convergence and successful memory behavior must be distinguished: an algorithm's eventual outcome still needs to be assessed for what it preserves. The paper contributes a probability-based examination of those outcomes and a strong characterization of failure.
summary.tldr: For unbiased random patterns, the paper analyzes unlearning outcomes and shows that failed unlearning causes total memory breakdown.

title: Some results on convergent unlearning algorithm

abstract: We examine the statistics of natural monochromatic images decomposed using a multi-scale wavelet basis. Although the coefficients of this rep(cid:173) resentation are nearly decorrelated, they exhibit important higher-order statistical dependencies that cannot be eliminated with purely linear pro(cid:173) c~ssing. In particular, rectified coefficients corresponding to basis func(cid:173) tions at neighboring spatial positions, orientations and scales are highly correlated. A method of removing these dependencies is to divide each coefficient by a weighted combination of its rectified neighbors. Sev(cid:173) eral successful models of the steady -state behavior of neurons in primary visual cortex are based on such "divisive normalization" computations, and thus our analysis provides a theoretical justification for these models. Perhaps more importantly, the statistical measurements explicitly specify the weights that should be used in computing the normalization signal. We demonstrate that this weighting is qualitatively consistent with re(cid:173) cent physiological experiments that characterize the suppressive effect of stimuli presented outside of the classical receptive field. Our obser(cid:173) vations thus provide evidence for the hypothesis that early visual neural processing is well matched to these statistical properties of images.

paragraphs: This paper connects the statistics of natural monochrome images with response suppression in primary visual cortex. The authors decompose images using wavelets at multiple scales. Although the resulting coefficients have little ordinary correlation, their rectified values remain strongly related across nearby positions, orientations, and scales. These higher-order dependencies survive purely linear processing.

The proposed statistical remedy is divisive normalization: divide each coefficient by a weighted combination of rectified neighboring coefficients. Similar computations already appear in models of visual neurons. The analysis gives those computations a statistical rationale and, more specifically, uses measured image dependencies to determine the weights contributing to the normalization signal.

The derived weighting is qualitatively consistent with physiological experiments showing that stimuli outside a neuron's classical receptive field can suppress its response. This links a property of natural images to a property of neural processing. The result supports the hypothesis that early vision is adapted to image statistics, with surrounding activity providing information relevant to normalizing a local response.
summary.tldr: Natural-image statistics determine divisive-normalization weights that qualitatively match observed surround suppression in visual cortex.

title: Modeling Surround Suppression in V1 Neurons with a Statistically Derived Normalization Model

abstract: We describe a method for learning an overcomplete set of basis functions for the purpose of modeling sparse structure in images. The sparsity of the basis function coefficients is modeled with a mixture-of-Gaussians distribution. One Gaussian captures non(cid:173) active coefficients with a small-variance distribution centered at zero, while one or more other Gaussians capture active coefficients with a large-variance distribution. We show that when the prior is in such a form, there exist efficient methods for learning the basis functions as well as the parameters of the prior. The performance of the algorithm is demonstrated on a number of test cases and also on natural images. The basis functions learned on natural images are similar to those obtained with other methods, but the sparse form of the coefficient distribution is much better described. Also, since the parameters of the prior are adapted to the data, no assumption about sparse structure in the images need be made a priori, rather it is learned from the data.

paragraphs: This paper learns an overcomplete collection of basis functions for representing sparse structure in images. The representation uses coefficients to determine how much each basis function contributes. Its central modeling choice is to describe these coefficients with a mixture of Gaussian distributions that separates inactive contributions from active ones.

A narrow Gaussian centered on zero captures coefficients associated with inactivity. One or more broader Gaussians capture active coefficients that can take larger values. The authors show that this prior structure permits efficient learning of both the basis functions and the parameters governing the coefficient distribution. The representation and its statistical description therefore adapt together.

Tests include constructed cases and natural images. On natural images, the learned basis functions resemble those obtained by other methods, while the sparse coefficient distribution is described substantially better. Because the prior parameters are learned from the data, the method does not require the sparse structure to be specified in advance. Its benefit concerns learning how coefficients are distributed as well as learning the image components themselves.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian-mixture coefficient prior enables efficient sparse-code learning while adapting the description of sparsity to the image data.

title: Learning Sparse Codes with a Mixture-of-Gaussians Prior

abstract: We introduce the mixture of Gaussian processes (MGP) model which is useful for applications in which the optimal bandwidth of a map is input dependent. The MGP is derived from the mixture of experts model and can also be used for modeling general conditional probability densities. We discuss how Gaussian processes -in particular in form of Gaussian process classification, the support vector machine and the MGP model(cid:173) can be used for quantifying the dependencies in graphical models.
originalAbstract: We introduce the mixture of Gaussian processes (MGP) model which is useful for applications in which the optimal bandwidth of a map is input dependent. The MGP is derived from the mixture of experts model and can also be used for modeling general conditional probability densities. We discuss how Gaussian processes -in particular in form of Gaussian process classification, the support vector machine and the MGP model(cid:173) can be used for quantifying the dependencies in graphical models.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a mixture of Gaussian processes for applications where the appropriate bandwidth of a mapping depends on the input. Bandwidth concerns the scale over which the mapping varies, so this setting calls for different behavior in different parts of the input space. The proposed model addresses that variation through a mixture construction.

The model is derived from the mixture-of-experts framework, connecting Gaussian-process modeling to an approach that combines multiple predictive components. Its stated scope also includes general conditional probability densities. This extends the intended use beyond describing a single predicted value, allowing the model to represent how a distribution of possible outcomes depends on the input.

The paper additionally discusses quantifying dependencies in graphical models using Gaussian-process classification, support vector machines, and the proposed mixture. This connects the new model to the broader task of specifying probabilistic relationships. The abstract's contribution is the model and these uses: it identifies input-dependent bandwidth and conditional-density modeling as reasons to consider mixtures of Gaussian processes.
summary.tldr: Mixtures of Gaussian processes address input-dependent bandwidth and can model conditional probability densities and dependencies in graphical models.

title: Mixtures of Gaussian Processes

abstract: We present an algorithm that induces a class of models with thin junction trees—models that are characterized by an upper bound on the size of the maximal cliques of their triangulated graph. By ensuring that the junction tree is thin, inference in our models remains tractable throughout the learning process. This allows both an efﬁcient implementation of an iterative scaling parameter estimation algorithm and also ensures that inference can be performed efﬁciently with the ﬁnal model. We illustrate the approach with applications in handwritten digit recognition and DNA splice site detection.

By ensuring that the junction tree is thin, inference in our models remains tractable throughout the learning process. This allows both an efﬁcient implementation of an iterative scaling parameter estimation algorithm and also ensures that inference can be performed efﬁciently with the ﬁnal model. We illustrate the approach with applications in handwritten digit recognition and DNA splice site detection.

paragraphs: The paper presents an algorithm for learning models whose junction trees remain thin. Thinness means imposing an upper bound on the largest cliques in the model's triangulated graph. This structural restriction matters because inference must be carried out within the model, and the authors use it to keep that computation tractable.

The restriction is maintained throughout learning, rather than applied only to the completed model. As a result, the authors can efficiently implement an iterative scaling algorithm for estimating parameters. The model structure and the parameter-learning procedure are therefore designed to work together: maintaining manageable inference supports the repeated computations needed during estimation.

The same structural property also allows efficient inference after learning has finished. The authors illustrate the approach through handwritten digit recognition and DNA splice-site detection. The contribution is a model-learning strategy that explicitly controls inference complexity at both stages of use, making tractability a property preserved by the learning process and retained by its final output.
summary.tldr: Bounding junction-tree clique sizes keeps inference tractable during model learning and in the final learned model.

title: Thin Junction Trees

abstract: This article presents a 2-phase computational learning model and appli- cation. As a demonstration, a system has been built, called CHIME for Computer Human Interacting Musical Entity. In phase 1 of training, re- current back-propagationtrains the machine to reproduce 3 jazz melodies. The recurrent network is expanded and is further trained in phase 2 with a reinforcement learning algorithm and a critique produced by a set of basic rules for jazz improvisation. After each phase CHIME can interactively improvise with a human in real time.

As a demonstration, a system has been built, called CHIME for Computer Human Interacting Musical Entity. In phase 1 of training, re- current back-propagationtrains the machine to reproduce 3 jazz melodies. paragraphs: The paper presents a two-phase learning approach for musical improvisation and demonstrates it in a system called CHIME, the Computer Human Interacting Musical Entity. The system is designed for interactive music-making with a human. Its training combines learning to reproduce musical examples with a later stage that evaluates improvisation using basic jazz rules.

In the first phase, recurrent back-propagation trains a network to reproduce three jazz melodies. This establishes a learned repertoire through a sequence-processing network. The network is then expanded for the second phase, where reinforcement learning uses a critique generated by a set of basic improvisation rules. The training objective thus changes from reproducing examples to learning under rule-based feedback.

CHIME can improvise interactively with a person in real time after either phase. This makes the application a demonstration of usable musical interaction at both stages of the learning process. The contribution is the combined computational model and working system, showing how example-based recurrent training and subsequent reinforcement learning can be brought together in an improvising musical application.
summary.tldr: CHIME combines recurrent training on jazz melodies with rule-guided reinforcement learning to improvise with a human in real time.

title: Improvisation and Learning

abstract: Side-chain prediction is an important subtask in the protein-folding problem. We show that finding a minimal energy side-chain con(cid:173) figuration is equivalent to performing inference in an undirected graphical model. The graphical model is relatively sparse yet has many cycles. We used this equivalence to assess the performance of approximate inference algorithms in a real-world setting. Specifi(cid:173) cally we compared belief propagation (BP), generalized BP (GBP) and naive mean field (MF). In cases where exact inference was possible, max-product BP al(cid:173) ways found the global minimum of the energy (except in few cases where it failed to converge), while other approximation algorithms of similar complexity did not. In the full protein data set, max(cid:173) product BP always found a lower energy configuration than the other algorithms, including a widely used protein-folding software (SCWRL).

paragraphs: Predicting protein side chains is one part of the larger protein-folding problem. This paper connects that task to probabilistic inference: finding the side-chain arrangement with minimum energy is equivalent to inference in an undirected graphical model. The resulting graph has relatively few connections but contains many cycles, making it a useful setting for studying approximate inference.

The authors use this connection to compare belief propagation, generalized belief propagation, and naive mean field on a concrete scientific problem. They give particular attention to max-product belief propagation, which searches for a best configuration. Where exact inference is feasible, it provides a reference for checking whether an approximate method reaches the true minimum.

In those tractable cases, max-product belief propagation found the global minimum whenever it converged, with a few convergence failures. Across the full protein dataset, it found lower-energy configurations than the other tested algorithms, including SCWRL. These results support its effectiveness on the studied task while preserving the distinction between strong observed performance and guaranteed convergence.
summary.tldr: Protein side-chain prediction becomes a graphical-model inference problem, where max-product belief propagation performs strongly in the reported comparisons.

title: Approximate Inference and Protein-Folding

abstract: A new feature extraction criterion, maximum margin criterion (MMC), is proposed in this paper. This new criterion is general in the sense that, when combined with a suitable constraint, it can actually give rise to the most popular feature extractor in the literature, linear discriminate analysis (LDA). We derive a new feature extractor based on MMC using a different constraint that does not depend on the nonsingularity of the within-class scatter matrix Sw. Such a dependence is a major drawback of LDA especially when the sample size is small. The kernelized (nonlin- ear) counterpart of this linear feature extractor is also established in this paper. Our preliminary experimental results on face images demonstrate that the new feature extractors are efﬁcient and stable.

This new criterion is general in the sense that, when combined with a suitable constraint, it can actually give rise to the most popular feature extractor in the literature, linear discriminate analysis (LDA). We derive a new feature extractor based on MMC using a different constraint that does not depend on the nonsingularity of the within-class scatter matrix Sw. Such a dependence is a major drawback of LDA especially when the sample size is small. The kernelized (nonlin- ear) counterpart of this linear feature extractor is also established in this paper. paragraphs: The paper proposes the maximum margin criterion as a basis for feature extraction. Feature extraction constructs a representation of data for subsequent analysis or classification. The authors show that their criterion is general enough to recover linear discriminant analysis when paired with a suitable constraint, connecting the proposal to an established method.

Using a different constraint, they derive a feature extractor that does not require the within-class scatter matrix to be nonsingular. That matrix describes variation within classes, and its nonsingularity is a problematic requirement for LDA, particularly when few samples are available. The new formulation therefore addresses a specific mathematical dependency rather than simply changing the feature-extraction objective.

The paper also establishes a kernelized, nonlinear counterpart to the linear extractor. Preliminary experiments on face images indicate that the proposed extractors are efficient and stable. Those findings provide initial empirical support for the formulations, while the structural contribution is the alternative constraint that removes the stated matrix requirement and extends to a nonlinear version.
summary.tldr: A maximum-margin feature-extraction criterion yields linear and nonlinear methods that avoid LDA’s nonsingular within-class scatter requirement, with promising preliminary face-image results.

title: Efficient and Robust Feature Extraction by Maximum Margin Criterion

abstract: This paper investigates a new learning model in which the input data is corrupted with noise. We present a general statistical framework to tackle this problem. Based on the statistical reasoning, we propose a novel formulation of support vector classiﬁcation, which allows uncer- tainty in input data. We derive an intuitive geometric interpretation of the proposed formulation, and develop algorithms to efﬁciently solve it. Empirical results are included to show that the newly formed method is superior to the standard SVM for problems with noisy input.
originalAbstract: This paper investigates a new learning model in which the input data is corrupted with noise. We present a general statistical framework to tackle this problem. Based on the statistical reasoning, we propose a novel formulation of support vector classiﬁcation, which allows uncer- tainty in input data. We derive an intuitive geometric interpretation of the proposed formulation, and develop algorithms to efﬁciently solve it. Empirical results are included to show that the newly formed method is superior to the standard SVM for problems with noisy input.

paragraphs: Classification methods must sometimes learn from input measurements corrupted by noise. This paper treats that corruption as uncertainty to be incorporated into the learning model. It develops a general statistical framework for the problem and uses that reasoning to reformulate support vector classification.

The resulting classifier allows uncertainty in the inputs as part of its formulation. The authors also derive a geometric interpretation, connecting the statistical construction to an intuitive view of the classification problem. They develop algorithms to solve the formulation efficiently, linking the proposed modeling change to a practical computational procedure.

Empirical results show the new method outperforming the standard SVM on the noisy-input problems studied. This supports the usefulness of representing input uncertainty explicitly in those settings. The paper's contribution spans the statistical model, its geometric meaning, and the algorithms needed to fit it; the performance finding is empirical evidence for the tested problems rather than a guarantee for every possible kind of noise.
summary.tldr: A statistical reformulation of support vector classification explicitly accommodates input uncertainty and outperforms a standard SVM on the reported noisy-input problems.

title: Support Vector Classification with Input Data Uncertainty

abstract: We present a novel approach to collaborative prediction, using low-norm instead of low-rank factorizations. The approach is inspired by, and has strong connections to, large-margin linear discrimination. We show how to learn low-norm factorizations by solving a semi-deﬁnite program, and discuss generalization error bounds for them.

The approach is inspired by, and has strong connections to, large-margin linear discrimination. We show how to learn low-norm factorizations by solving a semi-deﬁnite program, and discuss generalization error bounds for them.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a matrix-factorization approach to collaborative prediction. Its central change is how it controls the factorization: it favors low norm rather than low rank. Rank and norm describe different aspects of a matrix representation, so this changes the kind of restriction used to guide learning from the available observations.

The approach is inspired by large-margin linear discrimination and has strong connections to it. This places collaborative prediction in contact with a classification principle centered on margins. The paper's contribution is therefore both a factorization formulation and a conceptual connection: it brings a form of magnitude control associated with large-margin learning into the matrix prediction setting.

The authors show that low-norm factorizations can be learned by solving a semidefinite program, giving the proposal an explicit optimization route. They also discuss generalization-error bounds, connecting the learned representation with questions about prediction beyond observed data. These are methodological and theoretical contributions; the abstract's stated results concern the formulation, its optimization, and its generalization analysis.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces low-norm matrix factorization for collaborative prediction, linking it to large-margin learning and semidefinite optimization.

title: Maximum-Margin Matrix Factorization

abstract: We present a reduction framework from ordinal regression to binary classification based on extended examples. The framework consists of three steps: extracting extended examples from the original examples, learning a binary classifier on the extended examples with any binary classification algorithm, and constructing a ranking rule from the binary classifier. A weighted 0/1 loss of the binary classifier would then bound the mislabeling cost of the ranking rule. Our framework allows not only to design good ordinal regression algorithms based on well-tuned binary classification approaches, but also to derive new generalization bounds for ordinal regression from known bounds for binary classification. In addition, our framework unifies many existing ordinal regression algorithms, such as perceptron ranking and support vector ordinal regression. When compared empirically on benchmark data sets, some of our newly designed algorithms enjoy advantages in terms of both training speed and generalization performance over existing algorithms, which demonstrates the usefulness of our framework.

paragraphs: This paper gives a general way to solve ordinal regression, where labels have an order, using binary classification. The framework first derives extended examples from the original training data. It then trains a binary classifier on those examples and converts the classifier into a rule for assigning ordered labels.

The reduction comes with a mathematical connection between the two tasks: a weighted binary classification error bounds the ranking rule's mislabeling cost. This allows established binary classification methods to support ordinal prediction. It also lets known binary-classification generalization bounds be used to derive new bounds for ordinal regression.

The result supports the usefulness of the reduction as both an analytical framework and a practical design method, with the empirical advantages applying to the reported algorithms and comparisons.
summary.tldr: A reduction from ordinal regression to binary classification transfers learning methods and error bounds while yielding competitive new algorithms.

title: Ordinal Regression by Extended Binary Classification

abstract: Policy gradient methods are reinforcement learning algorithms that adapt a param- eterized policy by following a performance gradient estimate. Conventional pol- icy gradient methods use Monte-Carlo techniques to estimate this gradient. Since Monte Carlo methods tend to have high variance, a large number of samples is required, resulting in slow convergence. In this paper, we propose a Bayesian framework that models the policy gradient as a Gaussian process. This reduces the number of samples needed to obtain accurate gradient estimates. Moreover, estimates of the natural gradient as well as a measure of the uncertainty in the gradient estimates are provided at little extra cost.

In this paper, we propose a Bayesian framework that models the policy gradient as a Gaussian process. This reduces the number of samples needed to obtain accurate gradient estimates. paragraphs: Policy gradient methods improve a reinforcement learning policy by estimating how changes to its parameters affect performance. Conventional methods use Monte Carlo sampling to estimate that direction of improvement. Because these estimates tend to have high variance, obtaining a sufficiently accurate direction can require many samples and slow learning.

This paper proposes a Bayesian framework that models the policy gradient as a Gaussian process. The aim is to use the available observations more effectively when estimating how the policy should change. The authors report that the framework reduces the number of samples required to obtain accurate gradient estimates, directly addressing the sampling burden of conventional methods.

The framework also supplies estimates of the natural gradient and quantifies uncertainty in its gradient estimates at little additional cost. Thus, its output includes both an improvement direction and information about how uncertain that direction is. The contribution combines greater sample efficiency in gradient estimation with additional information useful for understanding the reliability of a policy update.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian-process model of policy gradients reduces the samples needed for accurate estimates and provides natural gradients and uncertainty at little extra cost.

title: Bayesian Policy Gradient Algorithms

abstract: We propose a family of kernels for structured objects which is based on the bag-ofcomponents paradigm. However, rather than decomposing each complex object into the single histogram of its components, we use for each object a family of nested histograms, where each histogram in this hierarchy describes the object seen from an increasingly granular perspective. We use this hierarchy of histograms to define elementary kernels which can detect coarse and fine similarities between the objects. We compute through an efficient averaging trick a mixture of such specific kernels, to propose a final kernel value which weights efficiently local and global matches. We propose experimental results on an image retrieval experiment which show that this mixture is an effective template procedure to be used with kernels on histograms.

We use this hierarchy of histograms to define elementary kernels which can detect coarse and fine similarities between the objects. We compute through an efficient averaging trick a mixture of such specific kernels, to propose a final kernel value which weights efficiently local and global matches. paragraphs: The paper proposes a way to compare structured objects using more than one histogram of their components. A single bag-of-components histogram gives one summary of an object. Here, each object instead receives a hierarchy of nested histograms, describing it at progressively finer levels of detail.

The authors use this hierarchy to construct elementary kernels that respond to similarities at different scales. Coarser views can contribute broad matches, while finer views can contribute more detailed ones. An efficient averaging procedure combines these individual kernels into a final similarity value that weights both local and global matches. The hierarchy therefore participates directly in the comparison rather than serving only as a collection of separate descriptions.

An image-retrieval experiment provides evidence that the mixture is an effective general procedure for histogram-based kernels. The contribution is the combination of a multilevel representation and an efficient way to aggregate its comparisons. It offers a framework for retaining different granularities of similarity when a single component histogram would provide only one view.
summary.tldr: Nested histograms support an efficiently averaged kernel that combines coarse, fine, local, and global similarities.

title: Kernels on Structured Objects Through Nested Histograms

abstract: Over the past few years, the notion of stability in data clustering has received growing attention as a cluster validation criterion in a sample-based framework. However, recent work has shown that as the sample size increases, any clustering model will usually become asymptotically stable. This led to the conclusion that stability is lacking as a theoretical and practical tool. The discrepancy between this conclusion and the success of stability in practice has remained an open ques- tion, which we attempt to address. Our theoretical approach is that stability, as used by cluster validation algorithms, is similar in certain respects to measures of generalization in a model-selection framework. In such cases, the model cho- sen governs the convergence rate of generalization bounds. By arguing that these rates are more important than the sample size, we are led to the prediction that stability-based cluster validation algorithms should not degrade with increasing sample size, despite the asymptotic universal stability. This prediction is substan- tiated by a theoretical analysis as well as some empirical results. We conclude that stability remains a meaningful cluster validation criterion over ﬁnite samples.

paragraphs: Cluster stability is used to assess whether a clustering remains consistent across samples. A theoretical objection is that, as sample sizes grow, almost any clustering model usually becomes stable. If all models eventually share this property, stability might appear unable to distinguish useful choices. Yet stability-based validation has worked in practice, creating the discrepancy this paper investigates.

The authors connect stability-based validation to generalization in model selection. Their central point concerns convergence rates: different models can approach their large-sample behavior at different speeds. Those differences can matter at finite sample sizes even when the models share a stable limiting outcome. The eventual destination alone therefore does not settle whether stability is informative during convergence.

This reasoning predicts that stability-based validation should not deteriorate merely because sample sizes increase. The paper supports that prediction with theoretical analysis and some empirical results. Its conclusion is that stability remains meaningful for finite samples, reconciling its practical usefulness with the observation that asymptotic stability is widespread.
summary.tldr: Differences in convergence rates help explain why cluster stability can remain informative for finite samples despite widespread asymptotic stability.

title: Cluster Stability for Finite Samples

abstract: The recently proposed \emph{additive noise model} has advantages over previous structure learning algorithms, when attempting to recover some true data generating mechanism, since it (i) does not assume linearity or Gaussianity and (ii) can recover a unique DAG rather than an equivalence class. However, its original extension to the multivariate case required enumerating all possible DAGs, and for some special distributions, e.g. linear Gaussian, the model is invertible and thus cannot be used for structure learning. We present a new approach which combines a PC style search using recent advances in kernel measures of conditional dependence with local searches for additive noise models in substructures of the equivalence class. This results in a more computationally efficient approach that is useful for arbitrary distributions even when additive noise models are invertible. Experiments with synthetic and real data show that this method is more accurate than previous methods when data are nonlinear and/or non-Gaussian.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering a directed acyclic graph that describes a data-generating mechanism. Additive noise models are attractive because they need not assume linear relationships or Gaussian data and can sometimes identify a unique graph. However, an earlier multivariate approach enumerated all possible graphs, and invertible cases such as linear Gaussian models cannot be resolved by that approach alone.

The proposed method combines a PC-style search with local additive-noise searches. Kernel measures of conditional dependence guide the first stage. The local searches then examine substructures within the resulting equivalence class, using additive-noise information where it can help distinguish directions.

This combination is more computationally efficient and remains useful for arbitrary distributions, including cases where additive noise models are invertible. That usefulness does not imply unique identification in every case. Experiments on synthetic and real data show greater accuracy than previous methods when relationships are nonlinear and/or data are non-Gaussian. The approach brings complementary sources of structural information into one search procedure.
summary.tldr: Combining conditional-dependence search with local additive-noise modeling improves efficiency and empirical graph recovery for nonlinear or non-Gaussian data.

title: Nonlinear directed acyclic structure learning with weakly additive noise models

abstract: The CUR decomposition provides an approximation of a matrix X that has low reconstruction error and that is sparse in the sense that the resulting approximation lies in the span of only a few columns of X. In this regard, it appears to be similar to many sparse PCA methods. However, CUR takes a randomized algorithmic approach whereas most sparse PCA methods are framed as convex optimization problems. In this paper, we try to understand CUR from a sparse optimization viewpoint. In particular, we show that CUR is implicitly optimizing a sparse regression objective and, furthermore, cannot be directly cast as a sparse PCA method. We observe that the sparsity attained by CUR possesses an interesting structure, which leads us to formulate a sparse PCA method that achieves a CUR-like sparsity.

In this paper, we try to understand CUR from a sparse optimization viewpoint. In particular, we show that CUR is implicitly optimizing a sparse regression objective and, furthermore, cannot be directly cast as a sparse PCA method. We observe that the sparsity attained by CUR possesses an interesting structure, which leads us to formulate a sparse PCA method that achieves a CUR-like sparsity.

paragraphs: CUR approximates a matrix using a representation that lies in the span of a small selection of its columns. This gives it a form of sparsity alongside low reconstruction error. The resemblance to sparse principal component analysis raises a natural question: are these methods solving essentially the same kind of optimization problem?

The paper investigates CUR through sparse optimization rather than only through its randomized algorithm. The authors show that CUR implicitly optimizes a sparse regression objective. They also show that it cannot be directly reformulated as a sparse PCA method. The distinction matters because similar-looking sparse representations do not by themselves imply equivalent underlying objectives.

The analysis then becomes a source of a new method. The authors identify a particular structure in the sparsity produced by CUR and formulate a sparse PCA approach that achieves a similar structure. Thus, the paper both clarifies the relationship between two matrix approximation approaches and transfers a useful representational property from CUR into a sparse PCA formulation.
summary.tldr: CUR implicitly solves a sparse regression problem, and its sparsity structure inspires a new sparse PCA formulation.

title: CUR from a Sparse Optimization Viewpoint

abstract: Linear chains and trees are basic building blocks in many applications of graphical models. Although exact inference in these models can be performed by dynamic programming, this computation can still be prohibitively expensive with non-trivial target variable domain sizes due to the quadratic dependence on this size. Standard message-passing algorithms for these problems are inefficient because they compute scores on hypotheses for which there is strong negative local evidence. For this reason there has been significant previous interest in beam search and its variants; however, these methods provide only approximate inference. This paper presents new efficient exact inference algorithms based on the combination of it column generation and pre-computed bounds on the model's cost structure. Improving worst-case performance is impossible. However, our method substantially speeds real-world, typical-case inference in chains and trees. Experiments show our method to be twice as fast as exact Viterbi for Wall Street Journal part-of-speech tagging and over thirteen times faster for a joint part-of-speed and named-entity-recognition task. Our algorithm is also extendable to new techniques for approximate inference, to faster two-best inference, and new opportunities for connections between inference and learning.

paragraphs: Finding the most likely configuration in a chain or tree can be done exactly with dynamic programming. However, the computation grows quadratically with variable domain size, making large sets of possible labels expensive. This paper identifies wasted effort in scoring hypotheses that already have strong negative local evidence, while noting that beam-search alternatives sacrifice exactness.

The authors introduce exact inference algorithms combining column generation with precomputed bounds on the model's cost structure. The approach uses that structure to reduce computation in typical cases. It does not improve the worst-case performance, which the abstract states cannot be improved, but it retains exact inference while targeting the inefficiencies encountered in practical problems.

The approach also extends to approximate inference and faster two-best inference. The central finding is that exactness can be preserved alongside substantial practical speedups, even when worst-case complexity remains unchanged.
summary.tldr: Column generation and cost bounds accelerate exact inference in chains and trees in practice without improving worst-case complexity.

title: MAP Inference in Chains using Column Generation

abstract: In this paper we investigate the use of Langevin Monte Carlo methods on the probability simplex and propose a new method, Stochastic gradient Riemannian Langevin dynamics, which is simple to implement and can be applied online. We apply this method to latent Dirichlet allocation in an online setting, and demonstrate that it achieves substantial performance improvements to the state of the art online variational Bayesian methods.
originalAbstract: In this paper we investigate the use of Langevin Monte Carlo methods on the probability simplex and propose a new method, Stochastic gradient Riemannian Langevin dynamics, which is simple to implement and can be applied online. We apply this method to latent Dirichlet allocation in an online setting, and demonstrate that it achieves substantial performance improvements to the state of the art online variational Bayesian methods.

paragraphs: The paper investigates Langevin Monte Carlo on the probability simplex, the space of nonnegative probability vectors whose entries sum to one. This setting matters for inference involving distributions over categories: the quantities being estimated must remain meaningful probabilities. The work focuses on developing a sampling method for that space.

The proposed method is stochastic gradient Riemannian Langevin dynamics. The authors describe it as simple to implement and suitable for online use. Online applicability is a central part of the contribution, connecting a method for probability-valued quantities with a setting in which inference proceeds as data becomes available.

The paper applies the method to latent Dirichlet allocation in an online setting. In that application, it demonstrates substantial performance improvements over the state-of-the-art online variational Bayesian methods considered. This supplies empirical support for the proposed sampling approach in topic modeling. The stated result concerns that online LDA comparison, while the methodological contribution is the development of Langevin dynamics for the probability simplex.
summary.tldr: An online Langevin sampling method for probability vectors substantially improves performance over the compared online variational methods in latent Dirichlet allocation.

title: Stochastic Gradient Riemannian Langevin Dynamics on the Probability Simplex

abstract: A central result in statistical theory is Pinsker's theorem, which characterizes the minimax rate in the normal means model of nonparametric estimation. In this paper, we present an extension to Pinsker's theorem where estimation is carried out under storage or communication constraints. In particular, we place limits on the number of bits used to encode an estimator, and analyze the excess risk in terms of this constraint, the signal size, and the noise level. We give sharp upper and lower bounds for the case of a Euclidean ball, which establishes the Pareto-optimal minimax tradeoff between storage and risk in this setting.

In this paper, we present an extension to Pinsker's theorem where estimation is carried out under storage or communication constraints. In particular, we place limits on the number of bits used to encode an estimator, and analyze the excess risk in terms of this constraint, the signal size, and the noise level. We give sharp upper and lower bounds for the case of a Euclidean ball, which establishes the Pareto-optimal minimax tradeoff between storage and risk in this setting.

paragraphs: Statistical estimation usually asks how accurately a signal can be recovered from noisy observations. This paper adds a resource constraint: the estimator must be encoded using a limited number of bits. The question becomes how estimation accuracy changes when the result must fit within a storage or communication budget.

The authors extend Pinsker's theorem, a minimax result for the normal means model, to this constrained setting. They analyze excess risk as a function of the bit budget, signal size, and noise level. These quantities jointly describe the statistical problem and the resources available to represent its answer.

For signals in a Euclidean ball, the paper establishes sharp upper and lower bounds. The upper bounds describe attainable performance, while the lower bounds establish limits that estimators cannot surpass in the minimax sense. Together, they characterize the Pareto-optimal tradeoff between storage and risk for this setting. The contribution makes the cost of representing an estimate part of the theoretical account of estimation accuracy.
summary.tldr: Sharp bounds characterize the optimal minimax tradeoff between encoding bits and estimation risk for Gaussian sequence models in Euclidean balls.

title: Quantized Estimation of Gaussian Sequence Models in Euclidean Balls

abstract: One crucial goal in kernel online learning is to bound the model size. Common approaches employ budget maintenance procedures to restrict the model sizes using removal, projection, or merging strategies. Although projection and merging, in the literature, are known to be the most effective strategies, they demand extensive computation whilst removal strategy fails to retain information of the removed vectors. An alternative way to address the model size problem is to apply random features to approximate the kernel function. This allows the model to be maintained directly in the random feature space, hence effectively resolve the curse of kernelization. However, this approach still suffers from a serious shortcoming as it needs to use a high dimensional random feature space to achieve a sufficiently accurate kernel approximation. Consequently, it leads to a significant increase in the computational cost. To address all of these aforementioned challenges, we present in this paper the Dual Space Gradient Descent (DualSGD), a novel framework that utilizes random features as an auxiliary space to maintain information from data points removed during budget maintenance. Consequently, our approach permits the budget to be maintained in a simple, direct and elegant way while simultaneously mitigating the impact of the dimensionality issue on learning performance. We further provide convergence analysis and extensively conduct experiments on five real-world datasets to demonstrate the predictive performance and scalability of our proposed method in comparison with the state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Kernel online learning must control model growth as data arrive. Budget maintenance can remove, project, or merge stored vectors, but these choices involve tradeoffs. Removal loses information, while projection and merging can be computationally expensive. Replacing the kernel entirely with random features controls size, but accurate approximation may require a costly, high-dimensional representation.

Dual Space Gradient Descent, or DualSGD, uses random features as an auxiliary space rather than relying on them for the whole model. When budget maintenance removes a data point, this extra space retains information from it. The method therefore connects a bounded kernel representation with a separate mechanism for preserving information that simple deletion would discard.

This arrangement is intended to simplify budget maintenance while reducing the learning impact of the random-feature dimensionality issue. The paper supplies convergence analysis and experiments on five real-world datasets comparing predictive performance and scalability with existing methods. Its contribution is a framework for balancing information retention, model size, and computation, supported by both mathematical analysis and empirical evaluation.
summary.tldr: DualSGD uses an auxiliary random-feature space to preserve information from removed kernel vectors while controlling online model size.

title: Dual Space Gradient Descent for Online Learning

abstract: We study k-SVD that is to obtain the first k singular vectors of a matrix A. Recently, a few breakthroughs have been discovered on k-SVD: Musco and Musco [1] proved the first gap-free convergence result using the block Krylov method, Shamir [2] discovered the first variance-reduction stochastic method, and Bhojanapalli et al. [3] provided the fastest $O(\mathsf{nnz}(A) + \mathsf{poly}(1/\varepsilon))$-time algorithm using alternating minimization. In this paper, we put forward a new and simple LazySVD framework to improve the above breakthroughs. This framework leads to a faster gap-free method outperforming [1], and the first accelerated and stochastic method outperforming [2]. In the $O(\mathsf{nnz}(A) + \mathsf{poly}(1/\varepsilon))$ running-time regime, LazySVD outperforms [3] in certain parameter regimes without even using alternating minimization.

[3] provided the fastest $O(\mathsf{nnz}(A) + \mathsf{poly}(1/\varepsilon))$-time algorithm using alternating minimization. In this paper, we put forward a new and simple LazySVD framework to improve the above breakthroughs. paragraphs: LazySVD addresses the task of computing the first k singular vectors of a matrix. The paper presents a simple framework aimed at improving several recent algorithmic advances for this problem. Its results concern different kinds of convergence and runtime guarantees, rather than a single speed comparison that applies uniformly.

One outcome is a faster method with gap-free convergence, improving on a prior block Krylov result. Another is an accelerated stochastic method that improves on an earlier variance-reduction approach. These are distinct contributions: one advances the gap-free guarantee, while the other brings acceleration to the stochastic setting considered in the paper.

The framework also operates in a runtime regime consisting of the number of nonzero matrix entries plus a polynomial term in inverse accuracy. Within that regime, it improves on a previous alternating-minimization method for certain parameter settings, without itself using alternating minimization. The qualification about parameter settings is essential. Overall, LazySVD offers a common, simpler framework that strengthens several algorithmic results under their respective conditions.
summary.tldr: LazySVD provides a simple framework that improves several leading-singular-vector algorithms, with some speed advantages restricted to particular parameter regimes.

title: LazySVD: Even Faster SVD Decomposition Yet Without Agonizing Pain

abstract: Artificial neural networks are most commonly trained with the back-propagation algorithm, where the gradient for learning is provided by back-propagating the error, layer by layer, from the output layer to the hidden layers. A recently discovered method called feedback-alignment shows that the weights used for propagating the error backward don't have to be symmetric with the weights used for propagation the activation forward. In fact, random feedback weights work evenly well, because the network learns how to make the feedback useful. In this work, the feedback alignment principle is used for training hidden layers more independently from the rest of the network, and from a zero initial condition. The error is propagated through fixed random feedback connections directly from the output layer to each hidden layer. This simple method is able to achieve zero training error even in convolutional networks and very deep networks, completely without error back-propagation. The method is a step towards biologically plausible machine learning because the error signal is almost local, and no symmetric or reciprocal weights are required. Experiments show that the test performance on MNIST and CIFAR is almost as good as those obtained with back-propagation for fully connected networks. If combined with dropout, the method achieves 1.45% error on the permutation invariant MNIST task.

In fact, random feedback weights work evenly well, because the network learns how to make the feedback useful. The error is propagated through fixed random feedback connections directly from the output layer to each hidden layer. This simple method is able to achieve zero training error even in convolutional networks and very deep networks, completely without error back-propagation. paragraphs: Backpropagation trains hidden layers by passing an output error backward through successive layers. Feedback alignment had shown that backward connections can use random weights instead of matching forward weights. This paper extends that principle by sending the output error directly to each hidden layer through fixed random connections.

These direct connections let hidden layers learn more independently of the rest of the network, including from a zero initial condition. The method can reach zero training error in convolutional and very deep networks without backpropagating error layer by layer. The authors also present it as a step toward biological plausibility because its error signal is almost local and it needs no symmetric or reciprocal weights.

These findings distinguish the ability to fit training data from the reported generalization results, while showing that direct random feedback can provide useful learning signals.
summary.tldr: Fixed random connections can send output error directly to hidden layers and train deep networks without layer-by-layer error backpropagation.

title: Direct Feedback Alignment Provides Learning in Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Deep learning methods achieve state-of-the-art performance in many application scenarios. Yet, these methods require a significant amount of hyperparameters tuning in order to achieve the best results. In particular, tuning the learning rates in the stochastic optimization process is still one of the main bottlenecks. In this paper, we propose a new stochastic gradient descent procedure for deep networks that does not require any learning rate setting. Contrary to previous methods, we do not adapt the learning rates nor we make use of the assumed curvature of the objective function. Instead, we reduce the optimization process to a game of betting on a coin and propose a learning rate free optimal algorithm for this scenario. Theoretical convergence is proven for convex and quasi-convex functions and empirical evidence shows the advantage of our algorithm over popular stochastic gradient algorithms.

paragraphs: Choosing learning rates is a major source of tuning effort when training deep networks. This paper proposes a stochastic gradient procedure that requires no learning-rate setting. The objective is to remove that particular tuning decision from optimization, addressing a practical bottleneck in obtaining good results from deep-learning methods.

The approach reformulates optimization as a coin-betting game and develops an optimal algorithm for that game without a learning rate. It does not achieve this by adapting learning rates or relying on assumed curvature of the objective. The betting formulation instead supplies the basis for the update procedure, changing how the optimizer is designed.

The authors prove convergence for convex and quasi-convex functions and provide empirical evidence of advantages over popular stochastic gradient algorithms. These two kinds of support have distinct scopes: the convergence theory applies to the specified function classes, while experiments support practical use in deep-network training. The contribution combines removal of a familiar tuning parameter with theoretical analysis and observed optimization benefits.
summary.tldr: A coin-betting formulation yields a learning-rate-free optimizer with convergence guarantees for convex and quasi-convex functions and favorable empirical results.

title: Training Deep Networks without Learning Rates Through Coin Betting

abstract: We study algorithms for online nonparametric regression that learn the directions along which the regression function is smoother. Our algorithm learns the Mahalanobis metric based on the gradient outer product matrix $\boldsymbol{G}$ of the regression function (automatically adapting to the effective rank of this matrix), while simultaneously bounding the regret ---on the same data sequence--- in terms of the spectrum of $\boldsymbol{G}$. As a preliminary step in our analysis, we extend a nonparametric online learning algorithm by Hazan and Megiddo enabling it to compete against functions whose Lipschitzness is measured with respect to an arbitrary Mahalanobis metric.
originalAbstract: We study algorithms for online nonparametric regression that learn the directions along which the regression function is smoother. Our algorithm learns the Mahalanobis metric based on the gradient outer product matrix $\boldsymbol{G}$ of the regression function (automatically adapting to the effective rank of this matrix), while simultaneously bounding the regret ---on the same data sequence--- in terms of the spectrum of $\boldsymbol{G}$. As a preliminary step in our analysis, we extend a nonparametric online learning algorithm by Hazan and Megiddo enabling it to compete against functions whose Lipschitzness is measured with respect to an arbitrary Mahalanobis metric.

paragraphs: In online nonparametric regression, a learner makes predictions as a sequence of observations arrives. This paper studies how the learner can discover directions in which the regression function changes more smoothly. Rather than treating the geometry of the inputs as fixed, the method learns a distance measure while carrying out prediction.

The learned Mahalanobis metric is based on the regression function’s gradient outer product matrix, G. This matrix captures directional information about variation in the function. The algorithm automatically adapts to its effective rank, and the authors bound regret on the same data sequence in terms of G’s spectrum. Thus the prediction guarantee reflects the directional structure the method is learning.

A preliminary result extends an existing online nonparametric algorithm to compare against functions whose Lipschitz smoothness is measured using any Mahalanobis metric. That extension provides a basis for moving from a supplied geometry to a learned one. The main contribution joins metric adaptation and regret control within one online process, rather than treating learning the geometry as a separate prerequisite.
summary.tldr: An online regression algorithm learns directional smoothness while bounding regret through the spectrum of the regression function’s gradient structure.

title: Nonparametric Online Regression while Learning the Metric

abstract: We study the conditions under which one is able to efficiently apply variance-reduction and acceleration schemes on finite sums problems. First, we show that perhaps surprisingly, the finite sum structure, by itself, is not sufficient for obtaining a complexity bound of $\tilde{\cO}((n+L/\mu)\ln(1/\epsilon))$ for $L$-smooth and $\mu$-strongly convex finite sums - one must also know exactly which individual function is being referred to by the oracle at each iteration. Next, we show that for a broad class of first-order and coordinate-descent finite sums algorithms (including, e.g., SDCA, SVRG, SAG), it is not possible to get an `accelerated' complexity bound of $\tilde{\cO}((n+\sqrt{n L/\mu})\ln(1/\epsilon))$, unless the strong convexity parameter is given explicitly. Lastly, we show that when this class of algorithms is used for minimizing $L$-smooth and non-strongly convex finite sums, the optimal complexity bound is $\tilde{\cO}(n+L/\epsilon)$, assuming that (on average) the same update rule is used for any iteration, and $\tilde{\cO}(n+\sqrt{nL/\epsilon})$, otherwise.

paragraphs: This paper asks what information optimization algorithms need to obtain fast rates when an objective is a finite sum of functions. Its first result shows that finite-sum structure alone does not deliver the stated variance-reduction complexity for smooth, strongly convex problems. The algorithm must also know which individual function the oracle refers to at each iteration.

A second result concerns a broad class of first-order and coordinate-descent methods, including SDCA, SVRG, and SAG. Within this class, achieving the stated accelerated complexity requires explicit knowledge of the strong-convexity parameter. The restriction is therefore about both the algorithm family and the information supplied to it, rather than a universal impossibility of acceleration.

For smooth objectives without strong convexity, the optimal complexity also depends on whether the same update rule is used on average at every iteration. Up to suppressed logarithmic factors, the bounds are n + L/epsilon with that restriction and n + sqrt(nL/epsilon) otherwise. Here n is the number of terms, L describes smoothness, and epsilon is the target accuracy.
summary.tldr: Fast finite-sum optimization rates depend on component identities, parameter knowledge, and the permitted update rules.

title: Limitations on Variance-Reduction and Acceleration Schemes for Finite Sums Optimization

abstract: Latent models have become the default choice for recommender systems due to their performance and scalability. However, research in this area has primarily focused on modeling user-item interactions, and few latent models have been developed for cold start. Deep learning has recently achieved remarkable success showing excellent results for diverse input types. Inspired by these results we propose a neural network based latent model called DropoutNet to address the cold start problem in recommender systems. Unlike existing approaches that incorporate additional content-based objective terms, we instead focus on the optimization and show that neural network models can be explicitly trained for cold start through dropout. Our model can be applied on top of any existing latent model effectively providing cold start capabilities, and full power of deep architectures. Empirically we demonstrate state-of-the-art accuracy on publicly available benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/layer6ai-labs/DropoutNet.

paragraphs: Latent recommendation models are attractive for their accuracy and scalability, but much of their development has concentrated on user–item interactions. Cold start creates a different challenge: recommendations must remain useful when the interaction information normally supporting them is unavailable. DropoutNet introduces a neural latent model explicitly trained to handle that situation.

The main change concerns optimization. The authors use dropout to train neural networks for cold start, rather than adding separate content-based terms to the objective. This makes preparation for missing interaction information part of the training process. The proposed model can be placed on top of an existing latent model, extending it with cold-start capabilities and a deep architecture.

On publicly available benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art accuracy. The finding supports a training-centered approach to cold start and gives existing latent recommenders a route to handling it. The broader contribution is the observation that dropout can serve a task-specific purpose here: training the recommendation model to cope with the information conditions it will encounter during cold start.
summary.tldr: DropoutNet uses dropout to explicitly train latent recommenders for cold start and reports state-of-the-art benchmark accuracy.

title: DropoutNet: Addressing Cold Start in Recommender Systems

abstract: Random forests are learning algorithms that build large collections of random trees and make predictions by averaging the individual tree predictions. In this paper, we consider various tree constructions and examine how the choice of parameters affects the generalization error of the resulting random forests as the sample size goes to infinity. We show that subsampling of data points during the tree construction phase is important: Forests can become inconsistent with either no subsampling or too severe subsampling. As a consequence, even highly randomized trees can lead to inconsistent forests if no subsampling is used, which implies that some of the commonly used setups for random forests can be inconsistent. As a second consequence we can show that trees that have good performance in nearest-neighbor search can be a poor choice for random forests.

paragraphs: Random forests average predictions from many randomized trees. This paper examines how tree construction and parameter choices affect generalization as the amount of training data grows without bound. The focus is consistency: whether a forest's prediction behavior approaches the appropriate large-sample target, rather than merely whether it performs well on a particular finite dataset.

The analysis identifies subsampling during tree construction as important. Forests can be inconsistent when they use no subsampling, but they can also be inconsistent when subsampling is too severe. Even heavily randomized trees can produce inconsistent forests without subsampling. Thus, adding randomness to the trees does not by itself prevent the failure modes established by the analysis.

The results imply that some commonly used random-forest configurations can be inconsistent. They also show that tree constructions effective for nearest-neighbor search can be poor choices for random-forest prediction. These findings make the construction details consequential: a tree's usefulness for another task, or its high degree of randomization, does not establish the long-run predictive properties of the resulting forest.
summary.tldr: Random forests can be inconsistent with either absent or overly severe subsampling, even when their trees are highly randomized.

title: When do random forests fail?

abstract: Approximate inference in probabilistic graphical models (PGMs) can be grouped into deterministic methods and Monte-Carlo-based methods. The former can often provide accurate and rapid inferences, but are typically associated with biases that are hard to quantify. The latter enjoy asymptotic consistency, but can suffer from high computational costs. In this paper we present a way of bridging the gap between deterministic and stochastic inference. Specifically, we suggest an efficient sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithm for PGMs which can leverage the output from deterministic inference methods. While generally applicable, we show explicitly how this can be done with loopy belief propagation, expectation propagation, and Laplace approximations. The resulting algorithm can be viewed as a post-correction of the biases associated with these methods and, indeed, numerical results show clear improvements over the baseline deterministic methods as well as over "plain" SMC.

paragraphs: Approximate inference in graphical models often involves a tradeoff between fast deterministic calculations and computationally demanding sampling. Deterministic methods can be accurate but introduce biases that are difficult to measure. Monte Carlo methods offer asymptotic consistency, although obtaining useful results can require substantial computation.

This paper combines the two approaches through a sequential Monte Carlo algorithm that uses the output of deterministic inference. The authors explicitly develop this connection for loopy belief propagation, expectation propagation, and Laplace approximations. A deterministic approximation therefore becomes useful input to a stochastic inference procedure rather than only a final answer.

The resulting method can be understood as correcting bias left by the deterministic calculation. Numerical results show clear improvements over both the deterministic baselines and ordinary sequential Monte Carlo. These comparisons support the value of combining their strengths: an initial approximation can inform the sampling procedure, while the stochastic stage provides a way to refine inference beyond that approximation. The reported improvements are empirical results for the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A sequential Monte Carlo method uses deterministic approximations to improve graphical-model inference and correct their biases.

title: Graphical model inference: Sequential Monte Carlo meets deterministic approximations

abstract: Consider the situation where you are given an existing $k$-way clustering $\pi$. A challenge for explainable AI is to find a compact and distinct explanations of each cluster which in this paper is using instance-level descriptors/tags from a common dictionary. Since the descriptors/tags were not given to the clustering method, this is not a semi-supervised learning situation. We show that the \emph{feasibility} problem of just testing whether any distinct description (not the most compact) exists is generally intractable for just two clusters. This means that unless \textbf{P} = \cnp, there cannot exist an efficient algorithm for the cluster description problem. Hence, we explore ILP formulations for smaller problems and a relaxed but restricted setting that leads to a polynomial time algorithm for larger problems. We explore several extension to the basic setting such as the ability to ignore some instances and composition constraints on the descriptions of the clusters. We show our formulation's usefulness on Twitter data where the communities were found using social connectivity (i.e. \texttt{follower} relation) but the explanation of the communities is based on behavioral properties of the nodes (i.e. hashtag usage) not available to the clustering method.
