paragraphs: This paper asks how to explain clusters that have already been formed. Each instance has descriptive tags from a shared dictionary, and the goal is to give each cluster a compact, distinct description. The tags were unavailable to the clustering method, so the explanations provide a separate view of the groups rather than influencing how they were created.

The authors show that even deciding whether distinct descriptions exist is generally intractable for two clusters. Finding the most compact descriptions therefore faces a fundamental computational obstacle unless P equals NP. They respond with integer linear programming formulations for smaller problems and a relaxed, restricted setting that permits a polynomial-time algorithm for larger ones.

The framework also allows some instances to be ignored and supports constraints on description composition. A Twitter application demonstrates its usefulness: communities are formed from follower relationships, then explained using hashtag behavior. This example shows how the method can connect a grouping based on social structure to descriptions based on a different source of information.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes the computational difficulty of distinct cluster descriptions and develops exact formulations and a tractable restricted relaxation.

title: The Cluster Description Problem - Complexity Results, Formulations and Approximations

abstract: Meta-learning for few-shot learning entails acquiring a prior over previous tasks and experiences, such that new tasks be learned from small amounts of data. However, a critical challenge in few-shot learning is task ambiguity: even when a powerful prior can be meta-learned from a large number of prior tasks, a small dataset for a new task can simply be too ambiguous to acquire a single model (e.g., a classifier) for that task that is accurate. In this paper, we propose a probabilistic meta-learning algorithm that can sample models for a new task from a model distribution. Our approach extends model-agnostic meta-learning, which adapts to new tasks via gradient descent, to incorporate a parameter distribution that is trained via a variational lower bound. At meta-test time, our algorithm adapts via a simple procedure that injects noise into gradient descent, and at meta-training time, the model is trained such that this stochastic adaptation procedure produces samples from the approximate model posterior. Our experimental results show that our method can sample plausible classifiers and regressors in ambiguous few-shot learning problems. We also show how reasoning about ambiguity can also be used for downstream active learning problems.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning uses experience from previous tasks to learn a new task from little data. Even a strong learned prior cannot always remove ambiguity: several models may plausibly explain the small dataset. The paper addresses this by learning to produce a distribution of task models rather than committing to one model.

The method extends model-agnostic meta-learning, which adapts through gradient descent, with a parameter distribution trained using a variational lower bound. At test time, adaptation injects noise into gradient descent. Meta-training shapes this stochastic adaptation procedure so that it generates samples from an approximate posterior over models for the new task.

Experiments show that the method can generate plausible classifiers and regressors for ambiguous few-shot problems. The paper also demonstrates how reasoning about this ambiguity can support downstream active learning. Its contribution is to make uncertainty over the task model part of adaptation itself: the outputs represent multiple plausible interpretations of scarce evidence, and that uncertainty can inform subsequent learning decisions.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic meta-learning uses noisy gradient adaptation to sample plausible task models when a few examples leave the task ambiguous.

title: Probabilistic Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning

abstract: Continuous-time Bayesian networks (CTBNs) constitute a general and powerful framework for modeling continuous-time stochastic processes on networks. This makes them particularly attractive for learning the directed structures among interacting entities. However, if the available data is incomplete, one needs to simulate the prohibitively complex CTBN dynamics. Existing approximation techniques, such as sampling and low-order variational methods, either scale unfavorably in system size, or are unsatisfactory in terms of accuracy. Inspired by recent advances in statistical physics, we present a new approximation scheme based on cluster-variational methods that significantly improves upon existing variational approximations. We can analytically marginalize the parameters of the approximate CTBN, as these are of secondary importance for structure learning. This recovers a scalable scheme for direct structure learning from incomplete and noisy time-series data. Our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of scalability.

paragraphs: Continuous-time Bayesian networks describe interacting entities whose states evolve over time. Learning their directed connections can reveal the structure of those interactions. Incomplete observations make this difficult because learning must account for unobserved dynamics, and simulating the full network process can become prohibitively complex as the system grows.

The paper introduces an approximation based on cluster-variational methods, drawing inspiration from statistical physics. Its purpose is to improve the treatment of the network dynamics beyond existing variational approximations while retaining scalability. This addresses a trade-off identified in the abstract: available sampling and low-order variational approaches can be expensive for large systems or insufficiently accurate.

The authors also analytically integrate out parameters of the approximate network, since the primary target is the connection structure rather than those parameters themselves. Together, these steps produce a method for learning structure directly from incomplete, noisy time series. The paper reports improved variational approximation and better scalability than existing methods, making the contribution relevant to network discovery when fully observed trajectories are unavailable.
summary.tldr: Cluster-variational approximations enable scalable learning of continuous-time network structure from incomplete and noisy observations.

title: Cluster Variational Approximations for Structure Learning of Continuous-Time Bayesian Networks from Incomplete Data

abstract: We aim to better understand attention over nodes in graph neural networks (GNNs) and identify factors influencing its effectiveness. We particularly focus on the ability of attention GNNs to generalize to larger, more complex or noisy graphs. Motivated by insights from the work on Graph Isomorphism Networks, we design simple graph reasoning tasks that allow us to study attention in a controlled environment. We find that under typical conditions the effect of attention is negligible or even harmful, but under certain conditions it provides an exceptional gain in performance of more than 60% in some of our classification tasks. Satisfying these conditions in practice is challenging and often requires optimal initialization or supervised training of attention. We propose an alternative recipe and train attention in a weakly-supervised fashion that approaches the performance of supervised models, and, compared to unsupervised models, improves results on several synthetic as well as real datasets. Source code and datasets are available at https://github.com/bknyaz/graph attention pool.

paragraphs: Attention over graph nodes is intended to help a graph neural network focus on useful information. This paper asks when that mechanism actually improves performance, especially when models encounter larger, more complex, or noisier graphs. The authors create simple graph-reasoning tasks to study these effects under controlled conditions.

The results show that attention is often negligible or even harmful under typical conditions. Under certain conditions, however, it produces gains exceeding 60% on some classification tasks. Achieving those favorable conditions in practice is challenging and often requires optimal initialization or direct supervision of the attention mechanism. The benefit therefore depends strongly on how attention is learned.

The authors propose weakly supervised attention training as an alternative. It approaches the performance of supervised models and improves on unsupervised models across several synthetic and real datasets. The study provides both a diagnostic account of attention's uneven effectiveness and a training approach that helps realize its benefits without relying on the fully supervised setup.
summary.tldr: Controlled graph tasks reveal conditional benefits from attention, and weak supervision helps approach the performance of supervised attention.

title: Understanding Attention and Generalization in Graph Neural Networks

abstract: We consider the problem of computing the maximum likelihood multivariate log-concave distribution for a set of points. Specifically, we present an algorithm which, given $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and an accuracy parameter $\eps>0$, runs in time $\poly(n,d,1/\eps),$ and returns a log-concave distribution which, with high probability, has the property that the likelihood of the $n$ points under the returned distribution is at most an additive $\eps$ less than the maximum likelihood that could be achieved via any log-concave distribution. This is the first computationally efficient (polynomial time) algorithm for this fundamental and practically important task. Our algorithm rests on a novel connection with exponential families: the maximum likelihood log-concave distribution belongs to a class of structured distributions which, while not an exponential family, ``locally'' possesses key properties of exponential families. This connection then allows the problem of computing the log-concave maximum likelihood distribution to be formulated as a convex optimization problem, and solved via an approximate first-order method. Efficiently approximating the (sub) gradients of the objective function of this optimization problem is quite delicate, and is the main technical challenge in this work.

paragraphs: This paper tackles the computation of a log-concave probability distribution that best fits a collection of multidimensional observations under maximum likelihood. The goal is to optimize over the whole class of log-concave distributions. The authors present what they describe as the first polynomial-time algorithm for this task.

The central insight connects the optimal distribution to a structured class with local properties resembling those of exponential families. Although this class is not itself an exponential family, those local properties are enough to formulate the estimation problem as convex optimization. An approximate first-order method then solves that formulation. Efficiently approximating the gradients or subgradients is the main technical obstacle.

For n observations in d dimensions and positive accuracy tolerance epsilon, the runtime is polynomial in n, d, and inverse epsilon. With high probability, the returned distribution has likelihood within additive epsilon of the best achievable log-concave likelihood. This is an approximate, probabilistic guarantee that establishes computational efficiency while explicitly accounting for the requested accuracy.
summary.tldr: A connection to local exponential-family structure enables polynomial-time approximate maximum likelihood estimation of multivariate log-concave distributions.

title: A Polynomial Time Algorithm for Log-Concave Maximum Likelihood via Locally Exponential Families

abstract: We introduce a temperature into the exponential function and replace the softmax output layer of the neural networks by a high-temperature generalization. Similarly, the logarithm in the loss we use for training is replaced by a low-temperature logarithm. By tuning the two temperatures, we create loss functions that are non-convex already in the single layer case. When replacing the last layer of the neural networks by our bi-temperature generalization of the logistic loss, the training becomes more robust to noise. We visualize the effect of tuning the two temperatures in a simple setting and show the efficacy of our method on large datasets. Our methodology is based on Bregman divergences and is superior to a related two-temperature method that uses the Tsallis divergence.
originalAbstract: We introduce a temperature into the exponential function and replace the softmax output layer of the neural networks by a high-temperature generalization. Similarly, the logarithm in the loss we use for training is replaced by a low-temperature logarithm. By tuning the two temperatures, we create loss functions that are non-convex already in the single layer case. When replacing the last layer of the neural networks by our bi-temperature generalization of the logistic loss, the training becomes more robust to noise. We visualize the effect of tuning the two temperatures in a simple setting and show the efficacy of our method on large datasets. Our methodology is based on Bregman divergences and is superior to a related two-temperature method that uses the Tsallis divergence.

paragraphs: This paper changes the output transformation and training loss of a neural network to improve robustness to noise. The method introduces two temperature parameters into the mathematical functions used by logistic loss. One modifies the exponential function underlying the output layer, while the other modifies the logarithm used to evaluate the training loss.

The output layer uses a high-temperature generalization of softmax, and the loss uses a low-temperature logarithm. Tuning both parameters produces a family of losses that can be nonconvex even for a single-layer model. The construction is based on Bregman divergences, giving the two modifications a shared mathematical foundation.

The authors visualize how the temperatures affect behavior in a simple setting and demonstrate efficacy on large datasets. They report more noise-robust training when using the proposed final-layer and loss formulation, as well as superiority to a related two-temperature approach based on Tsallis divergence. The contribution provides two adjustable components for shaping the training objective and improving its empirical response to noise.
summary.tldr: A Bregman-based loss with separate output and loss temperatures makes neural-network training more robust to noise.

title: Robust Bi-Tempered Logistic Loss Based on Bregman Divergences

abstract: The data deluge comes with high demands for data labeling. Crowdsourcing (or, more generally, ensemble learning) techniques aim to produce accurate labels via integrating noisy, non-expert labeling from annotators. The classic Dawid-Skene estimator and its accompanying expectation maximization (EM) algorithm have been widely used, but the theoretical properties are not fully understood. Tensor methods were proposed to guarantee identification of the Dawid-Skene model, but the sample complexity is a hurdle for applying such approaches---since the tensor methods hinge on the availability of third-order statistics that are hard to reliably estimate given limited data. In this paper, we propose a framework using pairwise co-occurrences of the annotator responses, which naturally admits lower sample complexity. We show that the approach can identify the Dawid-Skene model under realistic conditions. We propose an algebraic algorithm reminiscent of convex geometry-based structured matrix factorization to solve the model identification problem efficiently, and an identifiability-enhanced algorithm for handling more challenging and critical scenarios. Experiments show that the proposed algorithms outperform the state-of-art algorithms under a variety of scenarios.

This paper instead builds a framework around pairwise co-occurrences: how responses from pairs of annotators appear together. The authors show that these simpler statistics can identify the Dawid-Skene model under realistic conditions. The approach naturally has lower sample complexity, addressing the data demands that make third-order statistics a practical obstacle.

The paper also develops an efficient algebraic identification algorithm related to structured matrix factorization and convex geometry. A second algorithm strengthens identifiability for more challenging scenarios. Experiments show improvements over existing methods across a variety of settings. The central finding is that pairwise information can support model identification under the stated conditions, enabling algorithms that demand less statistical information from the available annotations.
summary.tldr: Pairwise annotator response statistics can identify the Dawid-Skene crowdsourcing model under realistic conditions with lower sample demands.

title: Crowdsourcing via Pairwise Co-occurrences: Identifiability and Algorithms

abstract: Despite the exploding interest in graph neural networks there has been little effort to verify and improve their robustness. This is even more alarming given recent findings showing that they are extremely vulnerable to adversarial attacks on both the graph structure and the node attributes. We propose the first method for verifying certifiable (non-)robustness to graph perturbations for a general class of models that includes graph neural networks and label/feature propagation. By exploiting connections to PageRank and Markov decision processes our certificates can be efficiently (and under many threat models exactly) computed. Furthermore, we investigate robust training procedures that increase the number of certifiably robust nodes while maintaining or improving the clean predictive accuracy.

paragraphs: Graph-based prediction can be vulnerable to adversarial changes in connections or node information. This paper addresses the verification problem: determining whether a prediction is robust to graph perturbations within a specified threat model. Its scope includes a general class of models containing graph neural networks and methods that propagate labels or features.

The authors propose a method for certifying both robustness and non-robustness. Their approach exploits mathematical connections to PageRank and Markov decision processes to make certificate computation efficient. Under many threat models, the certificates can be computed exactly. That qualification matters because the exactness claim depends on the permitted perturbations, rather than applying without distinction to every possible attack setting.

The paper also investigates training procedures designed to improve certified robustness. These procedures increase the number of nodes that can be certified robust while preserving or improving predictive accuracy on clean data. Together, the results connect verification with training: certificates establish which predictions have protection under the threat model, while robust training expands that protected set.
summary.tldr: The paper develops efficient robustness certificates for graph-based models and training procedures that increase certified robustness while maintaining or improving clean accuracy.

title: Certifiable Robustness to Graph Perturbations

abstract: Stagewise training strategy is widely used for learning neural networks, which runs a stochastic algorithm (e.g., SGD) starting with a relatively large step size (aka learning rate) and geometrically decreasing the step size after a number of iterations. It has been observed that the stagewise SGD has much faster convergence than the vanilla SGD with a polynomially decaying step size in terms of both training error and testing error. {\it But how to explain this phenomenon has been largely ignored by existing studies.} This paper provides some theoretical evidence for explaining this faster convergence. In particular, we consider a stagewise training strategy for minimizing empirical risk that satisfies the Polyak-\L ojasiewicz (PL) condition, which has been observed/proved for neural networks and also holds for a broad family of convex functions. For convex loss functions and two classes of ``nice-behaviored" non-convex objectives that are close to a convex function, we establish faster convergence of stagewise training than the vanilla SGD under the PL condition on both training error and testing error. Experiments on stagewise learning of deep residual networks exhibits that it satisfies one type of non-convexity assumption and therefore can be explained by our theory.

It has been observed to improve training and testing error faster than standard SGD with a polynomially decreasing learning rate. This paper develops theoretical evidence explaining that advantage under specified conditions on the optimization objective.

The analysis assumes that empirical risk satisfies the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition. The explanation is conditional on the PL condition and the covered objective classes. Within that scope, the paper gives a mathematical basis for the observed benefits of reducing learning rates in stages.
summary.tldr: Under the PL condition and specified objective assumptions, stagewise training achieves faster training- and testing-error convergence than SGD with polynomial learning-rate decay.

title: Stagewise Training Accelerates Convergence of Testing Error Over SGD

abstract: One of the most important steps toward interpretability and explainability of neural network models is feature selection, which aims to identify the subset of relevant features. Theoretical results in the field have mostly focused on the prediction aspect of the problem with virtually no work on feature selection consistency for deep neural networks due to the model's severe nonlinearity and unidentifiability. This lack of theoretical foundation casts doubt on the applicability of deep learning to contexts where correct interpretations of the features play a central role. In this work, we investigate the problem of feature selection for analytic deep networks. We prove that for a wide class of networks, including deep feed-forward neural networks, convolutional neural networks and a major sub-class of residual neural networks, the Adaptive Group Lasso selection procedure with Group Lasso as the base estimator is selection-consistent. The work provides further evidence that Group Lasso might be inefficient for feature selection with neural networks and advocates the use of Adaptive Group Lasso over the popular Group Lasso.

paragraphs: Identifying which input features matter is a different challenge from predicting accurately. Deep networks complicate this distinction because their nonlinear structure and unidentifiability make theoretical analysis difficult. This paper studies feature selection for analytic deep neural networks, seeking a foundation for interpreting which inputs are relevant to a learned relationship.

The authors analyze Adaptive Group Lasso with Group Lasso used as its base estimator. They prove selection consistency for a broad class of networks. This is a statistical guarantee about recovering the relevant feature subset as the available data grow. The covered architectures include deep feed-forward networks, convolutional networks, and a major subclass of residual networks.

The result gives feature selection its own theoretical support rather than relying on predictive success as evidence of correct interpretation. The work also provides further evidence that ordinary Group Lasso might be inefficient for neural-network feature selection and favors its adaptive version. The guarantee concerns the analytic network classes studied, while the criticism of ordinary Group Lasso remains qualified.
summary.tldr: The paper proves feature-selection consistency for Adaptive Group Lasso across a broad class of analytic deep networks.

title: Consistent feature selection for analytic deep neural networks

abstract: Sampling from a log-concave distribution function is one core problem that has wide applications in Bayesian statistics and machine learning. While most gradient free methods have slow convergence rate, the Langevin Monte Carlo (LMC) that provides fast convergence requires the computation of gradients. In practice one uses finite-differencing approximations as surrogates, and the method is expensive in high-dimensions. A natural strategy to reduce computational cost in each iteration is to utilize random gradient approximations, such as random coordinate descent (RCD) or simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation (SPSA).We show by a counterexamplethat blindly applying RCD does not achieve the goal in the most general setting. The high variance induced by the randomness means a larger number of iterations are needed, and this balances out the saving in each iteration. We then introduce a new variance reduction approach, termed Randomized Coordinates Averaging Descent (RCAD), and incorporate it with both overdamped and underdamped LMC. The methods are termed RCAD-O-LMC and RCAD-U-LMC respectively. The methods still sit in the random gradient approximation framework, and thus the computational cost in each iteration is low. However, by employing RCAD, the variance is reduced, so the methods converge within the same number of iterations as the classical overdamped and underdamped LMC. This leads to a computational saving overall.

paragraphs: Langevin Monte Carlo can sample efficiently from log-concave distributions, but computing gradients can be costly when finite differences are used in many dimensions. Random gradient approximations offer cheaper individual iterations. This paper examines whether those local savings actually translate into a lower total computational cost.

A counterexample shows that straightforward random coordinate descent does not achieve that goal in the most general setting. The added randomness raises variance, requiring enough extra iterations to offset the cheaper updates. This identifies a specific obstacle: lowering the amount of work per iteration is insufficient if the approximation also slows convergence.

The authors introduce Randomized Coordinates Averaging Descent, or RCAD, and combine it with both overdamped and underdamped Langevin Monte Carlo. The resulting methods retain inexpensive random-gradient updates while reducing their variance. They converge within the same number of iterations as the corresponding classical Langevin methods, producing an overall computational saving. The contribution is therefore a way to preserve the benefit of cheaper updates by controlling the variance that would otherwise cancel it.
summary.tldr: RCAD reduces random-gradient variance so Langevin sampling can use cheaper iterations without requiring more iterations than its classical counterparts.

title: Variance reduction for Random Coordinate Descent-Langevin Monte Carlo

abstract: We study the problem of learning differentiable functions expressed as programs in a domain-specific language. Such programmatic models can offer benefits such as composability and interpretability; however, learning them requires optimizing over a combinatorial space of program "architectures". We frame this optimization problem as a search in a weighted graph whose paths encode top-down derivations of program syntax. Our key innovation is to view various classes of neural networks as continuous relaxations over the space of programs, which can then be used to complete any partial program. All the parameters of this relaxed program can be trained end-to-end, and the resulting training loss is an approximately admissible heuristic that can guide the combinatorial search. We instantiate our approach on top of the A* and Iterative Deepening Depth-First Search algorithms and use these algorithms to learn programmatic classifiers in three sequence classification tasks. Our experiments show that the algorithms outperform state-of-the-art methods for program learning, and that they discover programmatic classifiers that yield natural interpretations and achieve competitive accuracy.

paragraphs: Models expressed as programs can offer interpretable structure and reusable components, but finding a good program requires searching many possible architectures. This paper represents that search as movement through a weighted graph. Each path builds program syntax from the top down, turning program learning into a structured search over possible derivations.

The key idea is to fill unfinished parts of a candidate program with neural networks. These networks act as continuous relaxations of the remaining program choices, allowing the completed relaxed model to be trained end to end. Its training loss supplies an approximately admissible heuristic for guiding the search toward promising program structures.

The authors incorporate this heuristic into A* and Iterative Deepening Depth-First Search and evaluate the resulting methods on three sequence-classification tasks. They report better performance than leading program-learning methods, along with classifiers that offer natural interpretations and competitive accuracy. The approach uses neural optimization to inform discrete program construction, while retaining programmatic models as the final objects being learned.
summary.tldr: Neural completions of partial programs provide approximately admissible heuristics that guide search toward accurate, interpretable programmatic classifiers.

title: Learning Differentiable Programs with Admissible Neural Heuristics

abstract: We consider an underdetermined noisy linear regression model where the minimum-norm interpolating predictor is known to be consistent, and ask: can uniform convergence in a norm ball, or at least (following Nagarajan and Kolter) the subset of a norm ball that the algorithm selects on a typical input set, explain this success? We show that uniformly bounding the difference between empirical and population errors cannot show any learning in the norm ball, and cannot show consistency for any set, even one depending on the exact algorithm and distribution. But we argue we can explain the consistency of the minimal-norm interpolator with a slightly weaker, yet standard, notion: uniform convergence of zero-error predictors in a norm ball. We use this to bound the generalization error of low- (but not minimal-)norm interpolating predictors.

paragraphs: The paper examines a noisy linear regression setting with more freedom in the predictor than the observations can determine. In this setting, the minimum-norm predictor that fits the training data exactly is known to be consistent. The question is whether uniform convergence arguments over norm-bounded predictors can explain that successful generalization.

The authors show that uniformly controlling the difference between training error and population error cannot establish learning across the norm ball. Restricting attention to a set chosen using the algorithm and distribution still cannot establish consistency through this kind of bound. These negative results identify a mismatch between a particular proof strategy and the behavior of the interpolating predictor.

They then argue that a weaker, standard form of uniform convergence can explain consistency when applied specifically to zero-training-error predictors within the norm ball. This perspective also yields generalization bounds for interpolators with low, but not necessarily minimal, norm. The contribution thus narrows the relevant predictor class while retaining a uniform-convergence-based explanation of learning.
summary.tldr: A weaker uniform convergence notion focused on zero-error predictors can explain low-norm interpolation where uniform error-gap bounds fail.

title: On Uniform Convergence and Low-Norm Interpolation Learning

abstract: Offline methods for reinforcement learning have a potential to help bridge the gap between reinforcement learning research and real-world applications. They make it possible to learn policies from offline datasets, thus overcoming concerns associated with online data collection in the real-world, including cost, safety, or ethical concerns. In this paper, we propose a benchmark called RL Unplugged to evaluate and compare offline RL methods. RL Unplugged includes data from a diverse range of domains including games e.g., Atari benchmark) and simulated motor control problems (e.g., DM Control Suite). The datasets include domains that are partially or fully observable, use continuous or discrete actions, and have stochastic vs. deterministic dynamics. We propose detailed evaluation protocols for each domain in RL Unplugged and provide an extensive analysis of supervised learning and offline RL methods using these protocols. We will release data for all our tasks and open-source all algorithms presented in this paper. We hope that our suite of benchmarks will increase the reproducibility of experiments and make it possible to study challenging tasks with a limited computational budget, thus making RL research both more systematic and more accessible across the community. Moving forward, we view RL Unplugged as a living benchmark suite that will evolve and grow with datasets contributed by the research community and ourselves. Our project page is available on github.

RL Unplugged provides a benchmark suite for evaluating and comparing methods that learn under this offline setting.

The authors provide domain-specific evaluation protocols and analyze supervised learning and offline reinforcement learning methods using them. They also state plans to release the datasets and implementations. The intended benefits are more reproducible comparisons and access to challenging research tasks with limited computation. The paper presents the suite as an evolving resource that can grow through contributions from the authors and the research community.
summary.tldr: RL Unplugged supplies diverse datasets and evaluation protocols to make offline reinforcement learning comparisons more systematic and reproducible.

title: RL Unplugged: A Suite of Benchmarks for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: To guide behavior, the brain extracts relevant features from high-dimensional data streamed by sensory organs. Neuroscience experiments demonstrate that the processing of sensory inputs by cortical neurons is modulated by instructive signals which provide context and task-relevant information. Here, adopting a normative approach, we model these instructive signals as supervisory inputs guiding the projection of the feedforward data. Mathematically, we start with a family of Reduced-Rank Regression (RRR) objective functions which include Reduced Rank (minimum) Mean Square Error (RRMSE) and Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA), and derive novel offline and online optimization algorithms, which we call Bio-RRR. The online algorithms can be implemented by neural networks whose synaptic learning rules resemble calcium plateau potential dependent plasticity observed in the cortex. We detail how, in our model, the calcium plateau potential can be interpreted as a backpropagating error signal. We demonstrate that, despite relying exclusively on biologically plausible local learning rules, our algorithms perform competitively with existing implementations of RRMSE and CCA.

paragraphs: The paper asks how cortical networks might learn which features of incoming sensory information matter for a task. It treats contextual or instructive signals as supervision that guides the compression of sensory inputs. Its normative approach starts with a mathematical learning objective and derives network behavior from that objective.

The authors use a family of reduced-rank regression objectives that includes reduced-rank minimum mean square error and canonical correlation analysis. These objectives provide different ways to learn a lower-dimensional relationship between inputs and supervisory information. From them, the authors derive offline and online optimization algorithms collectively called Bio-RRR.

The online algorithms can be implemented with networks that update connections using biologically plausible local information. Their learning rules resemble cortical plasticity associated with calcium plateau potentials. Within the model, those potentials can be interpreted as backward-propagating error signals. The algorithms perform competitively with existing implementations of the two named objectives, supporting the possibility that local biological learning rules can approximate useful supervised computations.
summary.tldr: Bio-RRR derives competitive supervised learning algorithms whose local neural updates resemble calcium plateau dependent cortical plasticity.

title: A simple normative network approximates local non-Hebbian learning in the cortex

abstract: Variational mutual information (MI) estimators are widely used in unsupervised representation learning methods such as contrastive predictive coding (CPC). A lower bound on MI can be obtained from a multi-class classification problem, where a critic attempts to distinguish a positive sample drawn from the underlying joint distribution from (m-1) negative samples drawn from a suitable proposal distribution. Using this approach, MI estimates are bounded above by \log m, and could thus severely underestimate unless m is very large. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel estimator based on a multi-label classification problem, where the critic needs to jointly identify \emph{multiple} positive samples at the same time. We show that using the same amount of negative samples, multi-label CPC is able to exceed the \log m bound, while still being a valid lower bound of mutual information. We demonstrate that the proposed approach is able to lead to better mutual information estimation, gain empirical improvements in unsupervised representation learning, and beat the current state-of-the-art in knowledge distillation over 10 out of 13 tasks.

paragraphs: Contrastive predictive coding can estimate mutual information by asking a critic to distinguish a positive sample from negative samples. In the multiclass formulation discussed here, the resulting estimate cannot exceed log m, where the classification problem contains m candidates. This ceiling can severely underestimate mutual information unless the number of candidates is very large.

The paper changes the classification task so that the critic must identify several positive samples jointly. This multi-label formulation can exceed the log m ceiling while using the same number of negative samples. Crucially, the authors show that the estimator remains a valid lower bound on mutual information. The change expands what the estimator can express without abandoning that theoretical interpretation.

The authors demonstrate improvements in mutual information estimation and empirical gains in unsupervised representation learning. They also report outperforming the then-current state of the art in knowledge distillation on ten of thirteen tasks. These results link the altered estimation objective to practical learning improvements, while preserving the distinction between a lower bound and an exact information estimate.
summary.tldr: Multi-label CPC identifies multiple positive samples jointly, exceeding the usual log m ceiling while remaining a valid mutual information lower bound.

title: Multi-label Contrastive Predictive Coding

abstract: Despite being the workhorse of deep learning, the backpropagation algorithm is no panacea. It enforces sequential layer updates, thus preventing efficient parallelization of the training process. Furthermore, its biological plausibility is being challenged. Alternative schemes have been devised; yet, under the constraint of synaptic asymmetry, none have scaled to modern deep learning tasks and architectures. Here, we challenge this perspective, and study the applicability of Direct Feedback Alignment (DFA) to neural view synthesis, recommender systems, geometric learning, and natural language processing. In contrast with previous studies limited to computer vision tasks, our findings show that it successfully trains a large range of state-of-the-art deep learning architectures, with performance close to fine-tuned backpropagation. When a larger gap between DFA and backpropagation exists, like in Transformers, we attribute this to a need to rethink common practices for large and complex architectures. At variance with common beliefs, our work supports that challenging tasks can be tackled in the absence of weight transport.

paragraphs: Backpropagation is the standard training method for deep networks, but the paper highlights its sequential layer updates and questions about biological plausibility. It investigates Direct Feedback Alignment, or DFA, as an alternative under synaptic asymmetry. The central question is whether this alternative can handle demanding contemporary architectures and tasks.

The study extends the scope of previous DFA work beyond computer vision. It examines neural view synthesis, recommendation, geometric learning, and natural language processing. Across this range, the authors find that DFA successfully trains many state-of-the-art architectures and often achieves performance close to carefully tuned backpropagation. This broadens the empirical evidence for learning without weight transport.

The results are qualified by architecture: Transformers show a larger performance gap. The authors attribute such gaps to a need to reconsider common training practices for large, complex models. Their findings support the feasibility of tackling challenging tasks without weight transport, while preserving a distinction between successful training across many architectures and matching backpropagation equally well in every case.
summary.tldr: Direct Feedback Alignment trains many modern architectures near backpropagation performance, though larger gaps remain for models such as Transformers.

title: Direct Feedback Alignment Scales to Modern Deep Learning Tasks and Architectures

abstract: This paper proposes a reliable neural network pruning algorithm by setting up a scientific control. Existing pruning methods have developed various hypotheses to approximate the importance of filters to the network and then execute filter pruning accordingly. To increase the reliability of the results, we prefer to have a more rigorous research design by including a scientific control group as an essential part to minimize the effect of all factors except the association between the filter and expected network output. Acting as a control group, knockoff feature is generated to mimic the feature map produced by the network filter, but they are conditionally independent of the example label given the real feature map. We theoretically suggest that the knockoff condition can be approximately preserved given the information propagation of network layers. Besides the real feature map on an intermediate layer, the corresponding knockoff feature is brought in as another auxiliary input signal for the subsequent layers. Redundant filters can be discovered in the adversarial process of different features. Through experiments, we demonstrate the superiority of the proposed algorithm over state-of-the-art methods. For example, our method can reduce 57.8% parameters and 60.2% FLOPs of ResNet-101 with only 0.01% top-1 accuracy loss on ImageNet. The code is available at https://github.com/huawei-noah/Pruning/tree/master/SCOP_NeurIPS2020.

paragraphs: Network pruning removes filters judged unnecessary, but that judgment often depends on a proxy for importance. SCOP introduces a scientific control into the process so that filter selection more directly tests the association between a feature and the desired output. The goal is to make pruning decisions more reliable.

For a real feature map, the method creates a knockoff feature that resembles it but is conditionally independent of the label given the real map. Both signals enter subsequent layers, allowing their competition to reveal redundant filters. The authors theoretically suggest that the knockoff condition can be approximately maintained as information moves through layers; this is an approximate preservation claim.

In the supplied example, SCOP removes 57.8% of ResNet-101's parameters and 60.2% of its FLOPs with a reported 0.01% top-1 accuracy loss on ImageNet. This illustrates substantial compression with little measured accuracy change in that evaluation, supporting the use of controlled feature comparisons for deciding what to remove.
summary.tldr: SCOP compares real features with knockoff controls to identify redundant filters and achieve substantial network compression in experiments.

title: SCOP: Scientific Control for Reliable Neural Network Pruning

abstract: Point completion refers to complete the missing geometries of objects from partial point clouds. Existing works usually estimate the missing shape by decoding a latent feature encoded from the input points. However, real-world objects are usually with diverse topologies and surface details, which a latent feature may fail to represent to recover a clean and complete surface. To this end, we propose a skeleton-bridged point completion network (SK-PCN) for shape completion. Given a partial scan, our method first predicts its 3D skeleton to obtain the global structure, and completes the surface by learning displacements from skeletal points. We decouple the shape completion into structure estimation and surface reconstruction, which eases the learning difficulty and benefits our method to obtain on-surface details. Besides, considering the missing features during encoding input points, SK-PCN adopts a local adjustment strategy that merges the input point cloud to our predictions for surface refinement. Comparing with previous methods, our skeleton-bridged manner better supports point normal estimation to obtain the full surface mesh beyond point clouds. The qualitative and quantitative experiments on both point cloud and mesh completion show that our approach outperforms the existing methods on various object categories.

paragraphs: Point completion reconstructs missing object geometry from a partial collection of three-dimensional points. Directly decoding a compressed feature representation can struggle with varied object structures and detailed surfaces. This paper introduces SK-PCN, which separates recovering the overall shape from reconstructing the surface.

Given a partial scan, the network first predicts a three-dimensional skeleton representing global structure. It then learns displacements from skeletal points to form the surface. A local adjustment stage merges the observed input points with the predictions to refine the result. This gives the original measurements a direct role in correcting the reconstructed surface.

The authors argue that separating structure estimation and surface reconstruction makes learning easier and helps recover surface detail. Their skeleton-based approach also better supports estimation of point normals, enabling full surface meshes as well as completed point clouds. Qualitative and quantitative experiments across several object categories report improvements over existing methods for both outputs, supporting the usefulness of this structured reconstruction process.
summary.tldr: SK-PCN completes partial 3D scans by predicting a skeleton, reconstructing its surface, and refining it with observed points.

title: Skeleton-bridged Point Completion: From Global Inference to Local Adjustment

abstract: Communication lays the foundation for human cooperation. It is also crucial for multi-agent cooperation. However, existing work focuses on broadcast communication, which is not only impractical but also leads to information redundancy that could even impair the learning process. To tackle these difficulties, we propose Individually Inferred Communication (I2C), a simple yet effective model to enable agents to learn a prior for agent-agent communication. The prior knowledge is learned via causal inference and realized by a feed-forward neural network that maps the agent's local observation to a belief about who to communicate with. The influence of one agent on another is inferred via the joint action-value function in multi-agent reinforcement learning and quantified to label the necessity of agent-agent communication. Furthermore, the agent policy is regularized to better exploit communicated messages. Empirically, we show that I2C can not only reduce communication overhead but also improve the performance in a variety of multi-agent cooperative scenarios, comparing to existing methods.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents need useful information from one another, but broadcasting every message can create unnecessary communication and redundant information. The paper introduces Individually Inferred Communication, or I2C, which learns whom an agent should communicate with. Its goal is to make communication selective while improving how agents cooperate.

I2C learns a communication prior through causal inference. It uses the joint action-value function to infer one agent's influence on another and turn that influence into labels indicating whether communication is necessary. A feed-forward network then maps an agent's local observation to a belief about suitable communication partners. The policy is also regularized to make better use of received messages.

Experiments across several cooperative multi-agent scenarios show lower communication overhead and better performance than the existing methods considered. The approach thus addresses both message selection and message use. Its reported findings indicate that reducing communication can accompany stronger cooperation when the selection mechanism is learned from relationships among the agents' actions and their joint value.
summary.tldr: I2C learns which agents should communicate, reducing communication overhead while improving cooperation in the evaluated scenarios.

title: Learning Individually Inferred Communication for Multi-Agent Cooperation

abstract: Coordinated ensemble spiking activity is widely observable in neural recordings and central in the study of population codes, with hypothesized roles including robust stimulus representation, interareal communication of neural information, and learning and memory formation. Model-free measures of synchrony characterize the coherence of pairwise activity, but not higher-order interactions; this limitation is transcended by statistical models of ensemble spiking activity. However, existing model-based analyses often impose assumptions about the relevance of higher-order interactions and require multiple repeated trials in order to characterize dynamics in the correlational structure of ensemble activity. To address these shortcomings, we propose an adaptive greedy filtering algorithm based on a discretized mark point-process model of ensemble spiking and a corresponding precise statistical inference framework to identify significant coordinated higher-order spiking activity. In the course of developing the statistical inference procedures, we also show that confidence intervals can be constructed for greedily estimated parameters. We demonstrate the utility of our proposed methods on simulated neuronal assemblies. Applied to multi-electrode recordings of human cortical ensembles, our proposed methods provide new insights into the dynamics underlying localized population activity during transitions between brain states.

paragraphs: Neurons often fire in coordinated groups, and understanding that coordination is important for studying population activity. Pairwise synchrony measures describe relationships between two neurons at a time, leaving interactions involving larger groups unresolved. Existing statistical approaches can capture those interactions, but often impose assumptions about their relevance or require repeated trials to track changes.

The authors propose an adaptive greedy filtering algorithm built on a discretized marked point-process model of ensemble spiking. It is paired with a statistical inference framework for identifying significant higher-order coordination. The method therefore addresses both estimating group activity and assessing the evidence for it. As part of that framework, the authors show that confidence intervals can be constructed for parameters estimated through a greedy procedure.

The paper demonstrates the method on simulated neuronal assemblies and applies it to multi-electrode recordings of human cortical ensembles. In those recordings, it provides insights into changing local population activity during transitions between brain states. The contribution concerns statistically supported descriptions of coordination and its dynamics, without establishing the hypothesized functional roles of coordinated firing.
summary.tldr: An adaptive spiking model and inference framework identify changing higher-order neuronal coordination and provide confidence intervals for greedily estimated parameters.

title: Dynamic Analysis of Higher-Order Coordination in Neuronal Assemblies via De-Sparsified Orthogonal Matching Pursuit

abstract: We revisit the problem of $n$-gram extraction in the differential privacy setting. In this problem, given a corpus of private text data, the goal is to release as many $n$-grams as possible while preserving user level privacy. Extracting $n$-grams is a fundamental subroutine in many NLP applications such as sentence completion, auto response generation for emails, etc. The problem also arises in other applications such as sequence mining, trajectory analysis, etc., and is a generalization of recently studied differentially private set union (DPSU) by Gopi et al. (2020). In this paper, we develop a new differentially private algorithm for this problem which, in our experiments, significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art. Our improvements stem from combining recent advances in DPSU, privacy accounting, and new heuristics for pruning in the tree-based approach initiated by Chen et al. (2012).

paragraphs: This paper studies how to extract and release sequences of text units, called n-grams, from a private corpus while preserving privacy at the user level. The objective is to release as many n-grams as possible under that privacy requirement. Such extraction is a building block for applications including sentence completion and automatic email responses.

The authors connect the task to differentially private set union, a related problem that n-gram extraction generalizes. Their algorithm combines advances in private set union with improved privacy accounting and new pruning heuristics for a tree-based extraction approach. The components address the shared challenge of finding useful sequences while managing the privacy implications of the overall procedure.

Experiments show that the resulting algorithm significantly outperforms the state of the art in the evaluated settings. The contribution is therefore a stronger extraction procedure assembled from complementary privacy and search techniques. Its relevance also extends beyond text: the abstract identifies sequence mining and trajectory analysis as applications where the same extraction problem arises. The stated goal remains useful release with user-level privacy, rather than unrestricted access to the underlying records.
summary.tldr: A new private n-gram extractor combines set-union methods, privacy accounting, and tree pruning to improve empirical extraction performance.

title: Differentially Private n-gram Extraction

abstract: The pre-trained language model (PrLM) demonstrates domination in downstream natural language processing tasks, in which multilingual PrLM takes advantage of language universality to alleviate the issue of limited resources for low-resource languages. Despite its successes, the performance of multilingual PrLM is still unsatisfactory, when multilingual PrLMs only focus on plain text and ignore obvious universal linguistic structure clues. Existing PrLMs have shown that monolingual linguistic structure knowledge may bring about better performance. Thus we propose a novel multilingual PrLM that supports both explicit universal dependency parsing and implicit language modeling. Syntax in terms of universal dependency parse serves as not only pre-training objective but also learned representation in our model, which brings unprecedented PrLM interpretability and convenience in downstream task use. Our model outperforms two popular multilingual PrLM, multilingual-BERT and XLM-R, on cross-lingual natural language understanding (NLU) benchmarks and linguistic structure parsing datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness and stronger cross-lingual modeling capabilities of our approach.

paragraphs: Multilingual language models can share knowledge across languages, helping languages with limited training resources. This paper argues that models trained only on plain text miss useful linguistic structure shared across languages. It proposes incorporating universal dependency syntax into multilingual pre-training so that grammatical relationships become an explicit part of what the model learns.

The proposed model supports both dependency parsing and language modeling. Universal dependency structure serves two roles: it is a training objective and part of the learned representation. This means syntactic information contributes directly to learning and remains available for downstream use. The authors also present this explicit structure as a source of improved interpretability.

Evaluations cover cross-lingual natural language understanding benchmarks and linguistic structure parsing datasets. The model outperforms multilingual-BERT and XLM-R in the reported comparisons. These findings support the usefulness of combining shared grammatical structure with multilingual language modeling. The contribution is therefore both representational and empirical: syntax is built into the model's learning process, and the resulting approach shows stronger cross-lingual performance in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Adding universal dependency syntax to multilingual pre-training improves reported cross-lingual understanding and parsing results.

title: Multilingual Pre-training with Universal Dependency Learning

abstract: Recently, Transformer has become a prevailing deep architecture for solving vehicle routing problems (VRPs). However, it is less effective in learning improvement models for VRP because its positional encoding (PE) method is not suitable in representing VRP solutions. This paper presents a novel Dual-Aspect Collaborative Transformer (DACT) to learn embeddings for the node and positional features separately, instead of fusing them together as done in existing ones, so as to avoid potential noises and incompatible correlations. Moreover, the positional features are embedded through a novel cyclic positional encoding (CPE) method to allow Transformer to effectively capture the circularity and symmetry of VRP solutions (i.e., cyclic sequences). We train DACT using Proximal Policy Optimization and design a curriculum learning strategy for better sample efficiency. We apply DACT to solve the traveling salesman problem (TSP) and capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP). Results show that our DACT outperforms existing Transformer based improvement models, and exhibits much better generalization performance across different problem sizes on synthetic and benchmark instances, respectively.

paragraphs: A routing improvement model learns how to revise an existing route to obtain a better solution. This paper identifies a representation problem when using Transformers for that task: conventional positional encoding does not suit the cyclic structure of vehicle routes. It proposes the Dual-Aspect Collaborative Transformer, or DACT, to represent route information more appropriately.

DACT learns separate embeddings for node features and positional features. Keeping these aspects separate is intended to avoid noise and incompatible correlations introduced by combining them directly. A cyclic positional encoding represents the circularity and symmetry of route solutions. The authors train the model with Proximal Policy Optimization and introduce a curriculum learning strategy to improve sample efficiency.

The evaluation covers the traveling salesman problem and the capacitated vehicle routing problem. DACT outperforms the existing Transformer-based improvement models tested and generalizes substantially better across problem sizes on synthetic and benchmark instances. The results support matching the model's representation to the structure of routes, with the architecture and training strategy together providing a learned approach to iterative solution improvement.
summary.tldr: DACT separates node and cyclic position representations to improve learned route refinement and generalization across problem sizes.

title: Learning to Iteratively Solve Routing Problems with Dual-Aspect Collaborative Transformer

abstract: Cryptic crosswords, the dominant crossword variety in the UK, are a promising target for advancing NLP systems that seek to process semantically complex, highly compositional language. Cryptic clues read like fluent natural language but are adversarially composed of two parts: a definition and a wordplay cipher requiring character-level manipulations. Expert humans use creative intelligence to solve cryptics, flexibly combining linguistic, world, and domain knowledge. In this paper, we make two main contributions. First, we present a dataset of cryptic clues as a challenging new benchmark for NLP systems that seek to process compositional language in more creative, human-like ways. After showing that three non-neural approaches and T5, a state-of-the-art neural language model, do not achieve good performance, we make our second main contribution: a novel curriculum approach, in which the model is first fine-tuned on related tasks such as unscrambling words. We also introduce a challenging data split, examine the meta-linguistic capabilities of subword-tokenized models, and investigate model systematicity by perturbing the wordplay part of clues, showing that T5 exhibits behavior partially consistent with human solving strategies. Although our curricular approach considerably improves on the T5 baseline, our best-performing model still fails to generalize to the extent that humans can. Thus, cryptic crosswords remain an unsolved challenge for NLP systems and a potential source of future innovation.

paragraphs: Cryptic crossword clues combine an answer’s definition with wordplay that can require manipulating individual characters. Their fluent surface wording disguises this structure, making them a demanding test of how language systems combine meaning and formal operations. The paper introduces a dataset of these clues as a benchmark for complex, compositional language understanding.

Initial evaluations find that three non-neural approaches and the T5 language model perform poorly. The authors then introduce a curriculum that first fine-tunes the model on related skills, including unscrambling words. They also create a challenging data split and examine how models using subword tokens handle operations on language itself. Perturbing the wordplay portion of clues provides another test of whether solving behavior is systematic.

The curriculum substantially improves the T5 baseline, and some observed behavior is partially consistent with human solving strategies. Nevertheless, the strongest model still falls short of human generalization. The benchmark therefore exposes a continuing gap between improving task performance and flexibly combining the knowledge needed to solve unfamiliar clues.
summary.tldr: A cryptic crossword benchmark and related-task curriculum improve language-model solving while revealing a persistent gap in human-like generalization.

title: Decrypting Cryptic Crosswords: Semantically Complex Wordplay Puzzles as a Target for NLP

abstract: Common approaches for task-agnostic exploration learn tabula-rasa --the agent assumes isolated environments and no prior knowledge or experience. However, in the real world, agents learn in many environments and always come with prior experiences as they explore new ones. Exploration is a lifelong process. In this paper, we propose a paradigm change in the formulation and evaluation of task-agnostic exploration. In this setup, the agent first learns to explore across many environments without any extrinsic goal in a task-agnostic manner.Later on, the agent effectively transfers the learned exploration policy to better explore new environments when solving tasks. In this context, we evaluate several baseline exploration strategies and present a simple yet effective approach to learning task-agnostic exploration policies. Our key idea is that there are two components of exploration: (1) an agent-centric component encouraging exploration of unseen parts of the environment based on an agent’s belief; (2) an environment-centric component encouraging exploration of inherently interesting objects. We show that our formulation is effective and provides the most consistent exploration across several training-testing environment pairs. We also introduce benchmarks and metrics for evaluating task-agnostic exploration strategies. The source code is available at https://github.com/sparisi/cbet/.

paragraphs: The paper treats exploration as a skill that can accumulate across environments. Instead of learning how to explore separately from scratch in each setting, an agent first trains across multiple environments without an external task goal. It later transfers its exploration policy to new environments while solving tasks, making previous exploration experience part of the evaluation.

The proposed approach combines two sources of exploratory motivation. One depends on the agent's beliefs and encourages visiting parts of the environment it has not seen. The other depends on the environment and encourages attention to inherently interesting objects. Together, these components account for both what remains unfamiliar to the agent and what in the scene attracts exploration.

The authors compare several exploration strategies and report that their formulation produces the most consistent exploration across the tested training–testing environment pairs. They also introduce benchmarks and evaluation metrics for this transfer setting. The findings support studying exploration through reusable policies, with performance judged partly by how well exploratory behavior carries into new environments.
summary.tldr: The paper learns transferable exploration policies by combining the pursuit of unseen places with interest in objects across environments.

title: Interesting Object, Curious Agent: Learning Task-Agnostic Exploration

abstract: Determinantal Point Process (DPPs) are statistical models for repulsive point patterns. Both sampling and inference are tractable for DPPs, a rare feature among models with negative dependence that explains their popularity in machine learning and spatial statistics. Parametric and nonparametric inference methods have been proposed in the finite case, i.e. when the point patterns live in a finite ground set. In the continuous case, only parametric methods have been investigated, while nonparametric maximum likelihood for DPPs -- an optimization problem over trace-class operators -- has remained an open question. In this paper, we show that a restricted version of this maximum likelihood (MLE) problem falls within the scope of a recent representer theorem for nonnegative functions in an RKHS. This leads to a finite-dimensional problem, with strong statistical ties to the original MLE. Moreover, we propose, analyze, and demonstrate a fixed point algorithm to solve this finite-dimensional problem. Finally, we also provide a controlled estimate of the correlation kernel of the DPP, thus providing more interpretability.

paragraphs: Determinantal point processes model patterns whose points tend to repel one another. They are useful partly because sampling and inference remain tractable, an unusual combination for models of negative dependence. This paper addresses learning such processes when points occupy a continuous domain and the model is not restricted to a fixed parametric family.

The main obstacle is that nonparametric maximum likelihood involves optimization over trace-class operators, an infinite-dimensional problem. The authors show that a restricted version fits a representer theorem for nonnegative functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This produces a finite-dimensional optimization problem with strong statistical connections to the original maximum-likelihood formulation.

The paper proposes, analyzes, and demonstrates a fixed-point algorithm for that finite problem. It also provides a controlled estimate of the process's correlation kernel, making the fitted model more interpretable. The contribution therefore links a continuous statistical estimation problem to a concrete computational procedure. Its reduction applies to the stated restricted formulation, rather than claiming an unrestricted solution to every continuous DPP likelihood problem.
summary.tldr: A representer theorem reduces restricted nonparametric continuous-DPP estimation to a finite problem with a fixed-point solver.

title: Nonparametric estimation of continuous DPPs with kernel methods

abstract: When faced with sequential decision-making problems, it is often useful to be able to predict what would happen if decisions were made using a new policy. Those predictions must often be based on data collected under some previously used decision-making rule. Many previous methods enable such off-policy (or counterfactual) estimation of the _expected_ value of a performance measure called the return. In this paper, we take the first steps towards a 'universal off-policy estimator' (UnO)---one that provides off-policy estimates and high-confidence bounds for _any_ parameter of the return distribution. We use UnO for estimating and simultaneously bounding the mean, variance, quantiles/median, inter-quantile range, CVaR, and the entire cumulative distribution of returns. Finally, we also discuss UnO's applicability in various settings, including fully observable, partially observable (i.e., with unobserved confounders), Markovian, non-Markovian, stationary, smoothly non-stationary, and discrete distribution shifts.
originalAbstract: When faced with sequential decision-making problems, it is often useful to be able to predict what would happen if decisions were made using a new policy. Those predictions must often be based on data collected under some previously used decision-making rule. Many previous methods enable such off-policy (or counterfactual) estimation of the _expected_ value of a performance measure called the return. In this paper, we take the first steps towards a 'universal off-policy estimator' (UnO)---one that provides off-policy estimates and high-confidence bounds for _any_ parameter of the return distribution. We use UnO for estimating and simultaneously bounding the mean, variance, quantiles/median, inter-quantile range, CVaR, and the entire cumulative distribution of returns. Finally, we also discuss UnO's applicability in various settings, including fully observable, partially observable (i.e., with unobserved confounders), Markovian, non-Markovian, stationary, smoothly non-stationary, and discrete distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation predicts how a new decision policy would perform using data collected under another policy. Many methods focus on expected return, which summarizes average performance. This paper takes steps toward a broader estimator that can describe multiple aspects of the return distribution and attach high-confidence bounds to those estimates.

The proposed estimator, UnO, is used to estimate and simultaneously bound the mean, variance, median and other quantiles, inter-quantile range, conditional value at risk, and the full cumulative distribution. These quantities describe different aspects of outcomes, including their spread and unfavorable tail, giving a fuller picture than the average alone.

The paper also discusses applicability across fully and partially observable settings, including unobserved confounders, as well as Markovian and non-Markovian processes. Other settings considered include stationary environments, smooth non-stationarity, and discrete distribution shifts. The contribution is a distribution-focused approach to counterfactual policy assessment, with the abstract presenting these broader settings as applicability discussions alongside the demonstrated estimation and bounding capabilities.
summary.tldr: UnO broadens off-policy evaluation from average return to distributional quantities with simultaneous high-confidence bounds.

title: Universal Off-Policy Evaluation

abstract: Unsupervised pre-training methods for large vision models have shown to enhance performance on downstream supervised tasks. Developing similar techniques for satellite imagery presents significant opportunities as unlabelled data is plentiful and the inherent temporal and multi-spectral structure provides avenues to further improve existing pre-training strategies. In this paper, we present SatMAE, a pre-training framework for temporal or multi-spectral satellite imagery based on Masked Autoencoder (MAE). To leverage temporal information, we include a temporal embedding along with independently masking image patches across time. In addition, we demonstrate that encoding multi-spectral data as groups of bands with distinct spectral positional encodings is beneficial. Our approach yields strong improvements over previous state-of-the-art techniques, both in terms of supervised learning performance on benchmark datasets (up to $\uparrow$ 7%), and transfer learning performance on downstream remote sensing tasks, including land cover classification (up to $\uparrow$ 14%) and semantic segmentation. Code and data are available on the project website: https://sustainlab-group.github.io/SatMAE/

paragraphs: Satellite imagery offers abundant unlabeled data, along with structure across time and spectral bands. SatMAE adapts masked-autoencoder pre-training to exploit those properties before supervised training on remote-sensing tasks. The paper investigates how to represent these additional dimensions so that pre-training benefits from information beyond an individual conventional image.

For temporal imagery, the framework adds temporal embeddings and masks image patches independently across time. For multispectral imagery, it groups spectral bands and assigns distinct spectral positional encodings to those groups. The authors find that this band-grouping representation is beneficial, making spectral identity an explicit part of the model's input representation.

The reported results improve on previous leading techniques in both supervised benchmark performance and transfer to downstream tasks. Improvements reach up to 7% on supervised benchmarks and up to 14% for land-cover classification, with gains also reported for semantic segmentation. Those figures describe reported upper improvements rather than uniform gains. The findings support pre-training choices tailored to the temporal and spectral organization of satellite data.
summary.tldr: SatMAE incorporates temporal and spectral structure into masked-autoencoder pre-training, improving performance and transfer on evaluated satellite-imagery tasks.

title: SatMAE: Pre-training Transformers for Temporal and Multi-Spectral Satellite Imagery

abstract: Empirical works show that for ReLU neural networks (NNs) with small initialization, input weights of hidden neurons (the input weight of a hidden neuron consists of the weight from its input layer to the hidden neuron and its bias term) condense onto isolated orientations. The condensation dynamics implies that the training implicitly regularizes a NN towards one with much smaller effective size. In this work, we illustrate the formation of the condensation in multi-layer fully connected NNs and show that the maximal number of condensed orientations in the initial training stage is twice the multiplicity of the activation function, where ``multiplicity'' indicates the multiple roots of activation function at origin. Our theoretical analysis confirms experiments for two cases, one is for the activation function of multiplicity one with arbitrary dimension input, which contains many common activation functions, and the other is for the layer with one-dimensional input and arbitrary multiplicity. This work makes a step towards understanding how small initialization leads NNs to condensation at the initial training stage.

paragraphs: Neural networks initialized with small weights can exhibit condensation: hidden neurons' input weights, including their biases, gather around a limited number of directions. When many neurons align this way, the network behaves as though it has a smaller effective size. This paper studies how that organization forms at the beginning of training.

The authors examine multilayer fully connected networks and connect the maximum number of condensed directions to the activation function's multiplicity at zero, meaning its root multiplicity there. They show that the maximum number is twice this multiplicity. This links an aspect of early network organization to a mathematical property of the activation.

The theoretical analysis confirms experiments in two settings: multiplicity-one activations with inputs of arbitrary dimension, and layers with one-dimensional inputs and arbitrary activation multiplicity. These specified cases provide a step toward explaining how small initialization induces early condensation. The result concerns the initial training stage and helps clarify one mechanism through which training can implicitly favor a smaller effective network.
summary.tldr: The paper connects early neural-network weight condensation under small initialization to the activation function's root multiplicity at zero.

title: Towards Understanding the Condensation of Neural Networks at Initial Training

abstract: Language models have achieved remarkable performance on a wide range of tasks that require natural language understanding. Nevertheless, state-of-the-art models have generally struggled with tasks that require quantitative reasoning, such as solving mathematics, science, and engineering questions at the college level. To help close this gap, we introduce Minerva, a large language model pretrained on general natural language data and further trained on technical content. The model achieves strong performance in a variety of evaluations, including state-of-the-art performance on the MATH dataset. We also evaluate our model on over two hundred undergraduate-level problems in physics, biology, chemistry, economics, and other sciences that require quantitative reasoning, and find that the model can correctly answer nearly a quarter of them.
