This paper introduces Minerva to address that gap. The model begins with general natural-language pretraining and then receives further training on technical content, focusing the investigation on quantitative problem solving.

The authors evaluate Minerva across several settings and report strong performance, including state-of-the-art results on the MATH dataset. This shows that the resulting model performs well on an established mathematics evaluation. The paper also broadens assessment beyond that dataset to questions drawn from undergraduate scientific subjects.

That broader evaluation contains more than two hundred problems in physics, biology, chemistry, economics, and other sciences requiring quantitative reasoning. Minerva correctly answers nearly a quarter of them. This result demonstrates an ability to solve some demanding problems across disciplines while also showing substantial remaining difficulty on that collection. The two evaluations together assess both mathematical benchmark performance and a wider range of technical questions.
summary.tldr: Minerva extends language-model training with technical content, achieving strong mathematics results and solving nearly a quarter of a broader undergraduate science problem set.

title: Solving Quantitative Reasoning Problems with Language Models

abstract: Clinical diagnosis of the eye is performed over multifarious data modalities including scalar clinical labels, vectorized biomarkers, two-dimensional fundus images, and three-dimensional Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) scans. Clinical practitioners use all available data modalities for diagnosing and treating eye diseases like Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) or Diabetic Macular Edema (DME). Enabling usage of machine learning algorithms within the ophthalmic medical domain requires research into the relationships and interactions between all relevant data over a treatment period. Existing datasets are limited in that they neither provide data nor consider the explicit relationship modeling between the data modalities. In this paper, we introduce the Ophthalmic Labels for Investigating Visual Eye Semantics (OLIVES) dataset that addresses the above limitation. This is the first OCT and near-IR fundus dataset that includes clinical labels, biomarker labels, disease labels, and time-series patient treatment information from associated clinical trials. The dataset consists of 1268 near-IR fundus images each with at least 49 OCT scans, and 16 biomarkers, along with 4 clinical labels and a disease diagnosis of DR or DME. In total, there are 96 eyes' data averaged over a period of at least two years with each eye treated for an average of 66 weeks and 7 injections. We benchmark the utility of OLIVES dataset for ophthalmic data as well as provide benchmarks and concrete research directions for core and emerging machine learning paradigms within medical image analysis.

Data cover 96 eyes, with an average observation period of at least two years; treatment averages are 66 weeks and seven injections per eye.

The authors benchmark the dataset's utility for ophthalmic analysis and provide benchmarks and research directions for machine learning in medical imaging. The contribution is a connected, longitudinal research resource, with imaging and clinical context available together.
summary.tldr: OLIVES links longitudinal eye imaging with biomarkers, clinical labels, diagnoses, and treatment histories for multimodal medical-image research.

title: OLIVES Dataset: Ophthalmic Labels for Investigating Visual Eye Semantics

abstract: Objective-space decomposition algorithms (ODAs) are widely studied for solving multi-objective integer programs. However, they often encounter difficulties in handling scalarized problems, which could cause infeasibility or repetitive nondominated points and thus induce redundant runtime. To mitigate the issue, we present a graph neural network (GNN) based method to learn the reduction rule in the ODA. We formulate the algorithmic procedure of generic ODAs as a Markov decision process, and parameterize the policy (reduction rule) with a novel two-stage GNN to fuse information from variables, constraints and especially objectives for better state representation. We train our model with imitation learning and deploy it on a state-of-the-art ODA. Results show that our method significantly improves the solving efficiency of the ODA. The learned policy generalizes fairly well to larger problems or more objectives, and the proposed GNN outperforms existing ones for integer programming in terms of test and generalization accuracy.

paragraphs: Multi-objective integer programs seek solutions under several objectives at once. Objective-space decomposition algorithms tackle them through smaller scalarized problems, but some of those problems can be infeasible or produce nondominated points already found. Such outcomes consume runtime without adding useful solutions. This paper learns a reduction rule intended to reduce that wasted work.

The authors describe the procedure of a generic decomposition algorithm as a Markov decision process. A two-stage graph neural network represents the policy that chooses reductions. Its representation combines information about variables, constraints, and objectives, with particular attention to the objectives. The policy is trained through imitation learning and then inserted into a state-of-the-art decomposition algorithm.

Reported results show a significant improvement in solving efficiency. The learned rule also generalizes fairly well to larger instances and problems with more objectives. The proposed network exceeds existing graph networks for integer programming in test and generalization accuracy. These findings support learning an internal solver decision while retaining the surrounding optimization procedure.
summary.tldr: A graph neural network learns reduction decisions that improve the efficiency of a multi-objective integer programming solver.

title: Graph Learning Assisted Multi-Objective Integer Programming

abstract: Recent advance in deep learning has led to rapid adoption of machine learning based NLP models in a wide range of applications. Despite the continuous gain in accuracy, backward compatibility is also an important aspect for industrial applications, yet it received little research attention. Backward compatibility requires that the new model does not regress on cases that were correctly handled by its predecessor. This work studies model update regression in structured prediction tasks. We choose syntactic dependency parsing and conversational semantic parsing as representative examples of structured prediction tasks in NLP. First, we measure and analyze model update regression in different model update settings. Next, we explore and benchmark existing techniques for reducing model update regression including model ensemble and knowledge distillation. We further propose a simple and effective method, Backward-Congruent Re-ranking (BCR), by taking into account the characteristics of structured output. Experiments show that BCR can better mitigate model update regression than model ensemble and knowledge distillation approaches.

paragraphs: A model update can improve overall accuracy while breaking cases that its predecessor handled correctly. This paper studies that problem as backward compatibility in structured language prediction. The relevant question is whether a replacement preserves earlier successes, an aspect of model quality that aggregate accuracy alone does not establish.

The authors use syntactic dependency parsing and conversational semantic parsing as representative tasks. They measure and analyze update regression across different update settings, then benchmark model ensembles and knowledge distillation as ways to reduce it. This establishes a comparison around the specific goal of avoiding new errors on previously correct cases.

They introduce Backward-Congruent Re-ranking, or BCR, which takes advantage of the structured nature of the outputs. Experiments show that BCR mitigates update regression better than the ensemble and distillation approaches considered. The contribution combines a way to evaluate update compatibility with a method tailored to structured predictions. Its results support treating preservation of existing behavior as an explicit objective when improving deployed NLP models.
summary.tldr: Backward-Congruent Re-ranking reduces newly introduced errors in structured NLP model updates better than the compared ensemble and distillation methods.

title: Measuring and Reducing Model Update Regression in Structured Prediction for NLP

abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are promising brain-inspired energy-efficient models. Recent progress in training methods has enabled successful deep SNNs on large-scale tasks with low latency. Particularly, backpropagation through time (BPTT) with surrogate gradients (SG) is popularly used to enable models to achieve high performance in a very small number of time steps. However, it is at the cost of large memory consumption for training, lack of theoretical clarity for optimization, and inconsistency with the online property of biological learning rules and rules on neuromorphic hardware. Other works connect the spike representations of SNNs with equivalent artificial neural network formulation and train SNNs by gradients from equivalent mappings to ensure descent directions. But they fail to achieve low latency and are also not online. In this work, we propose online training through time (OTTT) for SNNs, which is derived from BPTT to enable forward-in-time learning by tracking presynaptic activities and leveraging instantaneous loss and gradients. Meanwhile, we theoretically analyze and prove that the gradients of OTTT can provide a similar descent direction for optimization as gradients from equivalent mapping between spike representations under both feedforward and recurrent conditions. OTTT only requires constant training memory costs agnostic to time steps, avoiding the significant memory costs of BPTT for GPU training. Furthermore, the update rule of OTTT is in the form of three-factor Hebbian learning, which could pave a path for online on-chip learning. With OTTT, it is the first time that the two mainstream supervised SNN training methods, BPTT with SG and spike representation-based training, are connected, and meanwhile it is in a biologically plausible form. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and CIFAR10-DVS demonstrate the superior performance of our method on large-scale static and neuromorphic datasets in a small number of time steps. Our code is available at https://github.com/pkuxmq/OTTT-SNN.

abstract: We present a family $\{\widehat{\pi}_p\}_{p\ge 1}$ of pessimistic learning rules for offline learning of linear contextual bandits, relying on confidence sets with respect to different $\ell_p$ norms, where $\widehat{\pi}_2$ corresponds to Bellman-consistent pessimism (BCP), while $\widehat{\pi}_\infty$ is a novel generalization of lower confidence bound (LCB) to the linear setting. We show that the novel $\widehat{\pi}_\infty$ learning rule is, in a sense, adaptively optimal, as it achieves the minimax performance (up to log factors) against all $\ell_q$-constrained problems, and as such it strictly dominates all other predictors in the family, including $\widehat{\pi}_2$.

paragraphs: The paper studies offline learning for linear contextual bandits, where decisions must be learned from existing data. It considers pessimistic learning rules built from confidence sets. These sets represent uncertainty, and their geometry becomes a central design choice in the proposed family of rules.

The family uses different p-norms to define the confidence sets. Its two-norm member corresponds to Bellman-consistent pessimism. Its infinity-norm member provides a new extension of lower-confidence-bound learning to the linear setting. Placing these rules in one family allows the authors to compare their performance through a common mathematical framework.

The main result establishes a qualified form of adaptive optimality for the infinity-norm rule: it achieves minimax performance up to logarithmic factors across all q-norm-constrained problems considered. In this theoretical sense, it strictly dominates the other members of the family, including the two-norm rule. The result shows that the choice of confidence-set geometry can materially affect the strength and adaptability of offline learning guarantees.
summary.tldr: An infinity-norm pessimistic rule achieves adaptive minimax guarantees, up to logarithmic factors, across the studied constrained bandit problems.

title: Pessimism for Offline Linear Contextual Bandits using $\ell_p$ Confidence Sets

abstract: Recent studies show that transformer has strong capability of building long-range dependencies, yet is incompetent in capturing high frequencies that predominantly convey local information. To tackle this issue, we present a novel and general-purpose $\textit{Inception Transformer}$, or $\textit{iFormer}$ for short, that effectively learns comprehensive features with both high- and low-frequency information in visual data. Specifically, we design an Inception mixer to explicitly graft the advantages of convolution and max-pooling for capturing the high-frequency information to transformers. Different from recent hybrid frameworks, the Inception mixer brings greater efficiency through a channel splitting mechanism to adopt parallel convolution/max-pooling path and self-attention path as high- and low-frequency mixers, while having the flexibility to model discriminative information scattered within a wide frequency range. Considering that bottom layers play more roles in capturing high-frequency details while top layers more in modeling low-frequency global information, we further introduce a frequency ramp structure, i.e., gradually decreasing the dimensions fed to the high-frequency mixer and increasing those to the low-frequency mixer, which can effectively trade-off high- and low-frequency components across different layers. We benchmark the iFormer on a series of vision tasks, and showcase that it achieves impressive performance on image classification, COCO detection and ADE20K segmentation. For example, our iFormer-S hits the top-1 accuracy of 83.4% on ImageNet-1K, much higher than DeiT-S by 3.6%, and even slightly better than much bigger model Swin-B (83.3%) with only 1/4 parameters and 1/3 FLOPs. Code and models are released at https://github.com/sail-sg/iFormer.

paragraphs: Inception Transformer, or iFormer, combines mechanisms for capturing local visual detail and broad relationships. The paper starts from the observation that transformers handle long-range dependencies well but struggle with high-frequency information associated with local structure. Its Inception mixer adds convolution and max-pooling alongside self-attention so the model can represent information across a wider frequency range.

The mixer splits feature channels between parallel processing paths: convolution and max-pooling handle high-frequency information, while attention handles low-frequency information. A frequency ramp changes this allocation with depth. Earlier layers devote more dimensions to local detail, and later layers progressively allocate more to global information. This provides an explicit way to balance the two kinds of processing across the network.

Evaluations cover classification, object detection, and segmentation. On ImageNet-1K, iFormer-S reaches 83.4% top-1 accuracy, exceeding DeiT-S by 3.6 percentage points. It also slightly exceeds the reported 83.3% for Swin-B while using one-quarter of its parameters and one-third of its FLOPs, illustrating the proposed design's efficiency in that comparison.
summary.tldr: iFormer combines local-detail processing with self-attention and shifts their balance across layers to improve visual modeling efficiency.

title: Inception Transformer

abstract: We consider linear prediction with a convex Lipschitz loss, or more generally, stochastic convex optimization problems of generalized linear form, i.e.~where each instantaneous loss is a scalar convex function of a linear function. We show that in this setting, early stopped Gradient Descent (GD), without any explicit regularization or projection, ensures excess error at most $\varepsilon$ (compared to the best possible with unit Euclidean norm) with an optimal, up to logarithmic factors, sample complexity of $\tilde{O}(1/\varepsilon^2)$ and only $\tilde{O}(1/\varepsilon^2)$ iterations. This contrasts with general stochastic convex optimization, where $\Omega(1/\varepsilon^4)$ iterations are needed Amir et al. 2021. The lower iteration complexity is ensured by leveraging uniform convergence rather than stability. But instead of uniform convergence in a norm ball, which we show can guarantee suboptimal learning using $\Theta(1/\varepsilon^4)$ samples, we rely on uniform convergence in a distribution-dependent ball.

paragraphs: This paper asks how efficiently ordinary gradient descent can learn generalized linear prediction problems with convex losses. It includes linear prediction with a convex Lipschitz loss and considers losses formed by applying a scalar convex function to a linear function. The algorithm stops early and uses neither explicit regularization nor projection.

In this setting, the authors show that gradient descent achieves excess error at most epsilon relative to the best predictor with unit Euclidean norm. It needs order one over epsilon squared samples and iterations, up to logarithmic factors. The sample requirement is optimal to that precision. The iteration guarantee is substantially smaller than the one-over-epsilon-to-the-fourth requirement identified for general stochastic convex optimization.

The proof uses uniform convergence over a ball that depends on the data distribution. This choice matters: the authors show that uniform convergence over a norm ball can yield a suboptimal guarantee requiring order one over epsilon to the fourth samples. The result explains how the structure of generalized linear losses supports sharper learning guarantees for a simple optimization procedure.
summary.tldr: Early-stopped gradient descent achieves near-optimal sample complexity and fewer iterations for the studied generalized linear convex problems.

title: Thinking Outside the Ball: Optimal Learning with Gradient Descent for Generalized Linear Stochastic Convex Optimization

abstract: The problem of monotone submodular maximization has been studied extensively due to its wide range of applications. However, there are cases where one can only access the objective function in a distorted or noisy form because of the uncertain nature or the errors involved in the evaluation. This paper considers the problem of constrained monotone submodular maximization with noisy oracles introduced by Hassidim and Singer (2017). For a cardinality constraint, we propose an algorithm achieving a near-optimal (1-1/e-O(epsilon))-approximation guarantee (for arbitrary epsilon > 0) with only a polynomial number of queries to the noisy value oracle, which improves the exponential query complexity of Singer and Hassidim (2018). For general matroid constraints, we show the first constant approximation algorithm in the presence of noise. Our main approaches are to design a novel local search framework that can handle the effect of noise and to construct certain smoothing surrogate functions for noise reduction.

paragraphs: Many selection problems involve diminishing returns: adding an item helps less once similar benefits are already covered. Monotone submodular maximization formalizes this structure. This paper considers the harder situation where the value of a chosen set can only be evaluated through a noisy oracle, so the algorithm cannot rely on exact comparisons.

The authors develop a local search framework that accounts for noise and construct smoothed substitute objectives to reduce its effect. For a cardinality constraint, which limits the number of selected items, their algorithm achieves an approximation of 1-1/e-O(epsilon) for any positive epsilon. It requires only polynomially many queries to the noisy oracle, improving an earlier exponential query requirement.

The analysis also covers general matroid constraints, a broader framework for specifying which selections are permitted. Here the authors establish the first constant-factor approximation in the stated noisy setting. Together, the results show that carefully designed local search and smoothing can preserve meaningful optimization guarantees even when objective evaluations are distorted.
summary.tldr: Noise-aware local search and smoothing give efficient approximation guarantees for constrained submodular maximization with noisy evaluations.

title: Efficient Submodular Optimization under Noise: Local Search is Robust

abstract: Generative adversarial nets (GANs) have been remarkably successful at learning to sample from distributions specified by a given dataset, particularly if the given dataset is reasonably large compared to its dimensionality. However, given limited data, classical GANs have struggled, and strategies like output-regularization, data-augmentation, use of pre-trained models and pruning have been shown to lead to improvements. Notably, the applicability of these strategies is often constrained to particular settings, e.g., availability of a pretrained GAN, or increases training time, e.g., when using pruning. In contrast, we propose a Discriminator gradIent Gap regularized GAN (DigGAN) formulation which can be added to any existing GAN. DigGAN augments existing GANs by encouraging to narrow the gap between the norm of the gradient of a discriminator's prediction w.r.t. real images and w.r.t. the generated samples. We observe this formulation to avoid bad attractors within the GAN loss landscape, and we find DigGAN to significantly improve the results of GAN training when limited data is available.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial networks can struggle when the available training data are limited relative to their dimensionality. Existing remedies include augmentation, regularization, pretrained models, and pruning, but some depend on particular resources or increase training time. DigGAN introduces a regularization term that the authors describe as compatible with any existing GAN.

The method examines how sensitive the discriminator's prediction is to changes in its input. It compares the size of this gradient for real images with its size for generated samples, then encourages the gap between them to shrink. The target is therefore a difference in discriminator sensitivity across the two kinds of input.

The authors observe that this formulation helps avoid unfavorable attractors in the GAN optimization landscape and significantly improves training results with limited data. These are reported empirical findings, rather than a guarantee that every training run will avoid poor solutions. The approach matters because it supplies a broadly applicable modification focused on discriminator behavior when examples are scarce.
summary.tldr: DigGAN improves limited-data GAN training by encouraging similar discriminator gradient magnitudes for real and generated images.

title: DigGAN: Discriminator gradIent Gap Regularization for GAN Training with Limited Data

abstract: The distance matrix of a dataset $X$ of $n$ points with respect to a distance function $f$ represents all pairwise distances between points in $X$ induced by $f$. Due to their wide applicability, distance matrices and related families of matrices have been the focus of many recent algorithmic works. We continue this line of research and take a broad view of algorithm design for distance matrices with the goal of designing fast algorithms, which are specifically tailored for distance matrices, for fundamental linear algebraic primitives. Our results include efficient algorithms for computing matrix-vector products for a wide class of distance matrices, such as the $\ell_1$ metric for which we get a linear runtime, as well as an $\Omega(n^2)$ lower bound for any algorithm which computes a matrix-vector product for the $\ell_{\infty}$ case, showing a separation between the $\ell_1$ and the $\ell_{\infty}$ metrics. Our upper bound results in conjunction with recent works on the matrix-vector query model have many further downstream applications, including the fastest algorithm for computing a relative error low-rank approximation for the distance matrix induced by $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2^2$ functions and the fastest algorithm for computing an additive error low-rank approximation for the $\ell_2$ metric, in addition to applications for fast matrix multiplication among others. We also give algorithms for constructing distance matrices and show that one can construct an approximate $\ell_2$ distance matrix in time faster than the bound implied by the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma.

paragraphs: A distance matrix records the distance between every pair of points in a dataset. Although it can contain many entries, those entries arise from a shared geometric rule. This paper designs linear-algebra algorithms that exploit that structure, focusing on operations such as multiplying a distance matrix by a vector and constructing low-rank approximations.

A central finding is that the choice of distance function changes what computational savings are possible. The authors obtain linear runtime for matrix-vector multiplication with the ℓ1 metric, while proving a quadratic lower bound in the number of points for the ℓ∞ case. Thus, distance matrices do not all admit the same kinds of acceleration.

Combined with results about algorithms using matrix-vector queries, the methods yield the reported fastest low-rank approximation algorithms for several distance functions, with relative-error or additive-error guarantees depending on the case. The paper also develops matrix-construction algorithms, including approximate ℓ2 distance-matrix construction faster than the bound obtained through the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma. Together, the results connect geometric structure to concrete computational improvements.
summary.tldr: Algorithms tailored to distance matrices accelerate key linear-algebra operations, while lower bounds reveal sharp differences between distance functions.

title: Faster Linear Algebra for Distance Matrices

abstract: Pretraining a language model (LM) on text has been shown to help various downstream NLP tasks. Recent works show that a knowledge graph (KG) can complement text data, offering structured background knowledge that provides a useful scaffold for reasoning. However, these works are not pretrained to learn a deep fusion of the two modalities at scale, limiting the potential to acquire fully joint representations of text and KG. Here we propose DRAGON (Deep Bidirectional Language-Knowledge Graph Pretraining), a self-supervised approach to pretraining a deeply joint language-knowledge foundation model from text and KG at scale. Specifically, our model takes pairs of text segments and relevant KG subgraphs as input and bidirectionally fuses information from both modalities. We pretrain this model by unifying two self-supervised reasoning tasks, masked language modeling and KG link prediction. DRAGON outperforms existing LM and LM+KG models on diverse downstream tasks including question answering across general and biomedical domains, with +5% absolute gain on average. In particular, DRAGON achieves notable performance on complex reasoning about language and knowledge (+10% on questions involving long contexts or multi-step reasoning) and low-resource QA (+8% on OBQA and RiddleSense), and new state-of-the-art results on various BioNLP tasks. Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/michiyasunaga/dragon.

title: Deep Bidirectional Language-Knowledge Graph Pretraining

abstract: Large convolutional neural networks (CNN) can be difficult to train in the differentially private (DP) regime, since the optimization algorithms require a computationally expensive operation, known as the per-sample gradient clipping. We propose an efficient and scalable implementation of this clipping on convolutional layers, termed as the mixed ghost clipping, that significantly eases the private training in terms of both time and space complexities, without affecting the accuracy. The improvement in efficiency is rigorously studied through the first complexity analysis for the mixed ghost clipping and existing DP training algorithms.Extensive experiments on vision classification tasks, with large ResNet, VGG, and Vision Transformers (ViT), demonstrate that DP training with mixed ghost clipping adds $1\sim 10\%$ memory overhead and $<2\times$ slowdown to the standard non-private training. Specifically, when training VGG19 on CIFAR10, the mixed ghost clipping is $3\times$ faster than state-of-the-art Opacus library with $18\times$ larger maximum batch size. To emphasize the significance of efficient DP training on convolutional layers, we achieve 96.7\% accuracy on CIFAR10 and 83.0\% on CIFAR100 at $\epsilon=1$ using BEiT, while the previous best results are 94.8\% and 67.4\%, respectively. We open-source a privacy engine (\url{https://github.com/woodyx218/private_vision}) that implements DP training of CNN (including convolutional ViT) with a few lines of code.

paragraphs: Differentially private training can make large convolutional networks expensive to train because it requires clipping individual examples’ gradients. This paper introduces mixed ghost clipping, an efficient implementation of that operation for convolutional layers. The authors analyze its time and memory complexity alongside existing private-training algorithms, reporting efficiency improvements without affecting accuracy.

Experiments with large ResNet, VGG, and Vision Transformer models show private training with 1–10% additional memory use and less than twice the runtime of standard non-private training. For VGG19 on CIFAR10, the method runs three times faster than Opacus and supports an eighteenfold larger maximum batch size.

The paper also reports BEiT results at a privacy parameter of epsilon equal to one: 96.7% accuracy on CIFAR10 and 83.0% on CIFAR100, compared with previous best results of 94.8% and 67.4%. An accompanying privacy engine implements the method. The contribution links a costly low-level training operation to the practical feasibility of private training for larger vision models.
summary.tldr: Mixed ghost clipping reduces the time and memory overhead of differentially private vision-model training without affecting accuracy.

title: Scalable and Efficient Training of Large Convolutional Neural Networks with Differential Privacy

abstract: Quantum many-body physics simulation has important impacts on understanding fundamental science and has applications to quantum materials design and quantum technology. However, due to the exponentially growing size of the Hilbert space with respect to the particle number, a direct simulation is intractable. While representing quantum states with tensor networks and neural networks are the two state-of-the-art methods for approximate simulations, each has its own limitations in terms of expressivity and inductive bias. To address these challenges, we develop a novel architecture, Autoregressive Neural TensorNet (ANTN), which bridges tensor networks and autoregressive neural networks. We show that Autoregressive Neural TensorNet parameterizes normalized wavefunctions, allows for exact sampling, generalizes the expressivity of tensor networks and autoregressive neural networks, and inherits a variety of symmetries from autoregressive neural networks. We demonstrate our approach on quantum state learning as well as finding the ground state of the challenging 2D $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg model with different systems sizes and coupling parameters, outperforming both tensor networks and autoregressive neural networks. Our work opens up new opportunities for quantum many-body physics simulation, quantum technology design, and generative modeling in artificial intelligence.

paragraphs: Simulating a quantum system becomes difficult as its particle count grows because the space needed to describe its state expands exponentially. Tensor networks and neural networks provide approximate representations, but each brings different restrictions on what it can express and different structural preferences. This paper introduces Autoregressive Neural TensorNet, or ANTN, to combine these two approaches.

ANTN bridges tensor networks with autoregressive neural networks in a single architecture. The authors show that it represents normalized wavefunctions and supports exact sampling from its represented distribution. Its expressivity generalizes that of both component approaches, and it inherits a variety of symmetries from autoregressive networks. These properties connect representation flexibility with useful structure for quantum simulation.

The authors evaluate ANTN on quantum state learning and on finding ground states of the two-dimensional J1–J2 Heisenberg model across different system sizes and coupling parameters. It outperforms both tensor networks and autoregressive neural networks in these evaluations. Exact sampling is a property of the learned representation; the paper still concerns approximate simulation of the underlying quantum system.
summary.tldr: ANTN combines tensor networks and autoregressive neural networks to represent quantum states with exact sampling and improved empirical simulation performance.

title: ANTN: Bridging Autoregressive Neural Networks and Tensor Networks for Quantum Many-Body Simulation

abstract: We consider unconstrained minimization of smooth convex functions. We propose a novel variational perspective using forced Euler-Lagrange equation that allows for studying high-resolution ODEs. Through this, we obtain a faster convergence rate for gradient norm minimization using Nesterov's accelerated gradient method. Additionally, we show that Nesterov's method can be interpreted as a rate-matching discretization of an appropriately chosen high-resolution ODE. Finally, using the results from the new variational perspective, we propose a stochastic method for noisy gradients. Several numerical experiments compare and illustrate our stochastic algorithm with state of the art methods.

Through this, we obtain a faster convergence rate for gradient norm minimization using Nesterov's accelerated gradient method. Additionally, we show that Nesterov's method can be interpreted as a rate-matching discretization of an appropriately chosen high-resolution ODE. paragraphs: This paper studies how to minimize smooth convex functions without constraints. Its approach connects optimization algorithms, which move through discrete updates, with differential equations, which describe continuous motion. The authors introduce a variational perspective based on a forced Euler–Lagrange equation to study high-resolution ordinary differential equations. This provides a mathematical framework for examining the dynamics behind accelerated optimization.

Using that framework, the authors obtain a faster convergence rate for minimizing the gradient norm with Nesterov's accelerated gradient method. The gradient norm measures the size of the local slope, so reducing it concerns how quickly the algorithm approaches a point with little remaining slope. They also show that Nesterov's discrete updates can match the convergence rate of an appropriately selected high-resolution equation.

The authors then use these theoretical results to propose a stochastic method for settings with noisy gradients. Numerical experiments compare and illustrate this algorithm alongside state-of-the-art methods. The contribution therefore links a continuous mathematical description, a convergence result for an established algorithm, and the design of a method that accommodates gradient noise.
summary.tldr: A new variational framework explains accelerated optimization dynamics, improves a gradient-norm convergence result, and motivates an algorithm for noisy gradients.

title: A Variational Perspective on High-Resolution ODEs

abstract: The nonconvex formulation of the matrix completion problem has received significant attention in recent years due to its affordable complexity compared to the convex formulation. Gradient Descent (GD) is a simple yet efficient baseline algorithm for solving nonconvex optimization problems. The success of GD has been witnessed in many different problems in both theory and practice when it is combined with random initialization. However, previous works on matrix completion require either careful initialization or regularizers to prove the convergence of GD. In this paper, we study the rank-1 symmetric matrix completion and prove that GD converges to the ground truth when small random initialization is used. We show that in a logarithmic number of iterations, the trajectory enters the region where local convergence occurs. We provide an upper bound on the initialization size that is sufficient to guarantee the convergence, and show that a larger initialization can be used as more samples are available. We observe that the implicit regularization effect of GD plays a critical role in the analysis, and for the entire trajectory, it prevents each entry from becoming much larger than the others.

paragraphs: Matrix completion aims to recover a matrix from observed entries. Nonconvex formulations offer computational appeal, but previous convergence proofs for gradient descent have required careful initialization or explicit regularization. This paper studies the symmetric rank-one case and proves recovery of the ground truth from a sufficiently small random initialization.

The analysis follows the optimization trajectory before it reaches the region where local convergence applies. It shows that this region is entered within a logarithmic number of iterations. The authors also provide an upper bound on initialization size sufficient for convergence, and show that more observed samples allow a larger initialization.

A central mechanism is gradient descent's implicit regularization: throughout the trajectory, it prevents individual entries from becoming much larger than the others. This controlled behavior helps explain why the simple procedure can succeed without the additional safeguards used in earlier analyses. The result is specific to symmetric rank-one matrix completion, and the initialization bound is a sufficient condition rather than a claim that every larger initialization fails.
summary.tldr: For symmetric rank-one matrix completion, gradient descent provably recovers the ground truth from sufficiently small random initialization.

title: Rank-1 Matrix Completion with Gradient Descent and Small Random Initialization

abstract: The rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) recently empowered researchers to investigate hard mathematical problems which eluded traditional approaches for decades. Yet, the use of AI in Universal Algebra (UA)---one of the fields laying the foundations of modern mathematics---is still completely unexplored. This work proposes the first use of AI to investigate UA's conjectures with an equivalent equational and topological characterization. While topological representations would enable the analysis of such properties using graph neural networks, the limited transparency and brittle explainability of these models hinder their straightforward use to empirically validate existing conjectures or to formulate new ones. To bridge these gaps, we propose a general algorithm generating AI-ready datasets based on UA's conjectures, and introduce a novel neural layer to build fully interpretable graph networks. The results of our experiments demonstrate that interpretable graph networks: (i) enhance interpretability without sacrificing task accuracy, (ii) strongly generalize when predicting universal algebra's properties, (iii) generate simple explanations that empirically validate existing conjectures, and (iv) identify subgraphs suggesting the formulation of novel conjectures.

paragraphs: This paper applies AI to universal algebra conjectures that have both equational and topological descriptions. The topological view makes graph-based analysis possible, but ordinary graph neural networks can be difficult to interpret. For mathematical investigation, accurate predictions alone are insufficient: researchers also need explanations that can help assess existing conjectures or suggest new ones.

The authors develop an algorithm that generates datasets from these conjectures and introduce a neural layer for constructing fully interpretable graph networks. The two contributions connect mathematical problem formulation with a model designed to expose understandable structure. This makes interpretation part of the learning approach rather than relying solely on explanations added after a prediction.

Experiments report improved interpretability without sacrificing task accuracy, along with strong generalization when predicting universal algebra properties. The networks produce simple explanations that provide empirical support for existing conjectures and identify subgraphs suggesting new conjectures. These results describe a tool for mathematical exploration: empirical validation and candidate conjectures remain distinct from a mathematical proof that a statement always holds.
summary.tldr: Interpretable graph networks provide empirical support for universal algebra conjectures and identify structures that suggest new ones.

title: Interpretable Graph Networks Formulate Universal Algebra Conjectures

abstract: We study pure exploration with infinitely many bandit arms generated \iid from an unknown distribution. Our goal is to efficiently select a single high quality arm whose average reward is, with probability $1-\delta$, within $\varepsilon$ of being with the top $\eta$-fraction of arms; this is a natural adaptation of the classical PAC guarantee for infinite action sets. We consider both the fixed confidence and fixed budget settings, aiming respectively for optimal \emph{expected} and \emph{fixed} sample complexity.For fixed confidence, we give an algorithm with expected sample complexity $O\left(\frac{\log (1/\eta)\log (1/\delta)}{\eta\varepsilon^2}\right)$. This is optimal except for the $\log (1/\eta)$ factor, and the $\delta$-dependence closes a quadratic gap in the literature. For fixed budget, we show the asymptotically optimal sample complexity as $\delta\to 0$ is $c^{-1}\log(1/\delta)\big(\log\log(1/\delta)\big)^2$ to leading order; equivalently, the optimal failure probability with exactly $N$ samples decays as $\exp\big(-(1\pm o(1))\frac{cN}{\log^2 N}\big)$.The value of $c$ depends explicitly on the problem parameters (including the unknown arm distribution) through a certain Fisher information distance. Even the strictly super-linear dependence on $\log(1/\delta)$ was not known and resolves a question of Grossman-Moshkovitz (FOCS 2015).

paragraphs: When possible actions are unlimited, identifying the single best action is a different challenge from finding one that is reliably good. This paper studies the latter goal: select an action whose mean reward is within a chosen tolerance of the top fraction of actions. New actions are sampled independently from the same unknown distribution.

The authors distinguish two ways to control the search. With fixed confidence, sampling continues until a prescribed reliability target is met, and the concern is the expected number of samples. Their algorithm reaches a sample bound that is optimal apart from a logarithmic factor in the target fraction. Its dependence on failure probability improves a previously known quadratic gap.

With a fixed sampling budget, the optimal tradeoff is different. The paper establishes the leading asymptotic sample requirement as failure probability approaches zero, including an additional squared double-logarithmic factor. A constant determined by the problem and its unknown action distribution enters this expression through a Fisher information distance. These results clarify why expected sampling cost and a strict sample cap require distinct guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes nearly optimal expected sampling and asymptotically optimal fixed-budget guarantees for finding a high-quality action among infinitely many possibilities.

title: Asymptotically Optimal Quantile Pure Exploration for Infinite-Armed Bandits

abstract: The quality of training data impacts the performance of pre-trained large language models (LMs). Given a fixed budget of tokens, we study how to best select data that leads to good downstream model performance across tasks. We develop a new framework based on a simple hypothesis: just as humans acquire interdependent skills in a deliberate order, language models also follow a natural order when learning a set of skills from their training data. If such an order exists, it can be utilized for improved understanding of LMs and for data-efficient training. Using this intuition, our framework formalizes the notion of a skill and of an ordered set of skills in terms of the associated data. First, using both synthetic and real data, we demonstrate that these ordered skill sets exist, and that their existence enables more advanced skills to be learned with less data when we train on their prerequisite skills. Second, using our proposed framework, we introduce an online data sampling algorithm, Skill-It, over mixtures of skills for both continual pre-training and fine-tuning regimes, where the objective is to efficiently learn multiple skills in the former and an individual skill in the latter. On the LEGO synthetic in the continual pre-training setting, Skill-It obtains 37.5 points higher accuracy than random sampling. On the Natural Instructions dataset in the fine-tuning setting, Skill-It reduces the validation loss on the target skill by 13.6% versus training on data associated with the target skill itself. We apply our skills framework on the RedPajama dataset to continually pre-train a 3B-parameter LM, achieving higher accuracy on the LM Evaluation Harness with 1B tokens than the baseline approach of sampling uniformly over data sources with 3B tokens.

title: Skill-it! A data-driven skills framework for understanding and training language models

abstract: Recent neural architecture search (NAS) frameworks have been successful in finding optimal architectures for given conditions (e.g., performance or latency). However, they search for optimal architectures in terms of their performance on clean images only, while robustness against various types of perturbations or corruptions is crucial in practice. Although there exist several robust NAS frameworks that tackle this issue by integrating adversarial training into one-shot NAS, however, they are limited in that they only consider robustness against adversarial attacks and require significant computational resources to discover optimal architectures for a single task, which makes them impractical in real-world scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose a novel lightweight robust zero-cost proxy that considers the consistency across features, parameters, and gradients of both clean and perturbed images at the initialization state. Our approach facilitates an efficient and rapid search for neural architectures capable of learning generalizable features that exhibit robustness across diverse perturbations. The experimental results demonstrate that our proxy can rapidly and efficiently search for neural architectures that are consistently robust against various perturbations on multiple benchmark datasets and diverse search spaces, largely outperforming existing clean zero-shot NAS and robust NAS with reduced search cost.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search often selects networks for accuracy on clean images, even though deployed models may encounter many forms of perturbation or corruption. Existing robustness-focused searches can be computationally expensive and concentrate on adversarial attacks. This paper proposes a lightweight proxy for identifying architectures with broader robustness at a much lower search cost.

The proxy examines networks at initialization, comparing consistency across features, parameters, and gradients associated with clean and perturbed images. These signals are used to guide architecture selection before undertaking the expensive training involved in existing robust search methods. The intended target is an architecture capable of learning features that remain useful across different perturbations.

Experiments span multiple benchmark datasets and search spaces. The authors report that their proxy finds architectures with consistent robustness across varied perturbations and substantially outperforms existing clean zero-shot and robust search methods while reducing search cost. The findings support initialization-time consistency as a useful search signal in the tested settings, connecting efficient architecture selection with robustness beyond a single attack type.
summary.tldr: A lightweight initialization-time proxy guides architecture search toward robustness across diverse perturbations with reduced search cost.

title: Generalizable Lightweight Proxy for Robust NAS against Diverse Perturbations

abstract: Although we have witnessed great success of pre-trained models in natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision (CV), limited progress has been made for general time series analysis. Unlike NLP and CV where a unified model can be used to perform different tasks, specially designed approach still dominates in each time series analysis task such as classification, anomaly detection, forecasting, and few-shot learning. The main challenge that blocks the development of pre-trained model for time series analysis is the lack of a large amount of data for training. In this work, we address this challenge by leveraging language or CV models, pre-trained from billions of tokens, for time series analysis. Specifically, we refrain from altering the self-attention and feedforward layers of the residual blocks in the pre-trained language or image model. This model, known as the Frozen Pretrained Transformer (FPT), is evaluated through fine-tuning on all major types of tasks involving time series. Our results demonstrate that pre-trained models on natural language or images can lead to a comparable or state-of-the-art performance in all main time series analysis tasks, as illustrated in Figure1. We also found both theoretically and empirically that the self-attention module behaviors similarly to principle component analysis (PCA), an observation that helps explains how transformer bridges the domain gap and a crucial step towards understanding the universality of a pre-trained transformer. The code is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Pretrained-LM-for-TSForcasting-C561.

paragraphs: The paper explores whether models pretrained on language or images can provide a common foundation for time-series analysis. Tasks such as forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection often use separate specialized approaches. The authors identify the shortage of large-scale time-series training data as a barrier to developing a unified pretrained model.

Their Frozen Pretrained Transformer reuses models trained on billions of tokens while keeping the self-attention and feedforward layers in the residual blocks unchanged. They then evaluate the approach through fine-tuning across major time-series task types. This uses representations learned in other domains as a starting point for temporal data analysis.

The reported results are comparable to or better than the state of the art across the main task categories evaluated. The authors also find theoretical and empirical similarities between self-attention and principal component analysis. That observation offers an explanation for how pretrained Transformers can bridge domains, helping connect the practical transfer results with a proposed account of the shared processing behavior.
summary.tldr: Frozen language and vision Transformers transfer successfully to major time-series tasks, with attention behavior linked to principal component analysis.

title: One Fits All: Power General Time Series Analysis by Pretrained LM

abstract: We characterise the learning of a mixture of two clouds of data points with generic centroids via empirical risk minimisation in the high dimensional regime, under the assumptions of generic convex loss and convex regularisation. Each cloud of data points is obtained via a double-stochastic process, where the sample is obtained from a Gaussian distribution whose variance is itself a random parameter sampled from a scalar distribution $\varrho$. As a result, our analysis covers a large family of data distributions, including the case of power-law-tailed distributions with no covariance, and allows us to test recent ''Gaussian universality'' claims. We study the generalisation performance of the obtained estimator, we analyse the role of regularisation, and we analytically characterise the separability transition.

paragraphs: This paper studies classification when data have many features and may contain unusually extreme observations. It considers two clouds of points with general centers, and analyzes learning through empirical risk minimization under convex loss functions and convex regularization. These assumptions define the family of learning problems covered by the analysis.

The data model introduces randomness at two levels. Each observation is drawn from a Gaussian distribution, but its variance is itself sampled from another distribution. Changing that variance distribution produces a broad range of data behaviors, including power-law tails so heavy that a covariance matrix does not exist. This provides a framework for examining cases beyond ordinary Gaussian data.

Within this framework, the authors characterize generalization, investigate the effect of regularization, and analytically describe the transition to separability. The analysis also allows them to test claims of Gaussian universality: whether conclusions obtained for Gaussian features extend to other distributions. The contribution is a mathematical account of how classification behaves across this broader family.
summary.tldr: A random-variance data model enables analysis of high-dimensional classification across distributions that include very heavy tails.

title: Classification of Heavy-tailed Features in High Dimensions: a Superstatistical Approach

abstract: Relative entropy coding (REC) algorithms encode a sample from a target distribution $Q$ using a proposal distribution $P$ using as few bits as possible. Unlike entropy coding, REC does not assume discrete distributions and require quantisation.As such, it can be naturally integrated into communication pipelines such as learnt compression and differentially private federated learning. Unfortunately, despite their practical benefits, REC algorithms have not seen widespread application, due to their prohibitively slow runtimes or restrictive assumptions. In this paper, we make progress towards addressing these issues. We introduce Greedy Rejection Coding (GRC), which generalises the rejection sampling-based algorithm of Harsha et al. (2007) to arbitrary probability spaces and partitioning schemes. We first show that GRC terminates almost surely and returns unbiased samples from $Q$, and then focus on two variants of GRC, namely GRCS and GRCD. We show that for continuous $Q$ and $P$ over $\mathbb{R}$ with unimodal $dQ/dP$, the expected runtime of GRCS is upper bounded by $\beta D_{KL}(Q||P) + \mathcal{O}(1)$ where $\beta \approx 4.82$, and its expected codelength is optimal. This makes GRCS the first REC algorithm with guaranteed optimal runtime for this class of distributions, up to the multiplicative constant $\beta$. This significantly improves upon the previous state-of-the-art method, A* coding (Flamich et al., 2022). Under the same assumptions, we experimentally observe and conjecture that the expected runtime and codelength of GRCD are upper bounded by $D_{KL}(Q||P) + \mathcal{O}(1)$. Finally, we evaluate GRC in a compression pipeline with variational autoencoders on MNIST, and show that a modified training objective and a codelength-compression method can further improve compression efficiency.

paragraphs: Relative entropy coding communicates a sample from a target distribution using a proposal distribution while seeking a short bit representation. It can accommodate continuous distributions without quantization, making it relevant to learned compression and differentially private federated learning. However, slow execution and restrictive assumptions have hindered its use. The paper introduces Greedy Rejection Coding, or GRC, to address these obstacles.

GRC generalizes an earlier rejection-sampling approach to arbitrary probability spaces and partitioning schemes. The authors prove that it terminates almost surely and produces unbiased target samples. For continuous distributions on the real line with a unimodal target-to-proposal density ratio, the GRCS variant has optimal expected code length and a runtime bound proportional to KL divergence, with a multiplicative constant of approximately 4.82.

For GRCD, another variant, stronger runtime and code-length bounds are supported experimentally and conjectured under the same assumptions; they are not presented as established theorems. The authors also test GRC in a variational-autoencoder compression pipeline on MNIST. A modified training objective and an additional code-length compression method further improve efficiency, connecting the coding analysis to a working compression application.
summary.tldr: Greedy Rejection Coding improves relative entropy coding, with optimal-runtime guarantees for one variant under specific distributional assumptions.

title: Faster Relative Entropy Coding with Greedy Rejection Coding

abstract: This paper introduces a novel task called Cross Modal Generalization (CMG), which addresses the challenge of learning a unified discrete representation from paired multimodal data during pre-training. Then in downstream tasks, the model can achieve zero-shot generalization ability in other modalities when only one modal is labeled. Existing approaches in multimodal representation learning focus more on coarse-grained alignment or rely on the assumption that information from different modalities is completely aligned, which is impractical in real-world scenarios. To overcome this limitation, we propose \textbf{Uni-Code}, which contains two key contributions: the Dual Cross-modal Information Disentangling (DCID) module and the Multi-Modal Exponential Moving Average (MM-EMA). These methods facilitate bidirectional supervision between modalities and align semantically equivalent information in a shared discrete latent space, enabling fine-grained unified representation of multimodal sequences. During pre-training, we investigate various modality combinations, including audio-visual, audio-text, and the tri-modal combination of audio-visual-text. Extensive experiments on various downstream tasks, i.e., cross-modal event classification, localization, cross-modal retrieval, query-based video segmentation, and cross-dataset event localization, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods. The code is available at https://github.com/haihuangcode/CMG.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Cross Modal Generalization: pretrain on paired multimodal data, then use labels from just one modality to support downstream predictions in other modalities without additional labels there. The central challenge is learning a shared representation that preserves useful correspondences without assuming that every piece of information in one modality has an equivalent in another.

Uni-Code addresses this challenge through a shared discrete latent space. Its Dual Cross-modal Information Disentangling module and Multi-Modal Exponential Moving Average mechanism enable supervision in both directions between modalities. Together, they align semantically equivalent information and support detailed representations of multimodal sequences. This targets finer correspondences than a single broad alignment of whole inputs.

The authors investigate audio-visual, audio-text, and audio-visual-text pretraining. Experiments cover event classification and localization, cross-modal retrieval, query-based video segmentation, and event localization across datasets. The reported results support the effectiveness of the proposed representation methods across these tasks. The practical significance is that multimodal pretraining can make supervision supplied through one modality useful for another, reducing the need for separately labeled downstream data in each modality.
summary.tldr: Uni-Code learns shared discrete multimodal representations that support transfer to other modalities when only one has downstream labels.

title: Achieving Cross Modal Generalization with Multimodal Unified Representation

abstract: Fairness in machine learning has attracted increasing attention in recent years. The fairness methods improving algorithmic fairness for in-distribution data may not perform well under distribution shifts. In this paper, we first theoretically demonstrate the inherent connection between distribution shift, data perturbation, and model weight perturbation.Subsequently, we analyze the sufficient conditions to guarantee fairness (i.e., low demographic parity) for the target dataset, including fairness for the source dataset, and low prediction difference between the source and target datasets for each sensitive attribute group. Motivated by these sufficient conditions, we propose robust fairness regularization (RFR) by considering the worst case within the model weight perturbation ball for each sensitive attribute group. We evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed RFR algorithm on synthetic and real distribution shifts across various datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that RFR achieves better fairness-accuracy trade-off performance compared with several baselines. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/zhimengj0326/RFR_NeurIPS23}.

paragraphs: A model that meets a fairness objective on its training distribution may fail to do so when the data distribution changes. This paper studies how fairness can transfer from a source dataset to a target dataset, focusing on low demographic parity disparity. It begins by establishing theoretical connections among distribution changes, perturbations to data, and perturbations to model weights.

The analysis identifies sufficient conditions for target fairness. These include fairness on the source data and small differences between source and target predictions within each sensitive-attribute group. These conditions describe one route to a guarantee; they are not presented as requirements that every fair target model must satisfy.

The proposed robust fairness regularization, or RFR, uses this analysis to examine worst-case behavior within a ball of weight perturbations for each group. This turns the theoretical connection into a training objective. Across synthetic and real distribution shifts, the experiments report better fairness–accuracy trade-offs than several baselines, supporting the method's usefulness under the evaluated changes.
summary.tldr: RFR uses group-specific worst-case weight perturbations to improve empirical fairness–accuracy trade-offs under distribution shift.

title: Chasing Fairness Under Distribution Shift: A Model Weight Perturbation Approach

abstract: There is a growing interest in applying pre-trained large language models (LLMs) to planning problems. However, methods that use LLMs directly as planners are currently impractical due to several factors, including limited correctness of plans, strong reliance on feedback from interactions with simulators or even the actual environment, and the inefficiency in utilizing human feedback. In this work, we introduce a novel alternative paradigm that constructs an explicit world (domain) model in planning domain definition language (PDDL) and then uses it to plan with sound domain-independent planners. To address the fact that LLMs may not generate a fully functional PDDL model initially, we employ LLMs as an interface between PDDL and sources of corrective feedback, such as PDDL validators and humans. For users who lack a background in PDDL, we show that LLMs can translate PDDL into natural language and effectively encode corrective feedback back to the underlying domain model. Our framework not only enjoys the correctness guarantee offered by the external planners but also reduces human involvement by allowing users to correct domain models at the beginning, rather than inspecting and correcting (through interactive prompting) every generated plan as in previous work. On two IPC domains and a Household domain that is more complicated than commonly used benchmarks such as ALFWorld, we demonstrate that GPT-4 can be leveraged to produce high-quality PDDL models for over 40 actions, and the corrected PDDL models are then used to successfully solve 48 challenging planning tasks. Resources, including the source code, are released at: https://guansuns.github.io/pages/llm-dm.

paragraphs: This paper uses a large language model to construct an explicit description of a planning domain, then hands planning to a dedicated planner. The domain is written in PDDL, a language for specifying planning problems. This separates the work of describing how a world operates from finding a sequence of actions within that description.

Because the initial domain model may contain errors, the language model also mediates corrective feedback from validators and people. It can translate PDDL into natural language for users unfamiliar with the formalism and encode their corrections back into the model. Users can therefore repair a reusable domain description at the beginning instead of repeatedly correcting individual plans.

The framework inherits the correctness guarantees of sound external planners for planning with the supplied model. Across two IPC domains and a more complex Household domain, GPT-4 produces high-quality models covering over 40 actions. After correction, those models solve 48 challenging tasks, demonstrating how an editable world model can support repeated planning while reducing human involvement.
summary.tldr: LLMs build and help correct reusable PDDL world models, enabling sound external planners to solve tasks with less repeated human intervention.

title: Leveraging Pre-trained Large Language Models to Construct and Utilize World Models for Model-based Task Planning

abstract: Large text-to-image diffusion models have impressive capabilities in generating photorealistic images from text prompts. How to effectively guide or control these powerful models to perform different downstream tasks becomes an important open problem. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a principled finetuning method -- Orthogonal Finetuning (OFT), for adapting text-to-image diffusion models to downstream tasks. Unlike existing methods, OFT can provably preserve hyperspherical energy which characterizes the pairwise neuron relationship on the unit hypersphere. We find that this property is crucial for preserving the semantic generation ability of text-to-image diffusion models. To improve finetuning stability, we further propose Constrained Orthogonal Finetuning (COFT) which imposes an additional radius constraint to the hypersphere. Specifically, we consider two important finetuning text-to-image tasks: subject-driven generation where the goal is to generate subject-specific images given a few images of a subject and a text prompt, and controllable generation where the goal is to enable the model to take in additional control signals. We empirically show that our OFT framework outperforms existing methods in generation quality and convergence speed.

paragraphs: Adapting a text-to-image diffusion model requires changing its behavior while preserving the useful generation capabilities it already has. Orthogonal Finetuning, or OFT, approaches this through a geometric constraint on the model’s neurons. The paper focuses on preserving relationships within the network as it learns a downstream task.

OFT provably preserves hyperspherical energy, a quantity describing pairwise neuron relationships on a unit hypersphere. The authors find that this preservation is crucial for retaining semantic generation ability. They also introduce Constrained Orthogonal Finetuning, which adds a radius constraint to improve the stability of the adaptation process.

The method is studied in two settings: learning to generate a particular subject from a few example images and a text prompt, and enabling generation with additional control signals. In the reported experiments, OFT improves generation quality and convergence speed over existing methods. The geometric preservation is a formal property of the method; its benefits for generation are supported by the empirical comparisons in these adaptation tasks.
summary.tldr: Orthogonal Finetuning preserves a geometric measure of neuron relationships while adapting diffusion models, improving reported generation quality and convergence speed.

title: Controlling Text-to-Image Diffusion by Orthogonal Finetuning

abstract: Algorithms for playing in Stackelberg games have been deployed in real-world domains including airport security, anti-poaching efforts, and cyber-crime prevention. However, these algorithms often fail to take into consideration the additional information available to each player (e.g. traffic patterns, weather conditions, network congestion), a salient feature of reality which may significantly affect both players' optimal strategies. We formalize such settings as Stackelberg games with side information, in which both players observe an external context before playing. The leader commits to a (context-dependent) strategy, and the follower best-responds to both the leader's strategy and the context. We focus on the online setting in which a sequence of followers arrive over time, and the context may change from round-to-round. In sharp contrast to the non-contextual version, we show that it is impossible for the leader to achieve good performance (measured by regret) in the full adversarial setting. Motivated by our impossibility result, we show that no-regret learning is possible in two natural relaxations: the setting in which the sequence of followers is chosen stochastically and the sequence of contexts is adversarial, and the setting in which the sequence of contexts is stochastic and the sequence of followers is chosen by an adversary.

paragraphs: In a Stackelberg game, a leader commits to a strategy and a follower responds to it. Real decisions also depend on shared circumstances such as weather or network congestion. This paper incorporates that side information by allowing both players to observe a context before choosing their behavior.

The authors study repeated play with a sequence of followers and contexts that can change each round. The leader chooses a context-dependent strategy, and each follower best-responds to both that strategy and the observed context. They show that good regret performance is impossible when both sequences can be chosen adversarially, unlike the corresponding setting without context.

The paper then identifies two relaxations that allow no-regret learning. In one, followers are drawn stochastically while contexts remain adversarial. In the other, contexts are stochastic while followers are chosen adversarially. These results establish that which part of the environment has statistical regularity matters: either source of randomness can restore learnability in the respective setting despite adversarial variation in the other.
summary.tldr: Context makes fully adversarial Stackelberg learning impossible, but no-regret learning becomes possible when followers or contexts are stochastic.

title: Regret Minimization in Stackelberg Games with Side Information

abstract: In-context learning (ICL) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) are two common strategies for improving the performance of modern large language models (LLMs) on specific tasks. Despite their different natures, these strategies often lead to comparable performance gains. However, little is known about whether they induce similar representations inside LLMs. We approach this problem by analyzing the probability landscape of their hidden representations in the two cases. More specifically, we compare how LLMs solve the same question-answering task, finding that ICL and SFT create very different internal structures, in both cases undergoing a sharp transition in the middle of the network. In the first half of the network, ICL shapes interpretable representations hierarchically organized according to their semantic content. In contrast, the probability landscape obtained with SFT is fuzzier and semantically mixed. In the second half of the model, the fine-tuned representations develop probability modes that better encode the identity of answers, while less-defined peaks characterize the landscape of ICL representations. Our approach reveals the diverse computational strategies developed inside LLMs to solve the same task across different conditions, allowing us to make a step towards designing optimal methods to extract information from language models.

paragraphs: In-context learning and supervised fine-tuning can yield similar task improvements, but that does not establish that they organize information similarly inside a language model. This paper compares their hidden representations on the same question-answering task. It studies probability landscapes, using the organization of those representations to investigate the computational strategies associated with each approach.

The authors find markedly different internal structures, with both approaches showing a sharp transition around the middle of the network. In the first half, in-context learning produces interpretable representations arranged hierarchically by semantic content. Fine-tuning instead produces a less sharply organized landscape in which semantic information is more mixed.

In the second half, fine-tuned representations develop probability modes that encode answer identity more clearly, while the in-context-learning landscape has less distinct peaks. These observations show how similar improvements in task performance can accompany different internal organizations. The analysis offers a step toward choosing methods for extracting information from language models based on how their representations change across learning conditions.
summary.tldr: On the studied question-answering task, in-context learning and fine-tuning create different internal representation landscapes despite their potential for similar performance gains.

title: The Representation Landscape of Few-Shot Learning and Fine-Tuning in Large Language Models

abstract: Dense Associative Memories are high storage capacity variants of the Hopfield networks that are capable of storing a large number of memory patterns in the weights of the network of a given size. Their common formulations typically require storing each pattern in a separate set of synaptic weights, which leads to the increase of the number of synaptic weights when new patterns are introduced. In this work we propose an alternative formulation of this class of models using random features, commonly used in kernel methods. In this formulation the number of network's parameters remains fixed. At the same time, new memories can be added to the network by modifying existing weights. We show that this novel network closely approximates the energy function and dynamics of conventional Dense Associative Memories and shares their desirable computational properties.

paragraphs: Dense Associative Memories are variants of Hopfield networks designed to store many memory patterns. In common formulations, each stored pattern has its own set of synaptic weights. Adding memories therefore increases the number of weights, tying the model’s parameter count to the expanding collection of stored patterns.

This paper proposes a different formulation based on random features, a technique used in kernel methods. The network keeps a fixed number of parameters, and new memories are incorporated by changing existing weights. The important architectural shift is in how memories are represented: adding a pattern no longer requires adding a separate set of parameters.

The authors show that the resulting network closely approximates both the energy function and the dynamics of conventional Dense Associative Memories. It also shares their desirable computational properties. The result connects random-feature methods with associative memory and offers a fixed-parameter representation of this model family. The claim is about approximating the conventional models’ behavior while changing storage organization, rather than establishing an unlimited supply of perfectly recoverable memories.
summary.tldr: A random-feature formulation lets Dense Associative Memories add patterns by updating existing weights while closely approximating conventional models.

title: Dense Associative Memory Through the Lens of Random Features

abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated impressive capabilities in utilizing external tools and knowledge to boost accuracy and reduce hallucinations. However, developing prompting techniques that enable LLM agents to effectively use these tools and knowledge remains a heuristic and labor-intensive task. Here, we introduce AvaTaR, a novel and automated framework that optimizes an LLM agent to effectively leverage provided tools, improving performance on a given task. During optimization, we design a comparator module to iteratively deliver insightful and comprehensive prompts to the LLM agent by contrastively reasoning between positive and negative examples sampled from training data. We demon- strate AvaTaR on four complex multimodal retrieval datasets featuring textual, visual, and relational information, and three general question-answering (QA) datasets. We find AvaTaR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across all seven tasks, exhibiting strong generalization ability when applied to novel cases and achieving an average relative improvement of 14% on the Hit@1 metric for the retrieval datasets and 13% for the QA datasets. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/zou-group/avatar.
