paragraphs: AvaTaR tackles the manual effort involved in prompting language-model agents to use external tools effectively. Access to tools and knowledge can improve an agent’s answers, but deciding how to instruct the agent remains a separate challenge. The paper proposes an automated framework that improves tool use for a specified task.

Its central component is a comparator that reasons about positive and negative examples sampled from training data. By contrasting these examples, the comparator develops prompts intended to guide the agent toward more effective behavior. This process repeats during optimization, making the comparison of successful and unsuccessful examples a source of increasingly informative instructions.

The authors evaluate AvaTaR on four multimodal retrieval datasets involving text, images, and relational information, plus three question-answering datasets. They report improvements over state-of-the-art approaches on all seven tasks and strong generalization to new cases. Average relative gains are 14% in retrieval Hit@1 and 13% on the question-answering datasets. These results support contrastive prompt optimization as a practical method for improving tool-using agents.
summary.tldr: AvaTaR automatically improves tool-using agents by iteratively generating prompts from contrasts between positive and negative training examples.

title: AvaTaR: Optimizing LLM Agents for Tool Usage via Contrastive Reasoning

abstract: Machine unlearning (MU) empowers individuals with the `right to be forgotten' by removing their private or sensitive information encoded in machine learning models. However, it remains uncertain whether MU can be effectively applied to Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), particularly in scenarios of forgetting the leaked visual data of concepts. To overcome the challenge, we propose an efficient method, Single Image Unlearning (SIU), to unlearn the visual recognition of a concept by fine-tuning a single associated image for few steps. SIU consists of two key aspects: (i) Constructing Multifaceted fine-tuning data. We introduce four targets, based on which we construct fine-tuning data for the concepts to be forgotten; (ii) Joint training loss. To synchronously forget the visual recognition of concepts and preserve the utility of MLLMs, we fine-tune MLLMs through a novel Dual Masked KL-divergence Loss combined with Cross Entropy loss. Alongside our method, we establish MMUBench, a new benchmark for MU in MLLMs and introduce a collection of metrics for its evaluation. Experimental results on MMUBench show that SIU completely surpasses the performance of existing methods. Furthermore, we surprisingly find that SIU can avoid invasive membership inference attacks and jailbreak attacks. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to explore MU in MLLMs. We will release the code and benchmark in the near future.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove information already encoded in a trained model. This paper focuses on a multimodal version of that problem: making a model forget visual recognition of a particular concept. Single Image Unlearning, or SIU, uses one associated image and a few fine-tuning steps to pursue that goal efficiently.

The method constructs multifaceted fine-tuning data around four targets for the concept to be forgotten. Its training objective combines a Dual Masked KL-divergence loss with cross-entropy loss. These components are designed to support forgetting the targeted visual recognition while preserving the model's broader usefulness, making retention of utility part of the optimization rather than a separate concern.

The authors introduce MMUBench and evaluation metrics for unlearning in multimodal language models. On that benchmark, SIU outperforms existing methods, and the experiments also find that it can avoid membership inference and jailbreak attacks. These are reported empirical findings for the evaluated method and attacks. The contribution combines a low-data unlearning procedure with a benchmark for examining both forgetting and the continued utility of multimodal models.
summary.tldr: SIU uses one image and a few fine-tuning steps to reduce targeted visual recognition while preserving multimodal model utility.

title: Single Image Unlearning: Efficient Machine Unlearning in Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract: In the absence of class priors, recent deep clustering methods resort to data augmentation and pseudo-labeling strategies to generate supervision signals. Though achieved remarkable success, existing works struggle to discriminate hard samples at cluster boundaries, mining which is particularly challenging due to their unreliable cluster assignments. To break such a performance bottleneck, we propose incorporating user interaction to facilitate clustering instead of exhaustively mining semantics from the data itself. To be exact, we present Interactive Deep Clustering (IDC), a plug-and-play method designed to boost the performance of pre-trained clustering models with minimal interaction overhead. More specifically, IDC first quantitatively evaluates sample values based on hardness, representativeness, and diversity, where the representativeness avoids selecting outliers and the diversity prevents the selected samples from collapsing into a small number of clusters. IDC then queries the cluster affiliations of high-value samples in a user-friendly manner. Finally, it utilizes the user feedback to finetune the pre-trained clustering model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that IDC could remarkably improve the performance of various pre-trained clustering models, at the expense of low user interaction costs. The code could be accessed at pengxi.me.

paragraphs: Deep clustering methods often create their own supervision through data augmentation and estimated cluster labels. Samples near cluster boundaries remain difficult because their uncertain assignments make those supervision signals unreliable. This paper proposes using a small amount of user interaction to improve a pretrained clustering model at these difficult points.

Interactive Deep Clustering selects samples according to three properties: hardness, representativeness, and diversity. Hardness directs attention to difficult cases. Representativeness helps avoid spending interaction on outliers, while diversity prevents the selected examples from concentrating in only a few clusters. The system then asks users about the selected samples’ cluster affiliations and uses that feedback to fine-tune the model.

Experiments show substantial improvements across several pretrained clustering models with low interaction costs. The approach matters because it treats the choice of questions as part of the learning method: difficult examples are useful only when the selected set also represents the data and covers different clusters. Its plug-and-play design allows user feedback to refine models that have already been trained.
summary.tldr: Interactive Deep Clustering improves pretrained clustering models by requesting user feedback on difficult, representative, and diverse samples.

title: Interactive Deep Clustering via Value Mining

abstract: Online continual learning (OCL) requires the models to learn from constant, endless streams of data. While significant efforts have been made in this field, most were focused on mitigating the \textit{catastrophic forgetting} issue to achieve better classification ability, at the cost of a much heavier training workload. They overlooked that in real-world scenarios, e.g., in high-speed data stream environments, data do not pause to accommodate slow models. In this paper, we emphasize that \textit{model throughput}-- defined as the maximum number of training samples that a model can process within a unit of time -- is equally important. It directly limits how much data a model can utilize and presents a challenging dilemma for current methods. With this understanding, we revisit key challenges in OCL from both empirical and theoretical perspectives, highlighting two critical issues beyond the well-documented catastrophic forgetting: (\romannumeral1) Model's ignorance: the single-pass nature of OCL challenges models to learn effective features within constrained training time and storage capacity, leading to a trade-off between effective learning and model throughput; (\romannumeral2) Model's myopia: the local learning nature of OCL on the current task leads the model to adopt overly simplified, task-specific features and \textit{excessively sparse classifier}, resulting in the gap between the optimal solution for the current task and the global objective. To tackle these issues, we propose the Non-sparse Classifier Evolution framework (NsCE) to facilitate effective global discriminative feature learning with minimal time cost. NsCE integrates non-sparse maximum separation regularization and targeted experience replay techniques with the help of pre-trained models, enabling rapid acquisition of new globally discriminative features. Extensive experiments demonstrate the substantial improvements of our framework in performance, throughput and real-world practicality.

paragraphs: Online continual learning must keep up with a stream that does not stop while a model trains. This paper argues that preventing forgetting is only part of the problem: training throughput determines how many arriving examples the model can actually use. More expensive learning procedures can therefore sacrifice access to data even when they improve retention.

The authors identify two further challenges. Ignorance describes difficulty learning effective features from a single pass under limited time and storage. Myopia describes learning features and an excessively sparse classifier suited to the current task but poorly aligned with the overall objective. Their empirical and theoretical analysis examines these issues alongside forgetting.

The proposed Non-sparse Classifier Evolution framework combines non-sparse maximum-separation regularization with targeted experience replay and pretrained models. It aims to acquire features that distinguish classes across tasks while adding little training time. Experiments report substantial improvements in performance, throughput, and practical applicability. These findings support evaluating continual learners by both the quality of what they learn and their ability to process the available stream.
summary.tldr: NsCE addresses limited feature learning and task-local myopia alongside forgetting, improving reported accuracy and throughput in online continual learning.

title: Forgetting, Ignorance or Myopia: Revisiting Key Challenges in Online Continual Learning

abstract: We analyze the sample complexity of full-batch Gradient Descent (GD) in the setup of non-smooth Stochastic Convex Optimization. We show that the generalization error of GD, with common choice of hyper-parameters, can be $\tilde \Theta(d/m+1/\sqrt{m})$, where d is the dimension and m is the sample size. This matches the sample complexity of \emph{worst-case} empirical risk minimizers. That means that, in contrast with other algorithms, GD has no advantage over naive ERMs. Our bound follows from a new generalization bound that depends on both the dimension as well as the learning rate and number of iterations. Our bound also shows that, for general hyper-parameters, when the dimension is strictly larger than number of samples, $T=\Omega(1/\epsilon^4)$ iterations are necessary to avoid overfitting. This resolves an open problem by Schlisserman et al.23 and Amir er Al.21, and improves over previous lower bounds that demonstrated that the sample size must be at least square root of the dimension.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much training data full-batch gradient descent needs to generalize in non-smooth stochastic convex optimization. The distinction between fitting the observed sample and performing well on the underlying distribution is central. The analysis focuses on how dimension, sample size, learning rate, and iteration count jointly affect that distinction.

For common hyperparameter choices, the authors show that generalization error can scale as d/m + 1/√m, up to logarithmic factors, where d is dimension and m is sample size. This matches the sample complexity of worst-case empirical risk minimizers. In this setting, gradient descent therefore offers no better worst-case sample complexity than simply minimizing empirical risk.

A new bound also treats general hyperparameters. When dimension exceeds sample size, it establishes a necessary iteration count of order at least 1/ε⁴ to avoid overfitting at the target accuracy scale. This strengthens earlier lower bounds and resolves an open problem. The conclusions concern the specified non-smooth convex setting and expose how optimization choices interact with statistical generalization.
summary.tldr: In non-smooth stochastic convex optimization, full-batch gradient descent can match worst-case empirical risk minimizers’ sample complexity rather than improve it.

title: The Sample Complexity of Gradient Descent in Stochastic Convex Optimization

abstract: Data collection is often difficult in critical fields such as medicine, physics, and chemistry, yielding typically only small tabular datasets. However, classification methods tend to struggle with these small datasets, leading to poor predictive performance. Increasing the training set with additional synthetic data, similar to data augmentation in images, is commonly believed to improve downstream tabular classification performance. However, current tabular generative methods that learn either the joint distribution $ p(\mathbf{x}, y) $ or the class-conditional distribution $ p(\mathbf{x} \mid y) $ often overfit on small datasets, resulting in poor-quality synthetic data, usually worsening classification performance compared to using real data alone. To solve these challenges, we introduce TabEBM, a novel class-conditional generative method using Energy-Based Models (EBMs). Unlike existing tabular methods that use a shared model to approximate all class-conditional densities, our key innovation is to create distinct EBM generative models for each class, each modelling its class-specific data distribution individually. This approach creates robust energy landscapes, even in ambiguous class distributions. Our experiments show that TabEBM generates synthetic data with higher quality and better statistical fidelity than existing methods. When used for data augmentation, our synthetic data consistently leads to improved classification performance across diverse datasets of various sizes, especially small ones. Code is available at https://github.com/andreimargeloiu/TabEBM.

paragraphs: Small tabular datasets can make classification difficult, especially in fields where collecting observations is costly. Generating synthetic rows could help, but a generator trained on little data may overfit and produce examples that reduce classification accuracy. TabEBM addresses this problem with an approach that models each class separately.

The method builds a distinct energy-based generative model for every class, with each model learning its own class-specific data distribution. This differs from using one shared model to approximate all class-conditional distributions. The authors describe the resulting energy landscapes as robust even when class distributions are ambiguous, making the separation between class-specific generators central to the method.

Experiments report higher-quality synthetic data and better statistical fidelity than existing methods. Adding these generated examples to training data consistently improves classification across the evaluated datasets and sizes, with particular benefits for small datasets. The findings support separate class-specific energy models as a useful way to generate augmentation data when limited observations make shared generative modeling difficult.
summary.tldr: TabEBM trains a separate energy-based generator for each class to produce synthetic tabular data that improves classification, especially on small datasets.

title: TabEBM: A Tabular Data Augmentation Method with Distinct Class-Specific Energy-Based Models

abstract: This paper studies the scaling behavior of state-space models (SSMs) and their structured variants, such as Mamba, that have recently arisen in popularity as alternatives to transformer-based neural network architectures. Specifically, we focus on the capability of SSMs to learn features as their network width approaches infinity. Our findings reveal that established scaling rules, such as the Maximal Update Parameterization, fail to support feature learning as these models cannot be represented in the form of Tensor Programs. Additionally, we demonstrate that spectral scaling conditions, shown to be effective for feature learning in a host of other architectures, do not hold the same implications for SSMs. Through a detailed signal propagation analysis in SSMs, both forward and backward, we identify the appropriate scaling necessary for non-trivial feature evolution in the infinite-width limit. Our proposed scaling shows behavior akin to the Maximal Update Parameterization, such as improved stability, better generalization, and transferability of optimal hyper-parameters from small to large scale SSMs.

paragraphs: This paper examines how state-space models and structured variants such as Mamba should scale as network width grows. Its central question is whether their internal features continue to evolve meaningfully during training in the infinite-width limit. Answering this requires scaling rules suited to the architecture’s particular signal propagation.

The authors find that established rules, including Maximal Update Parameterization, fail to support feature learning for these models. They connect this failure to the models’ inability to fit the Tensor Programs framework. They also show that spectral scaling conditions useful for other architectures do not carry the same implications here. Familiar scaling criteria therefore need fresh analysis in the state-space setting.

By studying both forward signal propagation and backward training signals, the paper identifies scaling that supports nontrivial feature evolution at infinite width. The proposed scaling exhibits improved stability, better generalization, and transfer of optimal hyperparameters from smaller to larger state-space models. These findings connect an architecture-specific theoretical analysis with behaviors that matter when scaling model training.
summary.tldr: An analysis of state-space model signals yields scaling rules that preserve feature learning where established parameterizations fail.

title: On Feature Learning in Structured State Space Models

abstract: Recent advancements in Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) have shown promising results in mathematical reasoning within visual contexts, with models exceeding human-level performance on existing benchmarks such as MathVista. However, we observe significant limitations in the diversity of questions and breadth of subjects covered by these benchmarks. To address this issue, we present the MATH-Vision (MATH-V) dataset, a meticulously curated collection of 3,040 high-quality mathematical problems with visual contexts sourced from real math competitions. Spanning 16 distinct mathematical disciplines and graded across 5 levels of difficulty, our dataset provides a comprehensive and diverse set of challenges for evaluating the mathematical reasoning abilities of LMMs. Through extensive experimentation, we unveil a notable performance gap between current LMMs and human performance on \datasetname, underscoring the imperative for further advancements in LMMs. Moreover, our detailed categorization allows for a thorough error analysis of LMMs, offering valuable insights to guide future research and development. The dataset is released at [MathLLMs/MathVision](https://huggingface.co/datasets/MathLLMs/MathVision)

paragraphs: Strong results on existing visual mathematics benchmarks can leave uncertainty about how broadly a model reasons. The authors argue that limited question diversity and subject coverage make some existing evaluations incomplete. They introduce MATH-Vision, also called MATH-V, to assess mathematical reasoning that depends on visual context across a wider range of problems.

The dataset contains 3,040 problems drawn from actual mathematics competitions. Its organization covers 16 mathematical disciplines and five difficulty levels. This structure makes it possible to examine performance by mathematical area and challenge level, rather than relying only on one overall result. The visual contexts are part of the mathematical tasks that the models must solve.

The evaluation finds a notable gap between current large multimodal models and human performance on MATH-V. This contrasts with the strong performance reported on some existing benchmarks and shows that the new collection remains challenging. The detailed categories also support error analysis, helping researchers identify where failures occur and use those patterns to guide further work on multimodal mathematical reasoning.
summary.tldr: MATH-Vision evaluates visual mathematical reasoning with 3,040 competition problems and reveals a notable gap between tested models and humans.

title: Measuring Multimodal Mathematical Reasoning with MATH-Vision Dataset

abstract: Optimization of convex functions under stochastic zeroth-order feedback has been a major and challenging question in online learning. In this work, we consider the problem of optimizing second-order smooth and strongly convex functions where the algorithm is only accessible to noisy evaluations of the objective function it queries. We provide the first tight characterization for the rate of the minimax simple regret by developing matching upper and lower bounds. We propose an algorithm that features a combination of a bootstrapping stage and a mirror-descent stage. Our main technical innovation consists of a sharp characterization for the spherical-sampling gradient estimator under higher-order smoothness conditions, which allows the algorithm to optimally balance the bias-variance tradeoff, and a new iterative method for the bootstrapping stage, which maintains the performance for unbounded Hessian.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization when an algorithm can query noisy function values but cannot directly access derivatives. Its setting assumes strong convexity and second-order smoothness, with the title specifying a Lipschitz Hessian. The main question is how accurately an algorithm can identify a good solution from this restricted, noisy feedback.

The authors give matching upper and lower bounds for the minimax simple-regret rate. The upper bound describes performance an algorithm can achieve, while the lower bound establishes the corresponding worst-case difficulty. Their agreement provides a tight characterization of the rate within the stated problem setting. The proposed algorithm combines an initial bootstrapping stage with a mirror-descent stage.

A key technical result sharply characterizes a gradient estimator based on spherical sampling under higher-order smoothness. This lets the algorithm balance estimation bias against variance optimally for the analysis. A new iterative bootstrapping method also maintains performance when the Hessian is unbounded. The contribution therefore combines a characterization of fundamental sample requirements with an algorithm designed to attain them.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes matching minimax regret bounds and an attaining algorithm for strongly convex, second-order-smooth optimization using only noisy function evaluations.

title: Stochastic Zeroth-Order Optimization under Strongly Convexity and Lipschitz Hessian: Minimax Sample Complexity

abstract: Domain adaptive object detection (DAOD) aims to generalize detectors trained on an annotated source domain to an unlabelled target domain.As the visual-language models (VLMs) can provide essential general knowledge on unseen images, freezing the visual encoder and inserting a domain-agnostic adapter can learn domain-invariant knowledge for DAOD.However, the domain-agnostic adapter is inevitably biased to the source domain.It discards some beneficial knowledge discriminative on the unlabelled domain, \ie domain-specific knowledge of the target domain.To solve the issue, we propose a novel Domain-Aware Adapter (DA-Ada) tailored for the DAOD task.The key point is exploiting domain-specific knowledge between the essential general knowledge and domain-invariant knowledge.DA-Ada consists of the Domain-Invariant Adapter (DIA) for learning domain-invariant knowledge and the Domain-Specific Adapter (DSA) for injecting the domain-specific knowledge from the information discarded by the visual encoder.Comprehensive experiments over multiple DAOD tasks show that DA-Ada can efficiently infer a domain-aware visual encoder for boosting domain adaptive object detection.Our code is available at https://github.com/Therock90421/DA-Ada.

paragraphs: Domain adaptive object detection transfers a detector from a labeled source domain to a target domain without labels. Pretrained vision-language models supply general visual knowledge, and adapters can learn features shared across domains while keeping the visual encoder frozen. The paper argues that a domain-agnostic adapter remains biased toward the source and can discard information useful for distinguishing target-domain objects.

DA-Ada separates adaptation into two complementary components. The Domain-Invariant Adapter learns knowledge that transfers across domains. The Domain-Specific Adapter injects domain-specific information from what the visual encoder discards. Together, they aim to retain useful target-domain distinctions alongside the general knowledge and shared features that support transfer.

The approach matters because successful adaptation may require preserving differences as well as finding similarities. Experiments across multiple domain adaptive detection tasks show that DA-Ada can efficiently produce a domain-aware visual encoder that improves detection. The reported findings support combining shared and domain-specific knowledge when adapting to an unlabeled target.
summary.tldr: DA-Ada combines shared and domain-specific adapters to improve object detection in unlabeled target domains.

title: DA-Ada: Learning Domain-Aware Adapter for Domain Adaptive Object Detection

abstract: For constrained, not necessarily monotone submodular maximization, all known approximation algorithms with ratio greater than $1/e$ require continuous ideas, such as queries to the multilinear extension of a submodular function and its gradient, which are typically expensive to simulate with the original set function. For combinatorial algorithms, the best known approximation ratios for both size and matroid constraint are obtained by a simple randomized greedy algorithm of Buchbinder et al. [9]: $1/e \approx 0.367$ for size constraint and $0.281$ for the matroid constraint in $\mathcal O (kn)$ queries, where $k$ is the rank of the matroid. In this work, we develop the first combinatorial algorithms to break the $1/e$ barrier: we obtain approximation ratio of $0.385$ in $\mathcal O (kn)$ queries to the submodular set function for size constraint, and $0.305$ for a general matroid constraint. These are achieved by guiding the randomized greedy algorithm with a fast local search algorithm. Further, we develop deterministic versions of these algorithms, maintaining the same ratio and asymptotic time complexity. Finally, we develop a deterministic, nearly linear time algorithm with ratio $0.377$.

paragraphs: The paper studies choosing a valuable subset under constraints when the objective is submodular and need not improve whenever an item is added. Approximation ratios express how much of the optimal value an algorithm guarantees. Previously, ratios above 1/e required continuous techniques whose evaluations could be expensive to simulate using the original set function.

The authors guide randomized greedy selection with a fast local search procedure. Under a size constraint, the resulting combinatorial algorithm guarantees a ratio of 0.385 using O(kn) set-function queries, exceeding the earlier 1/e guarantee of about 0.367. For general matroid constraints, they obtain 0.305, improving the previous combinatorial ratio of 0.281.

They also construct deterministic versions retaining the same ratios and asymptotic time complexity, plus a deterministic nearly linear-time algorithm with ratio 0.377. The central advance is that discrete combinatorial methods can cross the 1/e threshold under the stated size constraint. The separate matroid result improves its corresponding guarantee without claiming to cross that threshold.
summary.tldr: Local-search guidance lets combinatorial submodular maximization exceed 1/e under size constraints and improve guarantees under matroid constraints.

title: Discretely beyond $1/e$: Guided Combinatorial Algortihms for Submodular Maximization

abstract: While widespread access to the Internet and the rapid advancement of generative models boost people's creativity and productivity, the risk of encountering inappropriate or harmful content also increases. To address the aforementioned issue, researchers managed to incorporate several harmful contents datasets with machine learning methods to detect harmful concepts. However, existing harmful datasets are curated by the presence of a narrow range of harmful objects, and only cover real harmful content sources. This restricts the generalizability of methods based on such datasets and leads to the potential misjudgment in certain cases. Therefore, we propose a comprehensive and extensive harmful dataset, **VHD11K**, consisting of 10,000 images and 1,000 videos, crawled from the Internet and generated by 4 generative models, across a total of 10 harmful categories covering a full spectrum of harmful concepts with non-trival definition. We also propose a novel annotation framework by formulating the annotation process as a multi-agent Visual Question Answering (VQA) task, having 3 different VLMs "debate" about whether the given image/video is harmful, and incorporating the in-context learning strategy in the debating process. Therefore, we can ensure that the VLMs consider the context of the given image/video and both sides of the arguments thoroughly before making decisions, further reducing the likelihood of misjudgments in edge cases. Evaluation and experimental results demonstrate that (1) the great alignment between the annotation from our novel annotation framework and those from human, ensuring the reliability of VHD11K;(2) our full-spectrum harmful dataset successfully identifies the inability of existing harmful content detection methods to detect extensive harmful contents and improves the performance of existing harmfulness recognition methods;(3) our dataset outperforms the baseline dataset, SMID, as evidenced by the superior improvement in harmfulness recognition methods.The entire dataset is publicly available: https://huggingface.co/datasets/denny3388/VHD11K

paragraphs: Recognizing harmful visual content requires attention to context, not just the presence of a small set of objects. This paper introduces VHD11K to broaden the content covered by harmfulness datasets. It contains 10,000 images and 1,000 videos across 10 harmful categories, combining Internet material with outputs from four generative models.

The authors also propose an annotation process framed as visual question answering. Three vision-language models debate whether an image or video is harmful, with in-context learning incorporated into that process. The aim is to consider contextual evidence and competing interpretations before assigning a label, reducing misjudgments in ambiguous cases.

The evaluation reports strong agreement between this annotation framework and human judgments. The dataset also exposes gaps in existing harmful-content detectors and improves recognition methods, with larger improvements than the SMID baseline dataset. These findings support both the annotation approach and the value of broader training and evaluation coverage, including generated content and harmful concepts that require contextual interpretation.
summary.tldr: VHD11K combines diverse real and generated visual content with multi-model contextual annotation to improve harmfulness recognition.

title: T2Vs Meet VLMs: A Scalable Multimodal Dataset for Visual Harmfulness Recognition

abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have recently shown outstanding capabilities in modeling complex image distributions, making them expressive image priors for solving Bayesian inverse problems. However, most existing DM-based methods rely on approximations in the generative process to be generic to different inverse problems, leading to inaccurate sample distributions that deviate from the target posterior defined within the Bayesian framework. To harness the generative power of DMs while avoiding such approximations, we propose a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that performs posterior sampling for general inverse problems by reducing it to sampling the posterior of a Gaussian denoising problem. Crucially, we leverage a general DM formulation as a unified interface that allows for rigorously solving the denoising problem with a range of state-of-the-art DMs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on six inverse problems (three linear and three nonlinear), including a real-world black hole imaging problem. Experimental results indicate that our proposed method offers more accurate reconstructions and posterior estimation compared to existing DM-based imaging inverse methods.

paragraphs: Image reconstruction from indirect measurements can have multiple plausible answers. Bayesian inverse methods describe this uncertainty through a posterior distribution, combining measurement evidence with prior knowledge about images. Diffusion models provide expressive image priors, but the authors identify a problem with many existing approaches: approximations used for flexibility can distort the distribution of reconstructed samples.

The paper proposes a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that reduces posterior sampling for general inverse problems to posterior sampling for Gaussian denoising. A general formulation of diffusion models provides a common interface for rigorously solving that denoising problem. This allows the method to use a range of diffusion models while avoiding the generative approximations targeted by the paper.

Evaluation covers six inverse problems, split between three linear and three nonlinear cases, including real-world black hole imaging. The authors report more accurate reconstructions and posterior estimates than the diffusion-based imaging methods compared. The contribution concerns both producing convincing reconstructed images and better representing the range of possibilities supported by the Bayesian formulation.
summary.tldr: A Monte Carlo method uses diffusion models through Gaussian denoising to improve Bayesian image reconstruction and posterior estimation.

title: Principled Probabilistic Imaging using Diffusion Models as Plug-and-Play Priors

abstract: Deep learning-based image stitching pipelines are typically divided into three cascading stages: registration, fusion, and rectangling. Each stage requires its own network training and is tightly coupled to the others, leading to error propagation and posing significant challenges to parameter tuning and system stability. This paper proposes the Simple and Robust Stitcher (SRStitcher), which revolutionizes the image stitching pipeline by simplifying the fusion and rectangling stages into a unified inpainting model, requiring no model training or fine-tuning. We reformulate the problem definitions of the fusion and rectangling stages and demonstrate that they can be effectively integrated into an inpainting task. Furthermore, we design the weighted masks to guide the reverse process in a pre-trained large-scale diffusion model, implementing this integrated inpainting task in a single inference. Through extensive experimentation, we verify the interpretability and generalization capabilities of this unified model, demonstrating that SRStitcher outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both performance and stability.

paragraphs: Image stitching commonly uses three successive stages: aligning images, fusing their content, and producing a rectangular result. When each stage has its own trained network, errors can propagate through the sequence, and the coupled components become difficult to tune. SRStitcher simplifies the latter two stages by expressing them as a single inpainting problem.

The authors reformulate fusion and rectangling so that a pretrained diffusion model can perform both together. Weighted masks guide the model's reverse generation process, directing how the integrated inpainting task is carried out. The method needs no additional model training or fine-tuning and completes the combined task in one inference.

This changes the organization of the stitching pipeline: two interacting processing stages become one coordinated operation, while registration remains a separate part of the setup. Extensive experiments support the unified model's interpretability and generalization, and report better performance and stability than state-of-the-art methods. The findings show that reusing a pretrained generative model can simplify this portion of stitching while improving the evaluated outputs.
summary.tldr: SRStitcher combines image fusion and rectangling into one guided diffusion-inpainting task without additional training.

title: Reconstructing the Image Stitching Pipeline: Integrating Fusion and Rectangling into a Unified Inpainting Model

abstract: Time series data are essential in a wide range of machine learning (ML) applications. However, temporal data are often scarce or highly sensitive, limiting data sharing and the use of data-intensive ML methods. A possible solution to this problem is the generation of synthetic datasets that resemble real data. In this work, we introduce Time Series Generative Modeling (TSGM), an open-source framework for the generative modeling and evaluation of synthetic time series datasets. TSGM includes a broad repertoire of machine learning methods: generative models, probabilistic, simulation-based approaches, and augmentation techniques. The framework enables users to evaluate the quality of the produced data from different angles: similarity, downstream effectiveness, predictive consistency, diversity, fairness, and privacy. TSGM is extensible and user-friendly, which allows researchers to rapidly implement their own methods and compare them in a shareable environment. The framework has been tested on open datasets and in production and proved to be beneficial in both cases. https://github.com/AlexanderVNikitin/tsgm

paragraphs: Time-series data are important for many machine learning applications, but limited availability and sensitivity can make them difficult to share or use at scale. Generating synthetic sequences that resemble real observations is one possible response. TSGM provides an open-source framework for both creating these datasets and evaluating their quality.

The framework includes generative machine learning models, probabilistic approaches, simulation-based methods, and data augmentation techniques. It also evaluates several distinct properties: similarity to real data, usefulness for downstream tasks, predictive consistency, diversity, fairness, and privacy. These dimensions make evaluation broader than checking whether generated sequences merely look like the original data.

TSGM is designed to be extensible so researchers can implement their own methods and compare them in a shared environment. The authors report that it has been useful in tests on open datasets and in production. Its contribution is therefore a common workflow spanning generation, evaluation, and comparison, helping users investigate which methods and data properties matter for their particular application.
summary.tldr: TSGM provides an extensible toolkit for generating synthetic time series and evaluating their utility, similarity, diversity, fairness, and privacy.

title: TSGM: A Flexible Framework for Generative Modeling of Synthetic Time Series

abstract: We propose a novel and general method to learn Bregman divergences from raw high-dimensional data that measure similarity between images in pixel space. As a prototypical application, we learn divergences that consider real-world corruptions of images (e.g., blur) as close to the original and noisy perturbations as far, even if in $L^p$-distance the opposite holds. We also show that the learned Bregman divergence excels on datasets of human perceptual similarity judgment, suggesting its utility in a range of applications. We then define adversarial attacks by replacing the projected gradient descent (PGD) with the mirror descent associated with the learned Bregman divergence, and use them to improve the state-of-the-art in robustness through adversarial training for common image corruptions. In particular, for the contrast corruption that was found problematic in prior work we achieve an accuracy that exceeds the $L^p$- and the LPIPS-based adversarially trained neural networks by a margin of 27.16\% on the CIFAR-10-C corruption data set.

paragraphs: Numerical distance between image pixels does not always reflect the kind of similarity useful for a task. A blurred image can remain recognizably close to its original even when a conventional distance measure ranks a noisy perturbation as closer. This paper learns Bregman divergences directly from high-dimensional data to express a different notion of image similarity.

In the demonstrated application, the learned divergence treats common corruptions such as blur as close to the original and noisy perturbations as far away. It also performs well on datasets of human perceptual similarity judgments. The authors then use the learned divergence to define adversarial attacks, replacing projected gradient descent with the corresponding mirror descent procedure.

Training with these attacks improves reported robustness to common image corruptions. For contrast corruption on CIFAR-10-C, the authors report an accuracy advantage of 27.16% over Lp-based and LPIPS-based adversarially trained networks. The results connect learning a suitable image geometry with constructing training attacks that improve robustness in the evaluated corruption setting.
summary.tldr: Learned Bregman divergences provide image similarity measures that support adversarial training with improved robustness to common corruptions.

title: Learning Bregman Divergences with Application to Robustness

abstract: Given the damping factor $\alpha$ and precision tolerance $\epsilon$, \citet{andersen2006local} introduced Approximate Personalized PageRank (APPR), the \textit{de facto local method} for approximating the PPR vector, with runtime bounded by $\Theta(1/(\alpha\epsilon))$ independent of the graph size. Recently, Fountoulakis \& Yang asked whether faster local algorithms could be developed using $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/(\sqrt{\alpha}\epsilon))$ operations. By noticing that APPR is a local variant of Gauss-Seidel, this paper explores the question of *whether standard iterative solvers can be effectively localized*. We propose to use the *locally evolving set process*, a novel framework to characterize the algorithm locality, and demonstrate that many standard solvers can be effectively localized. Let $\overline{\operatorname{vol}}{ (\mathcal S_t)}$ and $\overline{\gamma_t}$ be the running average of volume and the residual ratio of active nodes $\textstyle \mathcal{S_t}$ during the process. We show $\overline{\operatorname{vol}}{ (\mathcal S_t)}/\overline{\gamma_t} \leq 1/\epsilon$ and prove APPR admits a new runtime bound $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\overline{\operatorname{vol}}(\mathcal S_t)/(\alpha\overline{\gamma_t}))$ mirroring the actual performance. Furthermore, when the geometric mean of residual reduction is $\Theta(\sqrt{\alpha})$, then there exists $c \in (0,2)$ such that the local Chebyshev method has runtime $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\overline{\operatorname{vol}}(\mathcal{S_t})/(\sqrt{\alpha}(2-c)))$ without the monotonicity assumption. Numerical results confirm the efficiency of this novel framework and show up to a hundredfold speedup over corresponding standard solvers on real-world graphs.

This paper observes that it is also a local version of the Gauss-Seidel iterative solver. That connection motivates a broader question: can other standard iterative methods concentrate their work on locally active parts of a graph?

For a local Chebyshev method, the faster runtime guarantee is conditional on the geometric mean of residual reduction scaling as the square root of the damping factor. The result does not require a monotonicity assumption. Numerical experiments on real-world graphs show efficiency gains, including speedups of up to one hundred times over corresponding standard solvers.
summary.tldr: A framework for localizing iterative solvers yields refined runtime bounds and substantial empirical speedups on graph problems.

title: Iterative Methods via Locally Evolving Set Process

abstract: Gradient-based optimization methods have shown remarkable empirical success, yet their theoretical generalization properties remain only partially understood. In this paper, we establish a generalization bound for gradient flow that aligns with the classical Rademacher complexity bounds for kernel methods—specifically those based on the RKHS norm and kernel trace—through a data-dependent kernel called the loss path kernel (LPK). Unlike static kernels such as NTK, the LPK captures the entire training trajectory, adapting to both data and optimization dynamics, leading to tighter and more informative generalization guarantees. Moreover, the bound highlights how the norm of the training loss gradients along the optimization trajectory influences the final generalization performance. The key technical ingredients in our proof combine stability analysis of gradient flow with uniform convergence via Rademacher complexity. Our bound recovers existing kernel regression bounds for overparameterized neural networks and shows the feature learning capability of neural networks compared to kernel methods. Numerical experiments on real-world datasets validate that our bounds correlate well with the true generalization gap.

title: Generalization Bound of Gradient Flow through Training Trajectory and Data-dependent Kernel

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have facilitated a wide range of applications with distinct service-level objectives (SLOs), from latency-sensitive online tasks like interactive chatbots to throughput-oriented offline workloads like data synthesis. The existing deployment model, which dedicates machines to each workload, simplifies SLO management but often leads to poor resource utilization. This paper introduces HyGen, an interference-aware LLM serving system that enables efficient co-location of online and offline workloads while preserving SLOs. HyGen incorporates two key innovations: (1) performance control mechanisms, including a latency predictor to estimate batch execution time and an SLO-aware profiler to quantify latency interference, and (2) SLO-aware offline scheduling policies that maximize serving throughput and prevent starvation. Our evaluation on production workloads shows that HyGen achieves up to 3.9-5.8× throughput gains over online and hybrid serving baselines, while ensuring latency SLOs. The code of HyGen is publicly available at https://github.com/UIUC-MLSys/HyGen.

paragraphs: Interactive language-model applications need quick responses, while offline jobs such as data synthesis prioritize processing volume. Assigning separate machines to these workloads makes their service requirements easier to manage but can leave resources underused. HyGen is a serving system designed to run both workloads together while preserving their service-level objectives.

The system explicitly accounts for interference between requests. A latency predictor estimates how long a batch will execute, and an SLO-aware profiler measures the latency effects of sharing resources. These mechanisms inform offline scheduling policies that seek higher throughput while respecting service requirements and preventing offline requests from being indefinitely postponed.

Evaluations on production workloads report throughput gains of up to 3.9–5.8 times over online and hybrid serving baselines while meeting latency objectives. The result shows that coordinating workloads with different priorities can substantially improve utilization in the tested settings. HyGen's contribution is the combination of performance estimation and scheduling policies that make shared serving responsive to interference.
summary.tldr: HyGen co-locates interactive and offline LLM requests using interference-aware scheduling, reporting substantial throughput gains while maintaining latency objectives.

title: HyGen: Efficient LLM Serving via Elastic Online-Offline Request Co-location

abstract: Long chain-of-thought (LongCoT) has emerged as a powerful reasoning paradigm for enabling large language models (LLMs) to solve complex tasks through a systematic and thorough thinking phase. Although supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on high-quality LongCoT traces has proven effective to activate LongCoT abilities, we find that models trained in this way tend to overfit problem-specific knowledge and heuristics, leading to degraded out-of-distribution performance. To address this issue, we propose a Decoupled LongCoT Fine-Tuning (DLoFT) algorithm, which enables the model to learn generalizable LongCoT reasoning abilities while preventing overfitting to the reasoning content with problem-specific information. The key idea is to decouple the gradient into two orthogonal components: 1) a paradigm-relevant gradient corresponding to the general LongCoT paradigm and 2) a content-relevant gradient reflecting the problem-specific information, where only the former gradient is used to update model parameters. Specifically, by leveraging the unique two-phase composition (thinking and solution) of the LongCoT response, our gradient decoupling mechanism isolates the content-relevant gradient via a projection operation and separates the paradigm-relevant gradient through orthogonalization. Our DLoFT ensures the model concentrate on internalizing the LongCoT paradigm rather than memorizing problem-specific knowledge and heuristics. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our DLoFT significantly improves the generalization behavior of LongCoT abilities compared to SFT while maintaining strong in-distribution performance.

paragraphs: Training on extended reasoning examples can teach a model useful reasoning behavior while also encouraging it to absorb problem-specific shortcuts. The authors find that ordinary supervised fine-tuning on such examples can reduce performance outside the training distribution. DLoFT targets this problem by changing which part of the training signal updates the model.

The method separates the gradient into two orthogonal components: one associated with the general long-reasoning paradigm and another associated with specific problem content. It uses the response's thinking and solution phases to identify the content-related direction through projection. Orthogonalization then separates out the component intended to capture the broader reasoning pattern, and only that component updates model parameters.

This mechanism aims to teach the form of systematic reasoning while reducing memorization of the particular knowledge and heuristics in training examples. Experiments report significantly better generalization than supervised fine-tuning while maintaining strong performance on problems from the training distribution. The result supports the value of selecting training directions, rather than using the full gradient from every reasoning example.
summary.tldr: DLoFT separates training gradients to emphasize general long-form reasoning behavior and improve generalization beyond training problems.

title: DLoFT: Gradient-Decoupled Fine-Tuning for Generalizable Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

abstract: Sequential data—ranging from financial time series to natural language—has driven the growing adoption of autoregressive models. However, these algorithms rely on the presence of underlying patterns in the data, and their identification often depends heavily on human expertise. Misinterpreting these patterns can lead to model misspecification, resulting in increased generalization error and degraded performance. The recently proposed $\texttt{evolving pattern (EvoRate)}$ metric addresses this by using the mutual information between the next data point and its past to guide regression order estimation and feature selection. Building on this idea, we introduce a general framework based on predictive information—the mutual information between the past and the future, $\mathbf{I}(X_{\text{past}}; X_{\text{future}})$. This quantity naturally defines an information-theoretic learning curve, which quantifies the amount of predictive information available as the observation window grows. Using this formalism, we show that the presence or absence of temporal patterns fundamentally constrains the learnability of sequential models: even an optimal predictor cannot outperform the intrinsic information limit imposed by the data. We validate our framework through experiments on synthetic data, demonstrating its ability to assess model adequacy, quantify the inherent complexity of a dataset, and reveal interpretable structure in sequential data.

paragraphs: Sequence models depend on information in earlier observations that helps predict later ones. Choosing the wrong history length or misreading temporal patterns can therefore undermine generalization. This paper studies predictability as a property of the data itself, using predictive information: the mutual information shared between a sequence's past and its future.

The framework turns that quantity into an information-theoretic learning curve by tracking how much predictive information becomes available as the observation window grows. It extends an earlier idea based on information between the past and only the next observation. Looking at the broader future allows the framework to describe how temporal structure constrains what sequential models can learn.

The theoretical result is an intrinsic information limit: even an optimal predictor cannot exceed the predictive possibilities supplied by the data's patterns. Synthetic-data experiments demonstrate uses for assessing model adequacy, measuring inherent dataset complexity, and identifying interpretable sequence structure. The framework helps distinguish questions about a model's suitability from questions about how much predictive information the sequence contains in the first place.
summary.tldr: The paper uses information shared between past and future to characterize intrinsic limits on sequence predictability as observation windows grow.

title: How Patterns Dictate Learnability in Sequential Data

abstract: The practical performance of generative diffusion models depends on the appropriate choice of the noise scheduling function, which can also be equivalently expressed as a time reparameterization. In this paper, we present a time scheduler that selects sampling points based on entropy rather than uniform time spacing, ensuring that each point contributes an equal amount of information to the final generation. We prove that this time reparameterization does not depend on the initial choice of time. Furthermore, we provide a tractable exact formula to estimate this \emph{entropic time} for a trained model using the training loss without substantial overhead. Alongside the entropic time, inspired by the optimality results, we introduce a rescaled entropic time. In our experiments with mixtures of Gaussian distributions and ImageNet, we show that using the (rescaled) entropic times greatly improves the inference performance of trained models. In particular, we found that the image quality in pretrained EDM2 models, as evaluated by FID and FD-DINO scores, can be substantially increased by the rescaled entropic time reparameterization without increasing the number of function evaluations, with greater improvements in the few NFEs regime. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/DejanStancevic/Entropic-Time-Schedulers-for-Generative-Diffusion-Models}.

paragraphs: A diffusion model’s generation quality depends partly on where its sampling steps fall along the noise-removal process. This paper proposes choosing those points according to entropy, so that each contributes an equal amount of information to the final output. The resulting entropic time replaces uniform spacing in the original time coordinate.

The authors prove that this reparameterization is independent of the initial choice of time. They also provide a tractable exact formula for estimating entropic time from a trained model’s training loss without substantial overhead. Alongside this construction, they introduce a rescaled version motivated by optimality results.

Experiments on Gaussian mixtures and ImageNet show substantial inference improvements from the entropic schedules. For pretrained EDM2 models, rescaled entropic time improves image quality measured by FID and FD-DINO without increasing the number of function evaluations. The gains are greater when only a few evaluations are used. These findings show that allocating existing sampling steps more effectively can improve generation without spending more model evaluations.
summary.tldr: Entropy-based sampling schedules improve diffusion generation by reallocating existing evaluation steps according to information contribution.

title: Entropic Time Schedulers for Generative Diffusion Models

abstract: Multimodal time series forecasting is foundational in various fields, such as utilizing satellite imagery and numerical data for predicting typhoons in climate science. However, existing multimodal approaches primarily focus on utilizing text data to help time series forecasting, leaving the visual data in existing time series datasets underexplored. Furthermore, it is challenging for models to effectively capture the physical information embedded in visual data, such as satellite imagery's temporal and geospatial context, which extends beyond images themselves. To address this gap, we propose physics-informed positional encoding (PIPE), a lightweight method that embeds physical information into vision language models (VLMs). PIPE introduces two key innovations: (1) a physics-informed positional indexing scheme for mapping physics to positional IDs, and (2) a variant-frequency positional encoding mechanism for encoding frequency information of physical variables and sequential order of tokens within the embedding space. By preserving both the physical information and sequential order information, PIPE significantly improves multimodal alignment and forecasting accuracy. Through the experiments on the most representative and the largest open-sourced satellite image dataset, PIPE achieves state-of-the-art performance in both deep learning forecasting and climate domain methods, demonstrating superiority across benchmarks, including a 12\% improvement in typhoon intensity forecasting over prior works.

Their temporal and geographic context matters for interpreting them together with measurements. PIPE addresses this alignment problem through a lightweight positional-encoding method for vision-language models.

The method first maps physical information into positional identifiers. It then uses a variable-frequency encoding mechanism to represent information about physical variables while preserving the sequential order of tokens. These two components make position encoding carry both physical context and sequence structure, helping the model connect imagery with the accompanying time-series information.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance against deep-learning forecasting and climate-domain methods, including a 12% improvement in typhoon intensity forecasting over prior work. The contribution demonstrates how changing the representation of position can make physical context useful to a multimodal model, rather than leaving that context separate from its image representations.
summary.tldr: PIPE embeds physical context into positional encodings to improve satellite-image and time-series alignment for typhoon forecasting.

title: PIPE: Physics-Informed Position Encoding for Alignment of Satellite Images and Time Series in Typhoon Forecasting

abstract: We introduce a novel framework for decomposing interventional causal effects into synergistic, redundant, and unique components, building on the intuition of Partial Information Decomposition (PID) and the principle of Möbius inversion. While recent work has explored a similar decomposition of an observational measure, we argue that a proper causal decomposition must be interventional in nature. We develop a mathematical approach that systematically quantifies how causal power is distributed among variables in a system, using a recently derived closed-form expression for the Möbius function of the redundancy lattice. The formalism is then illustrated by decomposing the causal power in logic gates, cellular automata, and chemical reaction networks. Our results reveal how the distribution of causal power can be context- and parameter-dependent. The decomposition provides new insights into complex systems by revealing how causal influences are shared and combined among multiple variables, with potential applications ranging from attribution of responsibility in legal or AI systems, to the analysis of biological networks or climate models.

paragraphs: When several variables influence an outcome, their contributions can overlap, remain distinct, or depend on acting together. This paper develops a framework for separating those forms of causal influence into redundant, unique, and synergistic components. Its central position is that causal decomposition should be based on interventions, rather than solely on patterns observed in data.

The mathematics draws on Partial Information Decomposition and Möbius inversion. A closed-form expression for the Möbius function of the redundancy lattice makes it possible to systematically separate how causal power is distributed among variables. The purpose is to describe the organization of joint influence, giving more detail than a single measure of an overall causal effect.

The authors illustrate the framework with logic gates, cellular automata, and chemical reaction networks. These examples show that the distribution of causal power can change with context and system parameters. The decomposition therefore characterizes causal contributions in relation to a particular setting. Applications to responsibility attribution, biological networks, and climate models are proposed as possibilities, while the stated demonstrations focus on the three example systems.
summary.tldr: The paper decomposes intervention-based causal influence into shared, unique, and synergistic contributions that can vary with context.

title: Decomposing Interventional Causality into Synergistic, Redundant, and Unique Components

abstract: Simplicial complexes provide a powerful framework for modeling higher-order interactions in structured data, making them particularly suitable for applications such as trajectory prediction and mesh processing. However, existing simplicial neural networks (SNNs), whether convolutional or attention-based, rely primarily on discrete filtering techniques, which can be restrictive. In contrast, partial differential equations (PDEs) on simplicial complexes offer a principled approach to capture continuous dynamics in such structures. In this work, we introduce continuous simplicial neural network (COSIMO), a novel SNN architecture derived from PDEs on simplicial complexes. We provide theoretical and experimental justifications of COSIMO's stability under simplicial perturbations. Furthermore, we investigate the over-smoothing phenomenon—a common issue in geometric deep learning—demonstrating that COSIMO offers better control over this effect than discrete SNNs. Our experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that COSIMO achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art SNNs in complex and noisy environments. The implementation codes are available in https://github.com/ArefEinizade2/COSIMO.

paragraphs: COSIMO is a neural architecture for data represented by simplicial complexes, structures that capture interactions involving more than pairs of elements. Such representations are useful for problems including trajectory prediction and mesh processing. The paper examines how to learn on these structures using continuous dynamics instead of relying primarily on discrete filtering operations.

The architecture is derived from partial differential equations defined on simplicial complexes. This supplies a mathematical basis for how information evolves through the model. The authors provide theoretical and experimental support for its stability when the simplicial structure is perturbed. They also study over-smoothing, the tendency for learned representations to become excessively similar, and show that COSIMO offers better control of this effect than discrete simplicial networks.

Experiments on real-world datasets find performance competitive with state-of-the-art simplicial neural networks in complex and noisy settings. The contribution therefore combines a different modeling foundation with evidence about stability and representation quality. Its stated advantage is better control of over-smoothing alongside competitive task performance, rather than an across-the-board claim of higher accuracy.
summary.tldr: COSIMO derives simplicial neural networks from continuous equations, providing stability support and better control of over-smoothing with competitive performance.

title: Continuous Simplicial Neural Networks

abstract: Existing efforts in motion synthesis typically utilize either generative transformers with discrete representations or diffusion models with continuous representations. However, the discretization process in generative transformers can introduce motion errors, while the sampling process in diffusion models tends to be slow. In this paper, we propose a novel text-to-motion synthesis method GMMotion that combines a continuous motion representation with an autoregressive model, using the Gaussian mixture model (GMM) to represent the conditional probability distribution. Unlike autoregressive approaches relying on residual vector quantization, our model employs continuous motion representations derived from the VAE's latent space. This choice streamlines both the training and the inference processes. Specifically, we utilize a causal transformer to learn the distributions of continuous motion representations, which are modeled with a learnable Gaussian mixture model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our model surpasses existing state-of-the-art models in the motion synthesis task.

paragraphs: GMMotion generates motion from text while addressing two difficulties in existing approaches. Transformers that use discrete motion representations can introduce errors during discretization, while diffusion models working with continuous representations can be slow to sample. The paper combines continuous motion representations with autoregressive generation, aiming to retain the advantages of both choices.

The method obtains its motion representations from the latent space of a variational autoencoder. A causal transformer then learns conditional distributions over these continuous representations as generation proceeds. Instead of selecting entries from a discrete codebook, it uses a learnable Gaussian mixture model to describe the distribution from which motion representations are sampled.

This design gives an autoregressive model a way to generate continuous motion without residual vector quantization. The authors report that this choice simplifies training and inference, and that extensive experiments outperform existing state-of-the-art motion synthesis models. The stated contribution is therefore both a representation choice and a sampling mechanism that make continuous autoregressive text-to-motion generation effective.
summary.tldr: GMMotion generates continuous motion autoregressively using a learned Gaussian mixture distribution, avoiding motion discretization.

title: Autoregressive Motion Generation with Gaussian Mixture-Guided Latent Sampling

abstract: Transferring appearance to 3D assets using different representations of the appearance object - such as images or text - has garnered interest due to its wide range of applications in industries like gaming, augmented reality, and digital content creation. However, state-of-the-art methods still fail when the geometry between the input and appearance objects is significantly different. A straightforward approach is to directly apply a 3D generative model, but we show that this ultimately fails to produce appealing results. Instead, we propose a principled approach inspired by universal guidance. Given a pretrained rectified flow model conditioned on image or text, our training-free method interacts with the sampling process by periodically adding guidance. This guidance can be modeled as a differentiable loss function, and we experiment with two different types of guidance including part-aware losses for appearance and self-similarity. Our experiments show that our approach successfully transfers texture and geometric details to the input 3D asset, outperforming baselines both qualitatively and quantitatively. We also show that traditional metrics are not suitable for evaluating the task due to their inability of focusing on local details and comparing dissimilar inputs, in absence of ground truth data. We thus evaluate appearance transfer quality with a GPT-based system objectively ranking outputs, ensuring robust and human-like assessment, as further confirmed by our user study. Beyond showcased scenarios, our method is general and could be extended to different types of diffusion models and guidance functions. Project Page: *[https://sayands.github.io/guideflow3d](https://sayands.github.io/guideflow3d)*

paragraphs: Transferring an appearance described by an image or text onto a 3D asset becomes difficult when the source and target have substantially different geometry. The authors find that directly applying a 3D generative model does not produce appealing results in this setting. GuideFlow3D instead steers generation toward the desired transfer.

The method uses a pretrained rectified flow model without additional training. During sampling, it periodically applies guidance expressed as a differentiable loss. The authors explore guidance based on part-aware appearance losses and self-similarity. This gives the sampling process an explicit signal about which appearance relationships it should preserve or reproduce.

Experiments show successful transfer of textures and geometric details, with qualitative and quantitative improvements over baselines. The paper also argues that traditional metrics struggle with local detail and geometrically dissimilar inputs when ground truth is absent. It therefore uses GPT-based output rankings, with a user study supporting their human-like assessment. Extensions to other diffusion models and guidance functions are presented as possibilities.
summary.tldr: GuideFlow3D periodically guides a pretrained generative model to transfer appearance onto 3D assets with substantially different geometry.

title: GuideFlow3D: Optimization-Guided Rectified Flow For Appearance Transfer

abstract: Existing methods to enhance the reasoning capability of large language models predominantly rely on supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by reinforcement learning (RL) on reasoning-specific data. These approaches critically depend on external supervisions--such as labeled reasoning traces, verified golden answers, or pre-trained reward models. In this work, we propose Entropy Minimized Policy Optimization (EMPO), which makes an early attempt at fully unsupervised LLM reasoning incentivization. By minimizing the semantic entropy of LLMs on unlabeled questions, EMPO achieves competitive performance compared to supervised counterparts. Specifically, without any supervised signals, EMPO boosts the accuracy of Qwen2.5-Math-7B Base from 33.7\% to 51.6\% on math benchmarks and improves the accuracy of Qwen2.5-7B Base from 32.1\% to 50.1\% on MMLU-Pro. Primary analysis are also provided to interpret the effectiveness of EMPO. Code is available at https://github.com/QingyangZhang/EMPO.

paragraphs: Improving language-model reasoning commonly requires labeled reasoning traces, verified answers, or pretrained reward models. Entropy Minimized Policy Optimization, or EMPO, explores whether unlabeled questions alone can provide a useful training signal. The paper presents it as an early attempt at fully unsupervised reasoning incentivization, without those external sources of supervision.

EMPO minimizes semantic entropy on the model’s answers to unlabeled questions. This directs optimization toward reduced uncertainty at the level of answer meaning. The training objective therefore comes from the model’s responses rather than a supplied correct answer or externally trained evaluator. The paper also provides preliminary analysis intended to explain why this objective can help.

Reported accuracy rises from 33.7% to 51.6% for Qwen2.5-Math-7B Base on math benchmarks and from 32.1% to 50.1% for Qwen2.5-7B Base on MMLU-Pro. The authors describe the resulting performance as competitive with supervised counterparts. These experiments show that the proposed unsupervised objective can produce substantial reasoning gains in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: EMPO improves reasoning on tested benchmarks by minimizing semantic entropy on unlabeled questions without external supervisory signals.

title: Right Question is Already Half the Answer: Fully Unsupervised LLM Reasoning Incentivization

abstract: Global dependency modeling and spatial position modeling are two core issues of the foundational architecture design in current deep learning frameworks. Recently, Vision Transformers (ViTs) have achieved remarkable success in computer vision, leveraging the powerful global dependency modeling capability of the self-attention mechanism. Furthermore, Mamba2 has demonstrated its significant potential in natural language processing tasks by explicitly modeling the spatial adjacency prior through the structured mask. In this paper, we propose Polyline Path Masked Attention (PPMA) that integrates the self-attention mechanism of ViTs with an enhanced structured mask of Mamba2, harnessing the complementary strengths of both architectures. Specifically, we first ameliorate the traditional structured mask of Mamba2 by introducing a 2D polyline path scanning strategy and derive its corresponding structured mask, polyline path mask, which better preserves the adjacency relationships among image tokens. Notably, we conduct a thorough theoretical analysis on the structural characteristics of the proposed polyline path mask and design an efficient algorithm for the computation of the polyline path mask. Next, we embed the polyline path mask into the self-attention mechanism of ViTs, enabling explicit modeling of spatial adjacency prior. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks, including image classification, object detection, and segmentation, demonstrate that our model outperforms previous state-of-the-art approaches based on both state-space models and Transformers. For example, our proposed PPMA-T/S/B models achieve 48.7%/51.1%/52.3% mIoU on the ADE20K semantic segmentation task, surpassing RMT-T/S/B by 0.7%/1.3%/0.3%, respectively. Code is available at https://github.com/zhongchenzhao/PPMA.

Self-attention gives Vision Transformers strong global modeling capabilities, while structured masks can encode adjacency more explicitly. Polyline Path Masked Attention combines these ideas by incorporating a spatially informed mask into transformer attention.

The authors adapt Mamba2's structured mask using a two-dimensional polyline scanning strategy. The resulting mask better preserves adjacency relationships among image tokens. They analyze its structural properties theoretically and develop an efficient algorithm to compute it. Embedding this mask into self-attention adds an explicit spatial prior while retaining attention's ability to represent global dependencies.

summary.tldr: Polyline Path Masked Attention adds a two-dimensional adjacency-preserving mask to Vision Transformers and improves performance across evaluated vision tasks.

title: Polyline Path Masked Attention for Vision Transformer

abstract: A longstanding goal in safe reinforcement learning (RL) is a method to ensure the safety of a policy throughout the entire process, from learning to operation. However, existing safe RL paradigms inherently struggle to achieve this objective. We propose a method, called Provably Lifetime Safe RL (PLS), that integrates offline safe RL with safe policy deployment to address this challenge. Our proposed method learns a policy offline using return-conditioned supervised learning and then deploys the resulting policy while cautiously optimizing a limited set of parameters, known as target returns, using Gaussian processes (GPs). Theoretically, we justify the use of GPs by analyzing the mathematical relationship between target and actual returns. We then prove that PLS finds near-optimal target returns while guaranteeing safety with high probability. Empirically, we demonstrate that PLS outperforms baselines both in safety and reward performance, thereby achieving the longstanding goal to obtain high rewards while ensuring the safety of a policy throughout the lifetime from learning to operation.
