paragraphs: Safe reinforcement learning needs to address both how a policy is learned and what happens when it is used. This paper proposes Provably Lifetime Safe RL, or PLS, which connects offline policy learning with a cautious deployment procedure. Its central idea is to make safety part of the transition between those stages.

PLS first learns from offline data through return-conditioned supervised learning: the policy receives a target return that guides its behavior. During deployment, the method optimizes a limited set of these targets using Gaussian processes. This makes the target returns the focus of adaptation while the learned policy provides the underlying behavior.

The authors analyze the relationship between requested and actual returns to justify using Gaussian processes. They prove that PLS can identify near-optimal target returns while maintaining safety with high probability. Their experiments also report better safety and reward performance than baselines. The result combines a probabilistic safety guarantee with evidence that cautious deployment can still support strong rewards.
summary.tldr: PLS combines offline policy learning with cautious target-return optimization to achieve high rewards while guaranteeing safety with high probability.

title: A Provable Approach for End-to-End Safe Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Encountering shifted data at test time is a ubiquitous challenge when deploying predictive machine learning models. Test-time adaptation (TTA) methods aim to address this issue by continuously adapting a deployed model using only unlabeled test data. While TTA can help extend the model's deployment lifespan, there are scenarios where, despite adaptation, the drop in the model's performance remains significant enough to warrant taking the model offline and retraining. To detect such failure cases, we propose pairing TTA with risk monitoring frameworks that track predictive performance and raise alerts when predefined performance criteria are violated. Specifically, we extend existing monitoring tools based on sequential testing with confidence sequences to accommodate scenarios where the model is updated at test time and no test labels are available to estimate the performance metrics of interest. Our extensions unlock the application of rigorous statistical risk monitoring in TTA and we demonstrate applicability of our proposed TTA monitoring framework across a representative set of TTA methods, datasets and distribution shift types.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a deployed model using incoming data without labels, helping it respond when those data differ from its training distribution. Yet adaptation can leave performance low enough that continued deployment is inappropriate. This paper addresses how to recognize those cases, rather than assuming that ongoing updates keep the model sufficiently reliable.

The authors pair adaptation with statistical risk monitoring that tracks predictive performance and signals when predefined criteria are violated. They extend monitoring methods built on sequential tests and confidence sequences, tools for assessing evidence as observations arrive. The challenge is to accommodate both a changing model and the absence of test labels for directly measuring the performance quantities of interest.

The resulting framework makes rigorous statistical monitoring applicable to test-time adaptation. The authors demonstrate its use across a representative collection of adaptation methods, datasets, and distribution shifts. This separates two deployment functions: adaptation tries to maintain useful predictions, while monitoring checks whether performance still meets the chosen requirements and can indicate when taking the model offline for retraining is warranted.
summary.tldr: The paper extends statistical risk monitoring to detect performance failures in models adapting to unlabeled test data.

title: Monitoring Risks in Test-Time Adaptation

abstract: Transformers have gained attention in atmospheric time series forecasting (ATSF) for their ability to capture global spatial-temporal correlations. However, their complex architectures lead to excessive parameter counts and extended training times, limiting their scalability to large-scale forecasting. In this paper, we revisit ATSF from a theoretical perspective of atmospheric dynamics and uncover a key insight: spatial-temporal position embedding (STPE) can inherently model spatial-temporal correlations even without attention mechanisms. Its effectiveness arises from integrating geographical coordinates and temporal features, which are intrinsically linked to atmospheric dynamics. Based on this, we propose **STELLA**, a **S**patial-**T**emporal knowledge **E**mbedded **L**ightweight mode**L** for ASTF, utilizing only STPE and an MLP architecture in place of Transformer layers. With 10k parameters and one hour of training, STELLA achieves superior performance on five datasets compared to other advanced methods. The paper emphasizes the effectiveness of spatial-temporal knowledge integration over complex architectures, providing novel insights for ATSF.

paragraphs: Atmospheric forecasting requires capturing relationships across places and times. Transformers can model these broad relationships, but their complexity brings large parameter counts and lengthy training. This paper revisits the problem through atmospheric dynamics and asks how much useful structure can come from the representation of location and time itself.

The authors argue that spatial-temporal position embeddings can capture these correlations without attention mechanisms. Their explanation rests on combining geographic coordinates and temporal features that are intrinsically connected to atmospheric dynamics. STELLA uses this insight to build a forecasting model from those embeddings and a multilayer perceptron, replacing Transformer layers with a simpler architecture.

With 10,000 parameters and one hour of training, STELLA achieves better performance than other advanced methods on five datasets. These reported results show that the chosen representation can carry enough relevant structure to support strong forecasting with a small model. The paper's contribution is both architectural and conceptual: explicitly integrating spatial and temporal knowledge can reduce the need for architectural complexity in the evaluated atmospheric forecasting tasks.
summary.tldr: STELLA uses spatial-temporal embeddings and a small multilayer perceptron to achieve strong atmospheric forecasting without attention.

title: On the Integration of Spatial-Temporal Knowledge: A Lightweight Approach to Atmospheric Time Series Forecasting

abstract: This paper presents PipeFusion, an innovative parallel methodology to tackle the high latency issues associated with generating high-resolution images using diffusion transformers (DiTs) models. PipeFusion partitions images into patches and the model layers across multiple GPUs. It employs a patch-level pipeline parallel strategy to orchestrate communication and computation efficiently. By capitalizing on the high similarity between inputs from successive diffusion steps, PipeFusion reuses one-step stale feature maps to provide context for the current pipeline step. This approach notably reduces communication costs compared to existing DiTs inference parallelism, including tensor parallel, sequence parallel and DistriFusion. PipeFusion enhances memory efficiency through parameter distribution across devices, ideal for large DiTs like Flux.1. Experimental results demonstrate that PipeFusion achieves state-of-the-art performance on 8$\times$L40 PCIe GPUs for Pixart, Stable-Diffusion 3, and Flux.1 models. Our Source code is available at \url{https://github.com/xdit-project/xDiT}.

paragraphs: PipeFusion targets the latency of generating high-resolution images with diffusion transformers. It distributes work along two dimensions: image patches and model layers. These pieces are scheduled as a pipeline across multiple GPUs, coordinating computation with communication so that distributing the model does not require excessive data exchange.

The method uses the similarity between inputs at consecutive diffusion steps. Feature maps from the preceding step provide context for the current pipeline step, even though they are one step old. Reusing this context reduces communication relative to tensor parallelism, sequence parallelism, and DistriFusion. Distributing model parameters across devices also improves memory efficiency, which matters for large diffusion transformers such as Flux.1.

Experiments on eight L40 GPUs connected through PCIe report state-of-the-art performance for Pixart, Stable Diffusion 3, and Flux.1. These results demonstrate the benefits of combining patch scheduling, layer distribution, and reused features in the evaluated hardware setting. The core opportunity comes from exploiting similarity between diffusion steps when arranging work across GPUs.
summary.tldr: PipeFusion pipelines image patches and model layers across GPUs, reusing previous-step features to reduce diffusion-transformer communication and latency.

title: PipeFusion: Patch-level Pipeline Parallelism for Diffusion Transformers Inference

abstract: Truncation by death, a prevalent challenge in critical care, renders traditional dynamic treatment regime (DTR) evaluation inapplicable due to ill-defined potential outcomes. We introduce a principal stratification-based method, focusing on the always-survivor value function. We derive a semiparametrically efficient, multiply robust estimator for multi-stage DTRs, demonstrating its robustness and efficiency. Empirical validation and an application to electronic health records showcase its utility for personalized treatment optimization.

paragraphs: A dynamic treatment regime specifies treatment decisions across multiple stages. Evaluating such a regime becomes difficult when death makes a later outcome undefined. This problem, called truncation by death, is especially relevant in critical care. The paper addresses the resulting failure of traditional evaluation methods, whose potential outcomes may no longer be well defined.

The proposed approach uses principal stratification and focuses on an always-survivor value function. This changes the evaluation target to address the survival issue directly. The authors derive an estimator for treatment regimes with multiple stages and establish two statistical properties: semiparametric efficiency and multiple robustness. These properties concern how efficiently the estimator uses information and its robustness within the proposed estimation framework.

The paper combines methodological development with empirical validation and an application to electronic health records. These results demonstrate the method's utility for personalized treatment optimization under truncation by death. Its contribution is an evaluation and learning framework built around a defined survivor-focused target, allowing treatment strategies to be studied when death prevents conventional outcome comparisons.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a survivor-focused, efficient and multiply robust method for evaluating multi-stage treatment strategies when death makes outcomes undefined.

title: Evaluating and Learning Optimal Dynamic Treatment Regimes under Truncation by Death

abstract: The advent of foundation models in AI has significantly advanced general-purpose learning, enabling remarkable capabilities in zero-shot inference and in-context learning. However, training such models on physics data, including solutions to partial differential equations (PDEs), poses a unique challenge due to varying dimensionalities across different systems. Traditional approaches either fix a maximum dimension or employ separate encoders for different dimensionalities, resulting in inefficiencies. To address this, we propose a dimension-agnostic neural network architecture, the Axial Neural Network (XNN), inspired by parameter-sharing structures such as Deep Sets and Graph Neural Networks. XNN generalizes across varying tensor dimensions while maintaining computational efficiency. We convert existing PDE foundation models into axial neural networks and evaluate their performance across three training scenarios: training from scratch, pretraining on multiple PDEs, and fine-tuning on a single PDE. Our experiments show that XNNs perform competitively with original models and exhibit superior generalization to unseen dimensions, highlighting the importance of multidimensional pretraining for foundation models.

paragraphs: Foundation models for physical systems face a structural problem: data from different partial differential equations can have different numbers of dimensions. An architecture built around one fixed dimensionality does not naturally transfer across all these systems. Setting a maximum dimension or maintaining separate encoders introduces inefficiencies that complicate sharing a model across physics tasks.

The paper introduces the Axial Neural Network, or XNN, to handle varying tensor dimensionalities within a shared architecture. Its design draws on parameter sharing ideas associated with Deep Sets and graph neural networks. The aim is to reuse learned computation across dimensional settings while retaining computational efficiency, making dimensionality less of an architectural constraint.

The authors convert existing PDE foundation models into XNNs and study training from scratch, pretraining across multiple PDEs, and fine-tuning on one PDE. Their experiments report competitive performance against the original models and better generalization to unseen dimensions. These findings support both the architecture and the value of exposing physics foundation models to multiple dimensionalities during pretraining.
summary.tldr: Axial Neural Networks share computation across tensor dimensionalities, matching existing PDE models competitively while generalizing better to unseen dimensions.

title: Axial Neural Networks for Dimension-Free Foundation Models

abstract: The integration of language and 3D perception is critical for embodied AI and robotic systems to perceive, understand, and interact with the physical world. Spatial reasoning, a key capability for understanding spatial relationships between objects, remains underexplored in current 3D vision-language research. Existing datasets often mix semantic cues (e.g., object name) with spatial context, leading models to rely on superficial shortcuts rather than genuinely interpreting spatial relationships. To address this gap, we introduce Surprise3D, a novel dataset designed to evaluate language-guided spatial reasoning segmentation in complex 3D scenes. Surprise3D consists of more than 200k vision language pairs across 900+ detailed indoor scenes from ScanNet++ v2, including more than 2.8k unique object classes. The dataset contains 89k+ human-annotated spatial queries deliberately crafted without object name, thereby mitigating shortcut biases in spatial understanding. These queries comprehensively cover various spatial reasoning skills, such as relative position, narrative perspective, parametric perspective, and absolute distance reasoning. Initial benchmarks demonstrate significant challenges for current state-of-the-art expert 3D visual grounding methods and 3D-LLMs, underscoring the necessity of our dataset and the accompanying 3D Spatial Reasoning Segmentation (3D-SRS) benchmark suite. Surprise3D and 3D-SRS aim to facilitate advancements in spatially aware AI, paving the way for effective embodied interaction and robotic planning.

paragraphs: Surprise3D evaluates whether models can use language to identify regions in complex 3D scenes through spatial reasoning. The authors argue that existing datasets often let models exploit object names instead of interpreting spatial relationships. Their dataset deliberately removes object names from human-written spatial queries to reduce that source of shortcuts.

summary.tldr: Surprise3D uses object-name-free spatial queries to challenge 3D models on language-guided spatial reasoning and segmentation.

title: Surprise3D: A Dataset for Spatial Understanding and Reasoning in Complex 3D Scenes

abstract: Weak-to-strong generalization—where a student model trained on imperfect labels generated by a weaker teacher nonetheless surpasses that teacher—has been widely observed, but the mechanisms that enable it have remained poorly understood. In this paper, through a theoretical analysis of simple models, we uncover three core mechanisms that can drive this phenomenon. First, by analyzing ridge linear regression, we study the interplay between the teacher and student regularization parameters and prove that a student can compensate for a teacher’s under-regularization and achieve lower test error. We also analyze the role of the parameterization regime of the models and show that qualitatively different phenomena can happen in different regimes. Second, by analyzing weighted ridge linear regression, we show that a student model with a regularization structure better aligned to the target function, can outperform its teacher. Third, in a nonlinear multi‐index learning setting, we demonstrate that a student can learn easy, task-specific features from the teacher while leveraging its own broader pre-training to learn hard‐to‐learn features that the teacher cannot capture.

paragraphs: Weak-to-strong generalization occurs when a student trained on a weaker teacher’s imperfect labels nevertheless outperforms that teacher. This paper studies simple mathematical models to identify mechanisms that can make this possible. Its results explain several routes to improvement rather than claiming that learning from a weaker teacher always succeeds.

The first mechanism concerns regularization. In ridge linear regression, the authors prove that a student can compensate for a teacher that regularizes too little and attain lower test error. They also show that the models’ parameterization regimes can produce qualitatively different behavior. A weighted ridge analysis identifies another route: the student’s regularization structure can align better with the target function than the teacher’s does.

The third mechanism appears in a nonlinear multi-index learning setting. A student can obtain easier task-specific features from the teacher while using broader pretraining to learn difficult features the teacher cannot capture. Together, the analyses show how teacher supervision and student capabilities can play different roles. Improvement can arise from the student’s learning constraints or prior knowledge, even though its labels originate from a weaker model.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies regularization and pretrained feature learning as mechanisms that can let students outperform weaker teachers in analyzed models.

title: On the Mechanisms of Weak-to-Strong Generalization: A Theoretical Perspective

abstract: Unified multimodal large language models (U-MLLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance in end-to-end visual understanding and generation tasks. However, compared to generation-only systems (e.g., Stable Diffusion), the unified architecture of U-MLLMs introduces new risks of propagating demographic stereotypes. In this paper, we benchmark several state-of-the-art U-MLLMs and show that they exhibit significant gender and race biases in the generated outputs. To diagnose the source of these biases, we propose a locate-then-fix framework: we first audit the vision and language components — using techniques such as linear probing and controlled generation — and find that the language model appears to be a primary origin of the observed generative bias. Moreover, we observe a ``partial alignment'' phenomenon, where the U-MLLMs exhibit less bias in understanding tasks yet produce substantially biased images. To address this, we introduce a novel \emph{balanced preference loss} that enforces uniform generation probabilities across demographics by leveraging a synthetically balanced dataset. Extensive experiments show that our approach significantly reduces demographic bias while preserving semantic fidelity and image quality. Our findings underscore the need for targeted debiasing strategies in unified multimodal systems and introduce a practical approach to mitigate biases.

In this paper, we benchmark several state-of-the-art U-MLLMs and show that they exhibit significant gender and race biases in the generated outputs. To diagnose the source of these biases, we propose a locate-then-fix framework: we first audit the vision and language components — using techniques such as linear probing and controlled generation — and find that the language model appears to be a primary origin of the observed generative bias. Moreover, we observe a ``partial alignment'' phenomenon, where the U-MLLMs exhibit less bias in understanding tasks yet produce substantially biased images. To address this, we introduce a novel \emph{balanced preference loss} that enforces uniform generation probabilities across demographics by leveraging a synthetically balanced dataset. Extensive experiments show that our approach significantly reduces demographic bias while preserving semantic fidelity and image quality. Our findings underscore the need for targeted debiasing strategies in unified multimodal systems and introduce a practical approach to mitigate biases.

paragraphs: Unified multimodal models combine visual understanding and image generation, creating potential routes for demographic stereotypes to propagate between components. This paper benchmarks several leading unified models and finds significant gender and race biases in their generated images. It then investigates where those biases appear to originate.

The authors audit the vision and language components through linear probing and controlled generation. Their findings suggest that the language model is a primary source of the observed generative bias. They also identify partial alignment: models can show less bias when interpreting content while still generating substantially biased images. This makes understanding-task behavior an incomplete picture of the system's demographic behavior.

To address the generation problem, the paper introduces a balanced preference loss using a synthetically balanced dataset. The loss promotes uniform generation probabilities across demographic groups. Experiments report substantial bias reduction while preserving semantic fidelity and image quality. The results support targeted intervention in generation and retain the diagnostic qualification that the language component appears to be a major source of bias.
summary.tldr: The paper diagnoses demographic bias in unified multimodal image generation and reduces it with a balanced preference loss while preserving reported image quality.

title: On Fairness of Unified Multimodal Large Language Model for Image Generation

abstract: Inference scaling methods for LLMs often rely on decomposing problems into steps (or groups of tokens), followed by sampling and selecting the best next steps. However, these steps and their sizes are often predetermined or manually designed based on domain knowledge. We propose dynamic decomposition, a method that adaptively and automatically partitions solution and reasoning traces into manageable steps during inference. By more effectively allocating compute -- particularly through subdividing challenging steps and prioritizing their sampling -- dynamic decomposition significantly improves inference efficiency. Experiments on benchmarks such as APPS, MATH, and LiveCodeBench demonstrate that dynamic decomposition outperforms static approaches, including token-level, sentence-level, and single-step decompositions, reducing the pass@10 error rate by 5.0%, 6.7%, and 10.5% respectively. These findings highlight the potential of dynamic decomposition to improve a wide range of inference scaling techniques.

paragraphs: DISC studies how language models should divide reasoning into steps when additional computation is available during inference. Many inference-scaling methods sample several possible continuations and select promising next steps. Their effectiveness depends on the boundaries of those steps, yet existing approaches often fix the boundaries beforehand or rely on manual choices informed by domain knowledge.

Dynamic decomposition makes those boundaries adaptive. It partitions reasoning and solution traces automatically during inference, with particular attention to difficult portions. Challenging steps can be subdivided and receive more sampling effort. This connects the size of a reasoning unit to how much work it needs, giving the system a way to allocate computation more selectively.

Experiments on APPS, MATH, and LiveCodeBench show improvements over static decomposition approaches. Against token-level, sentence-level, and single-step decomposition, the abstract reports pass@10 error-rate reductions of 5.0%, 6.7%, and 10.5%, respectively. These results suggest that choosing where to divide a solution is itself an important part of inference scaling, alongside choosing how many candidate continuations to generate and evaluate.
summary.tldr: DISC adaptively divides reasoning into steps and concentrates sampling on difficult portions, improving inference efficiency over fixed decompositions.

title: DISC: Dynamic Decomposition Improves LLM Inference Scaling

abstract: Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs), such as CLIP, have shown promising zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) detection capabilities by leveraging semantic similarities between input images and textual labels. However, most existing approaches focus solely on expanding the label space in the text domain, ignoring complementary visual cues that can further enhance discriminative power. In this paper, we introduce DualCnst, a novel framework that integrates text-image dual consistency for improved zero-shot OOD detection. Specifically, we generate synthetic images from both ID and mined OOD textual labels using a text-to-image generative model, and jointly evaluate each test image based on (i) its semantic similarity to class labels and (ii) its visual similarity to the synthesized images. The resulting unified score function effectively combines multimodal information without requiring access to in-distribution images or additional training. We further provide theoretical analysis showing that incorporating multimodal negative labels reduces score variance and improves OOD separability. Extensive experiments across diverse OOD benchmarks demonstrate that DualCnst achieves state-of-the-art performance while remaining scalable, data-agnostic, and fully compatible with prior text-only VLM-based methods.

Vision-language models can do this by comparing images with textual class labels. DualCnst adds visual reference information to approaches that primarily expand the set of candidate labels in text.

The framework generates synthetic images for both expected classes and mined out-of-distribution labels using a text-to-image model. Each test image receives a combined score based on its semantic match to labels and its visual match to these synthesized examples. This adds a second source of evidence without requiring actual in-distribution images or additional training.

The theoretical analysis shows that incorporating negative labels through multiple modalities reduces score variance and improves separation between expected and unexpected inputs. Experiments across diverse benchmarks report state-of-the-art detection performance. The framework also remains compatible with earlier text-only methods, making the visual consistency signal a complementary component that can strengthen an existing label-based detection approach.
summary.tldr: DualCnst combines text-label similarity with similarity to generated reference images to improve zero-shot out-of-distribution detection.

title: DualCnst: Enhancing Zero-Shot Out-of-Distribution Detection via Text-Image Consistency in Vision-Language Models

abstract: This work introduces Clipout, a method for removing a target concept in pre-trained text-to-image models. By randomly clipping units from the learned data embedding and using a contrastive objective, models are encouraged to differentiate these clipped embedding vectors. Our goal is to remove private, copyrighted, inaccurate, or harmful concepts from trained models without the need for retraining. This is achieved by considering only negative samples and generating them in a bootstrapping-like manner, requiring minimal prior knowledge. Additionally, theoretical analyses are provided to further understand our proposed Clipout. Extensive experiments on text-to-image show that Clipout is simple yet highly effective and efficient compared with previous state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: Clipout addresses the problem of removing a target concept from an already trained text-to-image model. The motivating targets include private, copyrighted, inaccurate, or harmful content. Its objective is to remove such concepts without retraining the model, using only negative samples and requiring minimal prior knowledge about the target.

The method randomly clips units from a learned data embedding, creating altered embedding vectors. A contrastive objective encourages the model to distinguish these clipped representations. Negative samples are generated through a bootstrapping-like process, providing the material used by the removal procedure. The contribution combines this sample-generation strategy with an embedding-level operation and a contrastive learning objective.

The authors provide theoretical analysis to help explain Clipout and evaluate it extensively on text-to-image models. They report that the method is simple, effective, and efficient compared with previous state-of-the-art approaches. The findings support negative-only sample construction as a practical route to targeted concept removal, with the reported benefits covering both removal effectiveness and computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: Clipout combines random embedding clipping and contrastive learning to remove target concepts using only bootstrapped negative samples.

title: Removing Concepts from Text-to-Image Models with Only Negative Samples

abstract: We consider the two-sample testing problem for networks, where the goal is to determine whether two sets of networks originated from the same stochastic model. Assuming no vertex correspondence and allowing for different numbers of nodes, we address a fundamental network testing problem that goes beyond simple adjacency matrix comparisons. We adopt the stochastic block model (SBM) for network distributions, due to their interpretability and the potential to approximate more general models. The lack of meaningful node labels and vertex correspondence translate to a graph matching challenge when developing a test for SBMs. We introduce an efficient algorithm to match estimated network parameters, allowing us to properly combine and contrast information within and across samples, leading to a powerful test. We show that the matching algorithm, and the overall test are consistent, under mild conditions on the sparsity of the networks and the sample sizes, and derive a chi-squared asymptotic null distribution for the test. Through a mixture of theoretical insights and empirical validations, including experiments with both synthetic and real-world data, this study advances robust statistical inference for complex network data.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether two collections of networks were generated by the same stochastic model. It allows networks to have different numbers of nodes and assumes no correspondence between their vertices. Those conditions make direct adjacency-matrix comparison unsuitable because matching positions need not represent matching entities.

The authors model network distributions using stochastic block models, which describe connectivity through groups of nodes. Without meaningful node labels, comparing estimated model parameters creates a matching problem. They introduce an efficient parameter-matching algorithm that aligns the estimates so information can be combined within each sample and contrasted across the two samples.

Under stated mild conditions on network sparsity and sample sizes, the authors prove consistency of both the matching algorithm and the resulting test. They also derive a chi-squared asymptotic null distribution, describing the test statistic's limiting behavior when the samples share a model. Synthetic and real-world experiments complement the theory. The contribution makes statistical comparison possible through aligned model structure even when node-by-node correspondence is unavailable.
summary.tldr: An efficient parameter-matching method enables consistent two-sample testing for stochastic block models without vertex correspondence.

title: Network two-sample test for block models

abstract: Preference alignment in diffusion models has primarily focused on benign human preferences (e.g., aesthetic). In this paper, we propose a novel perspective: framing unrestricted adversarial example generation as a problem of aligning with adversary preferences. Unlike benign alignment, adversarial alignment involves two inherently conflicting preferences: visual consistency and attack effectiveness, which often lead to unstable optimization and reward hacking (e.g., reducing visual quality to improve attack success). To address this, we propose APA (Adversary Preferences Alignment), a two-stage framework that decouples conflicting preferences and optimizes each with differentiable rewards. In the first stage, APA fine-tunes LoRA to improve visual consistency using rule-based similarity reward. In the second stage, APA updates either the image latent or prompt embedding based on feedback from a substitute classifier, guided by trajectory-level and step-wise rewards. To enhance black-box transferability, we further incorporate a diffusion augmentation strategy. Experiments demonstrate that APA achieves significantly better attack transferability while maintaining high visual consistency, inspiring further research to approach adversarial attacks from an alignment perspective.

paragraphs: This paper treats the generation of unrestricted adversarial images as a preference-alignment problem. The desired output must satisfy two competing goals: remain visually consistent and successfully mislead a classifier. Optimizing both together can become unstable or encourage reward hacking, such as sacrificing image quality to increase attack success. Adversary Preferences Alignment, or APA, separates their optimization.

In the first stage, APA fine-tunes a LoRA adapter using a rule-based similarity reward to improve visual consistency. In the second, it adjusts an image latent representation or prompt embedding using feedback from a substitute classifier. Rewards operate both across the generation trajectory and at individual steps. A diffusion augmentation strategy additionally targets transferability to black-box classifiers.

The experiments report substantially improved attack transferability while preserving high visual consistency. This supports the paper’s central argument that separating conflicting preferences can improve the balance between appearance and attack effectiveness. The work also presents an alternative conceptual framing for adversarial generation: the objective is alignment with an adversary’s paired preferences, rather than a single success signal.
summary.tldr: APA separates visual-consistency and attack objectives to improve the transferability of diffusion-generated adversarial images.

title: Enhancing Diffusion-based Unrestricted Adversarial Attacks via Adversary Preferences Alignment

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as powerful tools for learning protein structures by capturing spatial relationships at the residue level. However, existing GNN-based methods often face challenges in learning multiscale representations and modeling long-range dependencies efficiently. In this work, we propose an efficient multiscale graph-based learning framework tailored to proteins. Our proposed framework contains two crucial components: (1) It constructs a hierarchical graph representation comprising a collection of fine-grained subgraphs, each corresponding to a secondary structure motif (e.g., $\alpha$-helices, $\beta$-strands, loops), and a single coarse-grained graph that connects these motifs based on their spatial arrangement and relative orientation. (2) It employs two GNNs for feature learning: the first operates within individual secondary motifs to capture local interactions, and the second models higher-level structural relationships across motifs. Our modular framework allows a flexible choice of GNN in each stage. Theoretically, we show that our hierarchical framework preserves the desired maximal expressiveness, ensuring no loss of critical structural information. Empirically, we demonstrate that integrating baseline GNNs into our multiscale framework remarkably improves prediction accuracy and reduces computational cost across various benchmarks.

paragraphs: Protein graph models commonly represent spatial relationships between individual residues. This paper addresses the difficulty of learning both local structure and longer-range relationships efficiently at that level. It introduces a hierarchy built around secondary-structure motifs, including alpha helices, beta strands, and loops, so the representation explicitly contains multiple structural scales.

Each motif becomes a fine-grained subgraph, while a coarse graph connects motifs according to their spatial arrangement and relative orientation. One graph neural network learns interactions within motifs; another learns relationships across motifs. The framework is modular, allowing different graph neural networks to be chosen for either stage rather than requiring one particular architecture.

The authors theoretically show that the hierarchy preserves the desired maximal expressiveness, supporting their claim that the construction retains critical structural information. Experiments show that placing baseline graph networks inside this framework improves prediction accuracy and lowers computational cost across benchmarks. The results support using protein structure itself to organize computation at both local and larger scales.
summary.tldr: A hierarchy of protein motifs and residue-level subgraphs improves graph-model accuracy and efficiency while preserving the framework’s desired expressiveness.

title: Towards Multiscale Graph-based Protein Learning with Geometric Secondary Structural Motifs

abstract: Reasoning models excel by generating long chain-of-thoughts, but decoding the resulting thousands of tokens is slow. Token-level specualtive decoding (SD) helps, but its benefit is capped, because the chance that an entire $\gamma$-token guess is correct falls exponentially as $\gamma$ grows. This means allocating more compute for longer token drafts faces an algorithmic ceiling -- making the speedup modest and hardware-agnostic. We raise this ceiling with lookahead reasoning, which exploits a second, step-level layer of parallelism. Our key insight is that reasoning models generate step-by-step, and each step needs only to be semantically correct, not exact token matching. In lookahead reasoning, a lightweight draft model proposes several future steps; the target model expands each proposal in one batched pass, and a verifier keeps semantically correct steps while letting the target regenerate any that fail. Token-level SD still operates within each reasoning step, so the two layers of parallelism multiply. We show lookahead reasoning lifts the peak speedup of SD both theoretically and empirically. Across GSM8K, AIME, and other benchmarks, lookahead reasoning improves the speedup of SD from 1.4x to 2.1x while preserving answer quality, and its speedup scales better with additional GPU throughput. Our code is available at https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/LookaheadReasoning

paragraphs: Long reasoning traces are slow to generate token by token. Speculative decoding accelerates generation with drafts, but longer drafts become increasingly unlikely to match the target model exactly. This paper adds another level of parallelism by exploiting the structure of reasoning steps, where semantic correctness can matter more than identical wording.

In lookahead reasoning, a lightweight model proposes several future reasoning steps. The target model expands those proposals in a single batch, and a verifier retains semantically correct steps while the target regenerates rejected ones. Token-level speculative decoding continues inside each step, allowing the step-level and token-level acceleration mechanisms to work together.

summary.tldr: Lookahead reasoning adds semantic step-level parallelism to speculative decoding, increasing reported speedup from 1.4× to 2.1× while preserving answer quality.

title: Scaling Speculative Decoding with Lookahead Reasoning

abstract: Tuning hyperparameters of learning algorithms is hard because gradients are usually unavailable. We compute exact gradients of cross-validation performance with respect to all hyperparameters by chaining derivatives backwards through the entire training procedure. These gradients allow us to optimize thousands of hyperparameters, including step-size and momentum schedules, weight initialization distributions, richly parameterized regularization schemes, and neural network architectures. We compute hyperparameter gradients by exactly reversing the dynamics of stochastic gradient descent with momentum.

These gradients allow us to optimize thousands of hyperparameters, including step-size and momentum schedules, weight initialization distributions, richly parameterized regularization schemes, and neural network architectures. We compute hyperparameter gradients by exactly reversing the dynamics of stochastic gradient descent with momentum.

paragraphs: Hyperparameters shape how a learning algorithm trains, but tuning them is difficult when gradients of validation performance are unavailable. This paper computes exact gradients of cross-validation performance with respect to hyperparameters by differentiating backward through the entire training procedure. Training itself becomes the sequence of computations through which the validation objective is traced.

The mechanism is exact reversal of stochastic gradient descent with momentum. By reversing those training dynamics and chaining derivatives backward, the method connects changes in training choices to changes in cross-validation performance. This gives a gradient-based route to adjusting the procedure that produced the trained model, in addition to adjusting the model's ordinary learned weights.

The resulting gradients allow optimization of thousands of hyperparameters. The examples include learning-rate and momentum schedules, initialization distributions, detailed regularization schemes, and neural network architectures. The contribution is the ability to obtain and use these gradients across a large hyperparameter space. Exact differentiation describes the gradient computation; it does not by itself assert that hyperparameter optimization reaches a global optimum.
summary.tldr: Exactly reversing momentum-based training enables gradients of validation performance for optimizing thousands of hyperparameters.

title: Gradient-based Hyperparameter Optimization through Reversible Learning

abstract: Generative models in vision have seen rapid progress due to algorithmic improvements and the availability of high-quality image datasets. In this paper, we offer contributions in both these areas to enable similar progress in audio modeling. First, we detail a powerful new WaveNet-style autoencoder model that conditions an autoregressive decoder on temporal codes learned from the raw audio waveform. Second, we introduce NSynth, a large-scale and high-quality dataset of musical notes that is an order of magnitude larger than comparable public datasets. Using NSynth, we demonstrate improved qualitative and quantitative performance of the WaveNet autoencoder over a well-tuned spectral autoencoder baseline. Finally, we show that the model learns a manifold of embeddings that allows for morphing between instruments, meaningfully interpolating in timbre to create new types of sounds that are realistic and expressive.

paragraphs: The paper advances musical-note generation through both a model and a dataset. Its WaveNet-style autoencoder learns temporal codes directly from raw audio waveforms, then uses those codes to condition an autoregressive decoder. The design connects a learned representation of a sound to a decoder that generates the audio sequence.

The authors also introduce NSynth, a large, high-quality collection of musical notes that is an order of magnitude larger than comparable public datasets. This addresses the availability of training and evaluation material alongside the modeling problem. On NSynth, the WaveNet autoencoder shows better qualitative and quantitative performance than a well-tuned spectral autoencoder baseline.

The learned embeddings also support morphing between instruments. Moving between representations can meaningfully interpolate timbre, producing new sounds that the authors describe as realistic and expressive. This finding matters because it demonstrates a use for the learned representation beyond reconstruction: it provides a space for generating variations in sound character. The paper thus links improved audio modeling with a concrete form of musical synthesis.
summary.tldr: A WaveNet autoencoder and the NSynth dataset improve musical-note modeling and enable meaningful timbre interpolation between instruments.

title: Neural Audio Synthesis of Musical Notes with WaveNet Autoencoders

abstract: Deep networks have been successfully applied to learn transferable features for adapting models from a source domain to a different target domain. In this paper, we present joint adaptation networks (JAN), which learn a transfer network by aligning the joint distributions of multiple domain-specific layers across domains based on a joint maximum mean discrepancy (JMMD) criterion. Adversarial training strategy is adopted to maximize JMMD such that the distributions of the source and target domains are made more distinguishable. Learning can be performed by stochastic gradient descent with the gradients computed by back-propagation in linear-time. Experiments testify that our model yields state of the art results on standard datasets.

paragraphs: Transferring a neural network from one domain to another requires representations that remain useful when the data distribution changes. This paper introduces joint adaptation networks, or JAN, to address that problem. Its central idea is to align the joint distributions of several domain-specific layers across the source and target domains.

The alignment criterion is joint maximum mean discrepancy, abbreviated JMMD. Considering multiple layers jointly makes their combined distribution the object of adaptation. The method also uses adversarial training to maximize JMMD, making differences between source and target distributions more distinguishable. This supplies a stronger discrepancy signal for the network’s distribution-alignment task.

The authors describe learning through stochastic gradient descent, with gradients computed by back-propagation in linear time. This connects the joint-distribution criterion to a practical neural-network training procedure. Experiments on standard datasets achieve results reported as state of the art. The findings support joint adaptation as an effective transfer-learning approach in those evaluations, alongside a computational formulation compatible with gradient-based training.
summary.tldr: Joint adaptation networks align distributions across multiple layers, using an adversarial discrepancy criterion to improve domain transfer.

title: Deep Transfer Learning with Joint Adaptation Networks

abstract: Along with the recent advances in scalable Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, sampling techniques that are based on Langevin diffusions have started receiving increasing attention. These so called Langevin Monte Carlo (LMC) methods are based on diffusions driven by a Brownian motion, which gives rise to Gaussian proposal distributions in the resulting algorithms. Even though these approaches have proven successful in many applications, their performance can be limited by the light-tailed nature of the Gaussian proposals. In this study, we extend classical LMC and develop a novel Fractional LMC (FLMC) framework that is based on a family of heavy-tailed distributions, called alpha-stable Levy distributions. As opposed to classical approaches, the proposed approach can possess large jumps while targeting the correct distribution, which would be beneficial for efficient exploration of the state space. We develop novel computational methods that can scale up to large-scale problems and we provide formal convergence analysis of the proposed scheme. Our experiments support our theory: FLMC can provide superior performance in multi-modal settings, improved convergence rates, and robustness to algorithm parameters.

paragraphs: Langevin Monte Carlo constructs sampling algorithms from stochastic dynamics driven by Brownian motion, leading to Gaussian proposals. These methods work well in many applications, but their light-tailed proposals can limit exploration. This paper develops a Fractional Langevin Monte Carlo framework that instead uses heavy-tailed alpha-stable Levy distributions.

The proposed dynamics can make large jumps while still targeting the intended distribution. Such jumps could help explore a state space more efficiently, particularly when useful regions are separated. The contribution therefore changes the underlying random motion used for sampling while preserving the goal of drawing from the correct target distribution.

The authors develop computational methods suitable for large-scale problems and provide a formal convergence analysis. Their experiments support the theory, showing that Fractional Langevin Monte Carlo can perform better in multimodal settings, improve convergence rates, and be robust to algorithm parameters. These are reported advantages of the proposed framework in the evaluated settings, supporting heavy-tailed dynamics as a useful extension of classical Langevin sampling.
summary.tldr: Fractional Langevin Monte Carlo uses heavy-tailed dynamics to enable large sampling jumps while targeting the correct distribution.

title: Fractional Langevin Monte Carlo: Exploring Levy Driven Stochastic Differential Equations for Markov Chain Monte Carlo

abstract: We apply basic statistical reasoning to signal reconstruction by machine learning - learning to map corrupted observations to clean signals - with a simple and powerful conclusion: it is possible to learn to restore images by only looking at corrupted examples, at performance at and sometimes exceeding training using clean data, without explicit image priors or likelihood models of the corruption. In practice, we show that a single model learns photographic noise removal, denoising synthetic Monte Carlo images, and reconstruction of undersampled MRI scans - all corrupted by different processes - based on noisy data only.

In practice, we show that a single model learns photographic noise removal, denoising synthetic Monte Carlo images, and reconstruction of undersampled MRI scans - all corrupted by different processes - based on noisy data only.

paragraphs: Image restoration aims to recover a clean signal from corrupted observations. Noise2Noise asks whether learning this mapping actually requires clean examples during training. Using statistical reasoning, the paper shows that it is possible to train restoration models using only corrupted data, with performance matching and sometimes exceeding training that uses clean data.

The approach does not require explicit image priors or likelihood models describing the corruption. This matters because the training setup can learn useful restoration behavior from noisy observations without supplying those additional models. The claim is that corrupted examples can be sufficient for successful learning, rather than that every possible corruption process must permit the same result.

The practical demonstrations cover photographic noise removal, denoising synthetic Monte Carlo images, and reconstruction of undersampled MRI scans. These involve different sources of corruption, yet the reported model learns restoration from noisy data alone. Together, the examples support the paper’s central finding across several restoration settings: clean training data need not always be the ingredient that makes accurate reconstruction possible.
summary.tldr: Noise2Noise shows that image restoration can be learned from corrupted data alone, sometimes matching or exceeding training with clean data.

title: Noise2Noise: Learning Image Restoration without Clean Data

abstract: Recent years have witnessed exciting progress in the study of stochastic variance reduced gradient methods (e.g., SVRG, SAGA), their accelerated variants (e.g, Katyusha) and their extensions in many different settings (e.g., online, sparse, asynchronous, distributed). Among them, accelerated methods enjoy improved convergence rates but have complex coupling structures, which makes them hard to be extended to more settings (e.g., sparse and asynchronous) due to the existence of perturbation. In this paper, we introduce a simple stochastic variance reduced algorithm (MiG), which enjoys the best-known convergence rates for both strongly convex and non-strongly convex problems. Moreover, we also present its efficient sparse and asynchronous variants, and theoretically analyze its convergence rates in these settings. Finally, extensive experiments for various machine learning problems such as logistic regression are given to illustrate the practical improvement in both serial and asynchronous settings.

paragraphs: Variance-reduced stochastic gradient methods aim to make optimization updates less noisy and thereby accelerate convergence. Accelerated versions can offer stronger convergence rates, but their updates often contain complicated dependencies. Those dependencies make it harder to adapt the methods to sparse data or asynchronous execution, where perturbations affect the optimization process.

The paper introduces MiG, a simpler stochastic variance-reduced algorithm. It achieves the best-known convergence rates reported in the paper for both strongly convex and non-strongly convex problems. Its contribution therefore combines a simpler algorithmic structure with strong theoretical rates, rather than treating simplicity and convergence speed as separate goals.

The authors also develop efficient sparse and asynchronous versions and analyze their convergence in those settings. Experiments across machine learning problems, including logistic regression, illustrate practical improvements in serial and asynchronous execution. Together, these results show why the method’s structure matters: the proposed algorithm supports extensions to important computing settings while retaining analyzed convergence behavior and demonstrating benefits in the evaluated applications.
summary.tldr: MiG combines a simple variance-reduced optimization algorithm with best-known convergence rates and analyzed sparse and asynchronous variants.

title: A Simple Stochastic Variance Reduced Algorithm with Fast Convergence Rates

abstract: Recent literature has demonstrated promising results for training Generative Adversarial Networks by employing a set of discriminators, in contrast to the traditional game involving one generator against a single adversary. Such methods perform single-objective optimization on some simple consolidation of the losses, e.g. an arithmetic average. In this work, we revisit the multiple-discriminator setting by framing the simultaneous minimization of losses provided by different models as a multi-objective optimization problem. Specifically, we evaluate the performance of multiple gradient descent and the hypervolume maximization algorithm on a number of different datasets. Moreover, we argue that the previously proposed methods and hypervolume maximization can all be seen as variations of multiple gradient descent in which the update direction can be computed efficiently. Our results indicate that hypervolume maximization presents a better compromise between sample quality and computational cost than previous methods.

paragraphs: A generative adversarial network can train its generator against several discriminators, each supplying a loss. Previous approaches often combine those losses through a simple operation such as averaging, then optimize the resulting single objective. This paper instead treats improving the losses from different discriminators as a multi-objective optimization problem.

The authors evaluate two approaches to that formulation: multiple gradient descent and hypervolume maximization. Both address how the generator should update when several discriminator objectives guide learning. They also argue that earlier methods and hypervolume maximization can be understood as variations of multiple gradient descent, with update directions that can be computed efficiently.

Experiments across several datasets indicate that hypervolume maximization offers a better balance between generated-sample quality and computational cost than previous methods. The finding is about that compromise, rather than a claim that every quality or cost measure improves independently. The broader contribution is to make the handling of multiple discriminator losses an explicit optimization choice, while connecting seemingly different training strategies within a shared framework.
summary.tldr: Treating multiple discriminator losses as separate objectives yields a hypervolume-based GAN training method with a better reported quality–cost compromise.

title: Multi-objective training of Generative Adversarial Networks with multiple discriminators

abstract: We consider the problem of learning representations that achieve group and subgroup fairness with respect to multiple sensitive attributes. Taking inspiration from the disentangled representation learning literature, we propose an algorithm for learning compact representations of datasets that are useful for reconstruction and prediction, but are also flexibly fair , meaning they can be easily modified at test time to achieve subgroup demographic parity with respect to multiple sensitive attributes and their conjunctions. We show empirically that the resulting encoder—which does not require the sensitive attributes for inference—allows for the adaptation of a single representation to a variety of fair classification tasks with new target labels and subgroup definitions.

paragraphs: Fair representation learning becomes more demanding when fairness must account for several sensitive attributes and their combinations. This paper addresses that problem by learning a compact representation that remains useful for reconstruction and prediction while supporting different fairness requirements. Its design draws inspiration from disentangled representation learning.

The proposed flexibility lies in modifying the representation at test time to achieve subgroup demographic parity for multiple sensitive attributes and their conjunctions. This means the intended fairness target can concern groups defined by combinations of attributes, as well as groups defined by individual attributes. The method is designed to adapt a learned representation to these different targets.

Empirical results show that a single representation can support fair classification tasks with new target labels and subgroup definitions. The resulting encoder does not require sensitive attributes during inference. These findings support the practical adaptability of the approach; the fairness criterion being addressed is subgroup demographic parity, so the result should be understood in terms of that specific goal.
summary.tldr: A disentanglement-inspired representation can be adapted at test time for subgroup demographic parity across multiple sensitive attributes and new classification tasks.

title: Flexibly Fair Representation Learning by Disentanglement

abstract: In this paper, we propose a faster stochastic alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) for nonconvex optimization by using a new stochastic path-integrated differential estimator (SPIDER), called as SPIDER-ADMM. Moreover, we prove that the SPIDER-ADMM achieves a record-breaking incremental first-order oracle (IFO) complexity for finding an $\epsilon$-approximate solution. As one of major contribution of this paper, we provide a new theoretical analysis framework for nonconvex stochastic ADMM methods with providing the optimal IFO complexity. Based on this new analysis framework, we study the unsolved optimal IFO complexity of the existing non-convex SVRG-ADMM and SAGA-ADMM methods, and prove their the optimal IFO complexity. Thus, the SPIDER-ADMM improves the existing stochastic ADMM methods. Moreover, we extend SPIDER-ADMM to the online setting, and propose a faster online SPIDER-ADMM. Our theoretical analysis also derives the IFO complexity of the online SPIDER-ADMM. Finally, the experimental results on benchmark datasets validate that the proposed algorithms have faster convergence rate than the existing ADMM algorithms for nonconvex optimization.

paragraphs: This paper improves stochastic ADMM for nonconvex optimization by incorporating the SPIDER estimator. The resulting method, SPIDER-ADMM, is designed to reach an approximate solution with fewer incremental first-order oracle calls. This complexity measure counts the gradient-information requests needed by the optimization procedure, making the theoretical comparison about computational work required to reach a specified accuracy.

Beyond analyzing their own method, they use it to establish optimal oracle-complexity results for existing SVRG-ADMM and SAGA-ADMM methods, resolving a previously unsettled question. They report that SPIDER-ADMM improves on existing stochastic ADMM methods and achieves record-setting oracle complexity for an epsilon-approximate solution.

The work extends the method to an online setting and derives an oracle-complexity result for that version as well. Benchmark experiments show faster convergence than existing ADMM algorithms for nonconvex optimization. The contribution combines a new optimizer, a reusable theoretical framework, and empirical support for the proposed methods’ convergence advantage.
summary.tldr: SPIDER-ADMM improves nonconvex stochastic optimization efficiency and introduces an analysis framework for oracle-complexity guarantees.

title: Faster Stochastic Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers for Nonconvex Optimization

abstract: This paper considers Safe Policy Improvement (SPI) in Batch Reinforcement Learning (Batch RL): from a fixed dataset and without direct access to the true environment, train a policy that is guaranteed to perform at least as well as the baseline policy used to collect the data. Our approach, called SPI with Baseline Bootstrapping (SPIBB), is inspired by the knows-what-it-knows paradigm: it bootstraps the trained policy with the baseline when the uncertainty is high. Our first algorithm, $\Pi_b$-SPIBB, comes with SPI theoretical guarantees. We also implement a variant, $\Pi_{\leq b}$-SPIBB, that is even more efficient in practice. We apply our algorithms to a motivational stochastic gridworld domain and further demonstrate on randomly generated MDPs the superiority of SPIBB with respect to existing algorithms, not only in safety but also in mean performance. Finally, we implement a model-free version of SPIBB and show its benefits on a navigation task with deep RL implementation called SPIBB-DQN, which is, to the best of our knowledge, the first RL algorithm relying on a neural network representation able to train efficiently and reliably from batch data, without any interaction with the environment.

paragraphs: The paper studies safe policy improvement from a fixed reinforcement learning dataset, with no direct access to the true environment. The safety objective is performance relative to the baseline policy that collected the data: learning should produce a policy that performs at least as well. Limited evidence makes this difficult because some proposed changes are more uncertain than others.

SPIBB addresses uncertainty by falling back on the baseline where uncertainty is high. The first algorithm, Pi_b-SPIBB, comes with theoretical safe policy improvement guarantees. A second variant, Pi_<=b-SPIBB, is reported to be even more efficient in practice. The shared principle is to preserve baseline behavior when the available data do not support confident improvement.

Experiments include a stochastic gridworld and randomly generated decision processes, where SPIBB shows advantages in both safety and mean performance over existing algorithms. The authors also implement a model-free deep version, SPIBB-DQN, and demonstrate benefits on navigation. This extends the practical investigation to neural representations trained from batch data without environment interaction.
summary.tldr: SPIBB learns from fixed data while retaining baseline behavior under high uncertainty, with safety guarantees for its first algorithm.

title: Safe Policy Improvement with Baseline Bootstrapping

abstract: Random Matrix Theory (RMT) is applied to analyze the weight matrices of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), including both production quality, pre-trained models such as AlexNet and Inception, and smaller models trained from scratch, such as LeNet5 and a miniature-AlexNet. Empirical and theoretical results clearly indicate that the empirical spectral density (ESD) of DNN layer matrices displays signatures of traditionally-regularized statistical models, even in the absence of exogenously specifying traditional forms of regularization, such as Dropout or Weight Norm constraints. Building on recent results in RMT, most notably its extension to Universality classes of Heavy-Tailed matrices, we develop a theory to identify 5+1 Phases of Training , corresponding to increasing amounts of Implicit Self-Regularization . For smaller and/or older DNNs, this Implicit Self-Regularization is like traditional Tikhonov regularization, in that there is a “size scale” separating signal from noise. For state-of-the-art DNNs, however, we identify a novel form of Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization , similar to the self-organization seen in the statistical physics of disordered systems. This implicit Self-Regularization can depend strongly on the many knobs of the training process. By exploiting the generalization gap phenomena, we demonstrate that we can cause a small model to exhibit all 5+1 phases of training simply by changing the batch size.

paragraphs: This paper studies neural-network weight matrices using random matrix theory. It examines both pretrained production models and smaller networks trained from scratch. The empirical spectral densities of their layer matrices show signatures associated with regularized statistical models, even when traditional regularizers such as dropout or weight-norm constraints are not explicitly imposed.

Smaller or older networks exhibit behavior resembling Tikhonov regularization, with a characteristic scale separating signal from noise. For the state-of-the-art networks studied, they identify heavy-tailed self-regularization, drawing on heavy-tailed random matrix theory and connections to disordered physical systems.

Training choices can strongly affect this implicit regularization. By changing batch size, the authors make a small model exhibit all 5+1 phases, using generalization-gap phenomena in the demonstration. The contribution is a framework for interpreting learned weight structure and relating it to training behavior. The batch-size result shows that these spectral regimes can change within a model as the training process changes.
summary.tldr: Random matrix analysis identifies traditional and heavy-tailed forms of neural-network self-regularization, with training phases that can shift through batch-size changes.

title: Traditional and Heavy Tailed Self Regularization in Neural Network Models

abstract: Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL) aims at classifying unlabeled objects by leveraging auxiliary knowledge, such as semantic representations. A limitation of previous approaches is that only intrinsic properties of objects, e.g. their visual appearance, are taken into account while their context, e.g. the surrounding objects in the image, is ignored. Following the intuitive principle that objects tend to be found in certain contexts but not others, we propose a new and challenging approach, context-aware ZSL, that leverages semantic representations in a new way to model the conditional likelihood of an object to appear in a given context. Finally, through extensive experiments conducted on Visual Genome, we show that contextual information can substantially improve the standard ZSL approach and is robust to unbalanced classes.

paragraphs: Zero-shot object recognition uses auxiliary semantic knowledge to classify objects without relying on labeled examples of every target category. This paper focuses on a source of evidence that earlier approaches overlooked: the context surrounding an object. An object's own appearance provides useful information, but the other objects in the image can also help establish what it is likely to be.

The authors propose context-aware zero-shot learning, using semantic representations to model how likely an object is to occur in a particular context. This changes the role of semantic information from describing the object alone to helping describe its relationship with its surroundings. The approach follows the observation that objects occur more naturally in some contexts than in others.

Experiments on Visual Genome show that contextual information can substantially improve standard zero-shot recognition. The paper also reports robustness to class imbalance, where categories have unequal representation. These findings support treating surrounding objects as useful recognition evidence, alongside the intrinsic properties of the object being classified.
summary.tldr: Modeling which objects fit a scene's context substantially improves zero-shot recognition in the reported Visual Genome experiments.

title: Context-Aware Zero-Shot Learning for Object Recognition

abstract: Machine Teaching studies how efficiently a Teacher can guide a Learner to a target hypothesis. We focus on the model of Machine Teaching with a black box learner introduced in [Dasgupta et al., ICML 2019], where the teaching is done interactively without having any knowledge of the Learner’s algorithm and class of hypotheses, apart from the fact that it contains the target hypothesis $h^*$. We first refine some existing results for this model and, then, we study new variants of it. Motivated by the realistic possibility that $h^*$ is not available to the learner, we consider the case where the teacher can only aim at having the learner converge to a best available approximation of $h^*$. We also consider weaker black box learners, where, in each round, the choice of the consistent hypothesis returned to the Teacher is not adversarial, and in particular, we show that better provable bounds can be obtained for a type of Learner that moves to the next hypothesis smoothly, preferring hypotheses that are close to the current one; and for another type of Learner that can provide to the Teacher hypotheses chosen at random among those consistent with the examples received so far. Finally, we present an empirical evaluation of our basic interactive teacher on real datasets.

paragraphs: Machine teaching studies how a teacher can efficiently guide a learner toward a desired hypothesis. This paper examines interactive teaching when the learner is a black box: the teacher does not know its algorithm or hypothesis class. In the starting model, the only relevant knowledge is that the target hypothesis belongs to that class.

The authors refine existing results and then relax parts of this setup. One variant allows the target to be unavailable to the learner, so the teaching objective becomes convergence to the best available approximation. Other variants consider learners whose choice among hypotheses consistent with the examples is not adversarial.

Better provable bounds are obtained for learners that favor hypotheses close to their current one and for learners that return a random consistent hypothesis. The paper also evaluates its basic interactive teacher on real datasets. Its central contribution is to show how teaching guarantees change with target availability and specific forms of learner behavior, even when the learner's internal algorithm remains unknown.
summary.tldr: The paper extends black-box machine teaching to approximate targets and proves better bounds for learners that change hypotheses smoothly or select them randomly.

title: Teaching with Limited Information on the Learner’s Behaviour

abstract: We study the computational and statistical tradeoffs in inferring combinatorial structures of high dimensional simple zero-field ferromagnetic Ising model. Under the framework of oracle computational model where an algorithm interacts with an oracle that discourses a randomized version of truth, we characterize the computational lower bounds of learning combinatorial structures in polynomial time, under which no algorithms within polynomial-time can distinguish between graphs with and without certain structures. This hardness of learning with limited computational budget is shown to be characterized by a novel quantity called vertex overlap ratio. Such quantity is universally valid for many specific graph structures including cliques and nearest neighbors. On the other side, we attain the optimal rates for testing these structures against empty graph by proposing the quadratic testing statistics to match the lower bounds. We also investigate the relationship between computational bounds and information-theoretic bounds for such problems, and found gaps between the two boundaries in inferring some particular structures, especially for those with dense edges.

paragraphs: This paper studies how difficult it is to detect graph structures in high-dimensional, simple, zero-field ferromagnetic Ising models. It separates two questions: whether the available information supports detection, and whether an algorithm with a polynomial computational budget can perform that detection.

The computational analysis uses an oracle model in which algorithms receive randomized information about the truth. Within that framework, the authors establish regimes where polynomial-time algorithms cannot distinguish graphs containing particular structures from graphs without them. A quantity called the vertex overlap ratio characterizes this difficulty and applies to several structures, including cliques and nearest neighbors.

The paper also constructs quadratic test statistics that achieve optimal rates when testing these structures against an empty graph. Comparing computational and information-theoretic boundaries reveals gaps for some structures, especially those with dense edges. The consequence is that statistical detectability and efficient computation can impose different requirements; the computational lower bounds are specifically established within the stated oracle framework.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes oracle-model computational barriers to detecting Ising graph structures and identifies gaps from statistical limits.

title: Computational and Statistical Tradeoffs in Inferring Combinatorial Structures of Ising Model

abstract: Monte-Carlo planning and Reinforcement Learning (RL) are essential to sequential decision making. The recent AlphaGo and AlphaZero algorithms have shown how to successfully combine these two paradigms to solve large-scale sequential decision problems. These methodologies exploit a variant of the well-known UCT algorithm to trade off the exploitation of good actions and the exploration of unvisited states, but their empirical success comes at the cost of poor sample-efficiency and high computation time. In this paper, we overcome these limitations by introducing the use of convex regularization in Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to drive exploration efficiently and to improve policy updates. First, we introduce a unifying theory on the use of generic convex regularizers in MCTS, deriving the first regret analysis of regularized MCTS and showing that it guarantees an exponential convergence rate. Second, we exploit our theoretical framework to introduce novel regularized backup operators for MCTS, based on the relative entropy of the policy update and, more importantly, on the Tsallis entropy of the policy, for which we prove superior theoretical guarantees. We empirically verify the consequence of our theoretical results on a toy problem. Finally, we show how our framework can easily be incorporated in AlphaGo and we empirically show the superiority of convex regularization, w.r.t. representative baselines, on well-known RL problems across several Atari games.
