paragraphs: Monte-Carlo Tree Search plans by exploring possible sequences of decisions. It must balance revisiting promising actions against investigating less-explored possibilities. The paper targets the sample and computational costs of this process, including the kind of search used alongside reinforcement learning in AlphaGo and AlphaZero.

The authors introduce a general theoretical framework for convex regularization in tree search. Regularization shapes exploration and policy updates rather than leaving those choices entirely to the usual search rule. Their analysis provides regret guarantees for regularized MCTS and establishes an exponential convergence rate. They then derive new backup operators, which determine how information from explored outcomes updates the search tree, using relative entropy and Tsallis entropy.

The Tsallis-based construction receives stronger theoretical guarantees in their framework. A toy problem illustrates consequences of the analysis, while experiments across several Atari games show advantages over representative baselines. The authors also describe how the framework can be incorporated into AlphaGo. The contribution connects a general mathematical treatment of regularization to concrete changes in how search explores and updates decisions.
summary.tldr: Convex regularization gives Monte-Carlo Tree Search new exploration and update rules with theoretical guarantees and reported Atari improvements.

title: Convex Regularization in Monte-Carlo Tree Search

abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a popular tool in training large-scale machine learning models. Its performance, however, is highly variable, depending crucially on the choice of the step sizes. Accordingly, a variety of strategies for tuning the step sizes have been proposed, ranging from coordinate-wise approaches (a.k.a. “adaptive” step sizes) to sophisticated heuristics to change the step size in each iteration. In this paper, we study two step size schedules whose power has been repeatedly confirmed in practice: the exponential and the cosine step sizes. For the first time, we provide theoretical support for them proving convergence rates for smooth non-convex functions, with and without the Polyak-Ł{}ojasiewicz (PL) condition. Moreover, we show the surprising property that these two strategies are \emph{adaptive} to the noise level in the stochastic gradients of PL functions. That is, contrary to polynomial step sizes, they achieve almost optimal performance without needing to know the noise level nor tuning their hyperparameters based on it. Finally, we conduct a fair and comprehensive empirical evaluation of real-world datasets with deep learning architectures. Results show that, even if only requiring at most two hyperparameters to tune, these two strategies best or match the performance of various finely-tuned state-of-the-art strategies.
originalAbstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a popular tool in training large-scale machine learning models. Its performance, however, is highly variable, depending crucially on the choice of the step sizes. Accordingly, a variety of strategies for tuning the step sizes have been proposed, ranging from coordinate-wise approaches (a.k.a. “adaptive” step sizes) to sophisticated heuristics to change the step size in each iteration. In this paper, we study two step size schedules whose power has been repeatedly confirmed in practice: the exponential and the cosine step sizes. For the first time, we provide theoretical support for them proving convergence rates for smooth non-convex functions, with and without the Polyak-Ł{}ojasiewicz (PL) condition. Moreover, we show the surprising property that these two strategies are \emph{adaptive} to the noise level in the stochastic gradients of PL functions. That is, contrary to polynomial step sizes, they achieve almost optimal performance without needing to know the noise level nor tuning their hyperparameters based on it. Finally, we conduct a fair and comprehensive empirical evaluation of real-world datasets with deep learning architectures. Results show that, even if only requiring at most two hyperparameters to tune, these two strategies best or match the performance of various finely-tuned state-of-the-art strategies.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent depends strongly on its step sizes: the amounts by which training updates change the model. This paper revisits exponential and cosine schedules, two simple ways of changing those amounts over training that already have practical support. Its central contribution is to explain theoretically when these schedules work well.

The authors prove convergence rates for smooth nonconvex objectives, both with and without the additional Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition. For objectives satisfying that condition, they also show that the schedules adapt to the noise in stochastic gradients. They achieve almost optimal performance without knowing the noise level or tuning their hyperparameters to it. This is a specific noise-adaptation result, rather than a claim that all tuning becomes unnecessary.

An empirical comparison on real datasets and deep learning architectures finds that the two schedules match or outperform several carefully tuned alternatives. Each requires at most two hyperparameters to tune. Together, the theory and experiments support these schedules as simple options whose performance can rival more elaborate strategies in the studied settings.
summary.tldr: Exponential and cosine step-size schedules receive convergence guarantees and, under the PL condition, adapt to gradient noise without noise-specific tuning.

title: A Second look at Exponential and Cosine Step Sizes: Simplicity, Adaptivity, and Performance

abstract: Unrolled computation graphs arise in many scenarios, including training RNNs, tuning hyperparameters through unrolled optimization, and training learned optimizers. Current approaches to optimizing parameters in such computation graphs suffer from high variance gradients, bias, slow updates, or large memory usage. We introduce a method called Persistent Evolution Strategies (PES), which divides the computation graph into a series of truncated unrolls, and performs an evolution strategies-based update step after each unroll. PES eliminates bias from these truncations by accumulating correction terms over the entire sequence of unrolls. PES allows for rapid parameter updates, has low memory usage, is unbiased, and has reasonable variance characteristics. We experimentally demonstrate the advantages of PES compared to several other methods for gradient estimation on synthetic tasks, and show its applicability to training learned optimizers and tuning hyperparameters.

paragraphs: Some learning problems optimize parameters through a sequence of computations, as in recurrent networks, learned optimizers, or hyperparameter tuning through training steps. Estimating gradients through these unrolled graphs can involve high memory use, slow updates, high variance, or bias. This paper proposes Persistent Evolution Strategies to improve that combination of tradeoffs.

PES divides the computation into shorter unrolls and performs an evolution-strategies update after each segment. Simply truncating a sequence can introduce bias. PES addresses that problem by accumulating correction terms across the entire sequence of unrolls, preserving information needed to eliminate the bias caused by those truncations.

The resulting estimator is described as unbiased, memory efficient, and capable of rapid parameter updates, with reasonable variance characteristics. Synthetic-task experiments demonstrate advantages over several other gradient-estimation methods. Further experiments show applicability to learned-optimizer training and hyperparameter tuning. The contribution is a way to update frequently from short computation segments while maintaining correction terms that account for the longer sequence.
summary.tldr: PES accumulates correction terms across truncated unrolls to obtain unbiased gradient estimates with low memory use and frequent updates.

title: Unbiased Gradient Estimation in Unrolled Computation Graphs with Persistent Evolution Strategies

abstract: As its width tends to infinity, a deep neural network’s behavior under gradient descent can become simplified and predictable (e.g. given by the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK)), if it is parametrized appropriately (e.g. the NTK parametrization). However, we show that the standard and NTK parametrizations of a neural network do not admit infinite-width limits that can *learn* features, which is crucial for pretraining and transfer learning such as with BERT. We propose simple modifications to the standard parametrization to allow for feature learning in the limit. Using the *Tensor Programs* technique, we derive explicit formulas for such limits. On Word2Vec and few-shot learning on Omniglot via MAML, two canonical tasks that rely crucially on feature learning, we compute these limits exactly. We find that they outperform both NTK baselines and finite-width networks, with the latter approaching the infinite-width feature learning performance as width increases.

paragraphs: Infinite-width limits can make neural-network training easier to characterize mathematically, but the parameterization determines what behavior survives that limit. This paper shows that standard and neural tangent kernel parameterizations do not yield infinite-width limits that learn features. That matters for tasks such as pretraining and transfer learning, where adapting representations is central.

The authors introduce simple modifications to standard parameterization that permit feature learning at infinite width. Using Tensor Programs, they derive explicit formulas for the resulting limits. This supplies a mathematically tractable description in which learned representations can change, extending the range of behavior captured by infinite-width analysis.

They compute these limits exactly for Word2Vec and for few-shot learning on Omniglot using MAML. In those tasks, the limits outperform both NTK baselines and finite-width networks, while the finite networks approach the feature-learning limit’s performance as width grows. The findings demonstrate that infinite width need not eliminate feature learning: the outcome depends on how the network is parameterized.
summary.tldr: Modified parameterizations preserve feature learning at infinite width and outperform tested NTK and finite-network baselines on two tasks.

title: Tensor Programs IV: Feature Learning in Infinite-Width Neural Networks

abstract: Robust loss functions are essential for training deep neural networks with better generalization power in the presence of noisy labels. Symmetric loss functions are confirmed to be robust to label noise. However, the symmetric condition is overly restrictive. In this work, we propose a new class of loss functions, namely asymmetric loss functions, which are robust to learning from noisy labels for arbitrary noise type. Subsequently, we investigate general theoretical properties of asymmetric loss functions, including classification-calibration, excess risk bound, and noise-tolerance. Meanwhile, we introduce the asymmetry ratio to measure the asymmetry of a loss function, and the empirical results show that a higher ratio will provide better robustness. Moreover, we modify several common loss functions, and establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for them to be asymmetric. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that asymmetric loss functions can outperform state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Incorrect training labels can push a neural network toward the wrong predictions, making the choice of training loss especially important. Symmetric loss functions offer robustness to label noise, but the symmetry requirement restricts which losses can be used. This paper introduces asymmetric loss functions as a broader class for learning with arbitrary types of label noise.

The authors study how these losses connect to classification quality through classification calibration, excess risk bounds, and noise tolerance. These properties address whether optimizing a loss supports good classification and how errors in that optimization relate to prediction errors. They also define an asymmetry ratio that measures a loss function's asymmetry and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for modified versions of several common losses to belong to the class.

Empirically, larger asymmetry ratios are associated with better robustness. Benchmark experiments also show that asymmetric losses can outperform previous leading methods. The contribution therefore combines a theoretical loss-design framework with evidence that its measurable properties can help guide practical learning from unreliable labels.
summary.tldr: Asymmetric losses broaden the design of noise-robust training objectives and can outperform existing methods on noisy-label benchmarks.

title: Asymmetric Loss Functions for Learning with Noisy Labels

abstract: The linearised Laplace method for estimating model uncertainty has received renewed attention in the Bayesian deep learning community. The method provides reliable error bars and admits a closed-form expression for the model evidence, allowing for scalable selection of model hyperparameters. In this work, we examine the assumptions behind this method, particularly in conjunction with model selection. We show that these interact poorly with some now-standard tools of deep learning–stochastic approximation methods and normalisation layers–and make recommendations for how to better adapt this classic method to the modern setting. We provide theoretical support for our recommendations and validate them empirically on MLPs, classic CNNs, residual networks with and without normalisation layers, generative autoencoders and transformers.

We provide theoretical support for our recommendations and validate them empirically on MLPs, classic CNNs, residual networks with and without normalisation layers, generative autoencoders and transformers.

paragraphs: The linearised Laplace method offers a way to attach uncertainty estimates to neural networks. It also supplies a closed-form model evidence expression, which makes it attractive for choosing hyperparameters at scale. This paper examines whether the assumptions supporting that approach remain appropriate when it is used with standard deep learning practices.

The authors identify problematic interactions with stochastic approximation methods and normalisation layers. These interactions matter especially for model selection: an uncertainty method can have an appealing mathematical expression while the assumptions behind using that expression fit the trained network poorly. The paper therefore focuses on adapting the method to the circumstances in which modern networks are actually trained and constructed.

The contribution includes recommendations supported by theory and empirical validation. The evaluations cover multilayer perceptrons, conventional convolutional networks, residual networks with and without normalisation, generative autoencoders, and transformers. This range examines the recommendations across several architectures. The stated finding is that the classic method needs considered adaptation when paired with these modern tools, particularly when its evidence is used to select models.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies assumption mismatches in linearised Laplace model selection and develops theoretically supported adaptations for modern neural networks.

title: Adapting the Linearised Laplace Model Evidence for Modern Deep Learning

abstract: Tensor decomposition is a dominant framework for multiway data analysis and prediction. Although practical data often contains timestamps for the observed entries, existing tensor decomposition approaches overlook or under-use this valuable time information. They either drop the timestamps or bin them into crude steps and hence ignore the temporal dynamics within each step or use simple parametric time coefficients. To overcome these limitations, we propose Bayesian Continuous-Time Tucker Decomposition. We model the tensor-core of the classical Tucker decomposition as a time-varying function, and place a Gaussian process prior to flexibly estimate all kinds of temporal dynamics. In this way, our model maintains the interpretability while is flexible enough to capture various complex temporal relationships between the tensor nodes. For efficient and high-quality posterior inference, we use the stochastic differential equation (SDE) representation of temporal GPs to build an equivalent state-space prior, which avoids huge kernel matrix computation and sparse/low-rank approximations. We then use Kalman filtering, RTS smoothing, and conditional moment matching to develop a scalable message passing inference algorithm. We show the advantage of our method in simulation and several real-world applications.

paragraphs: Tensor decomposition analyzes data involving several kinds of entities or dimensions together. Such observations often carry timestamps, but discarding time or grouping it into coarse intervals can hide changing relationships. This paper extends Tucker decomposition so that these relationships can evolve continuously, preserving temporal information that simpler treatments underuse.

The method makes the Tucker core a function of time and gives that function a Gaussian process prior. This provides a flexible way to represent temporal dynamics while retaining the decomposition's interpretability. The changing core captures how relationships among tensor nodes develop, rather than forcing them into fixed time bins or simple parametric coefficients.

Efficient inference comes from expressing temporal Gaussian processes through stochastic differential equations and an equivalent state-space prior. This avoids huge kernel-matrix computations and sparse or low-rank approximations. The authors combine Kalman filtering, RTS smoothing, and conditional moment matching into a scalable message-passing algorithm. Simulations and several real applications demonstrate advantages of the approach, supporting continuous-time modeling as a practical extension of tensor analysis.
summary.tldr: A time-varying Tucker core with a Gaussian process prior captures continuous temporal relationships, with state-space inference making the model scalable.

title: Bayesian Continuous-Time Tucker Decomposition

abstract: Researchers may perform regressions using a sketch of data of size m instead of the full sample of size n for a variety of reasons. This paper considers the case when the regression errors do not have constant variance and heteroskedasticity robust standard errors would normally be needed for test statistics to provide accurate inference. We show that estimates using data sketched by random projections will behave ’as if’ the errors were homoskedastic. Estimation by random sampling would not have this property. The result arises because the sketched estimates in the case of random projections can be expressed as degenerate U-statistics, and under certain conditions, these statistics are asymptotically normal with homoskedastic variance. We verify that the conditions hold not only in the case of least squares regression when the covariates are exogenous, but also in instrumental variables estimation when the covariates are endogenous. The result implies that inference can be simpler than the full sample case if the sketching scheme is appropriately chosen.

paragraphs: Regression is sometimes performed on a smaller sketch of a dataset instead of the full sample. This paper asks how that choice affects statistical inference when regression errors have unequal variances. In the full dataset, such heteroskedasticity would ordinarily call for robust standard errors to support accurate tests.

The authors show that estimates from random-projection sketches can behave as though the errors had constant variance. Random sampling does not share this property. Their explanation expresses the projected-data estimates as degenerate U-statistics and establishes that, under certain conditions, these statistics have asymptotically normal distributions with a homoskedastic form of variance.

The paper verifies the relevant conditions for least squares with exogenous covariates and for instrumental variables estimation with endogenous covariates. The implication is that an appropriately chosen sketch can simplify inference as well as reduce the data used for estimation. This is an asymptotic result under the stated conditions; its significance lies in how the sketching mechanism changes the estimator’s statistical behavior.
summary.tldr: Under stated conditions, random-projection sketches yield regression estimates with homoskedastic-form asymptotic variance even when original errors are heteroskedastic.

title: Least Squares Estimation using Sketched Data with Heteroskedastic Errors

abstract: Sparsely activated transformers, such as Mixture of Experts (MoE), have received great interest due to their outrageous scaling capability which enables dramatical increases in model size without significant increases in computational cost. To achieve this, MoE models replace the feedforward sub-layer with Mixture-of-Experts sub-layer in transformers and use a gating network to route each token to its assigned experts. Since the common practice for efficient training of such models requires distributing experts and tokens across different machines, this routing strategy often incurs huge cross-machine communication cost because tokens and their assigned experts likely reside in different machines. In this paper, we propose Gating Dropout , which allows tokens to ignore the gating network and stay at their local machines, thus reducing the cross-machine communication. Similar to traditional dropout, we also show that Gating Dropout has a regularization effect during training, resulting in improved generalization performance. We validate the effectiveness of Gating Dropout on multilingual machine translation tasks. Our results demonstrate that Gating Dropout improves a state-of-the-art MoE model with faster wall-clock time convergence rates and better BLEU scores for a variety of model sizes and datasets.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts transformers increase model capacity by routing each token to selected experts instead of activating every expert. When training distributes tokens and experts across machines, those routing decisions can require substantial data movement. A token may need processing by an expert located elsewhere, making communication an important cost despite the sparse computation.

Gating Dropout allows tokens to bypass the gating network and remain on their current machines. This reduces cross-machine communication by changing the routing behavior during training. The authors also find a regularization effect resembling traditional dropout: the altered training procedure improves generalization, giving the method a learning benefit alongside its communication savings.

The evaluation focuses on multilingual machine translation. Across several model sizes and datasets, adding Gating Dropout to a state-of-the-art mixture-of-experts model produces faster convergence in elapsed time and better BLEU scores. The results show that a routing modification can address both distributed execution costs and predictive quality within the tested translation settings.
summary.tldr: Gating Dropout keeps some token processing local, reducing communication while improving translation quality and training-time convergence in the reported experiments.

title: Gating Dropout: Communication-efficient Regularization for Sparsely Activated Transformers

abstract: We present Muse, a text-to-image Transformermodel that achieves state-of-the-art image genera-tion performance while being significantly moreefficient than diffusion or autoregressive models.Muse is trained on a masked modeling task indiscrete token space: given the text embeddingextracted from a pre-trained large language model(LLM), Muse learns to predict randomly maskedimage tokens. Compared to pixel-space diffusionmodels, such as Imagen and DALL-E 2, Muse issignificantly more efficient due to the use of dis-crete tokens and requires fewer sampling itera-tions; compared to autoregressive models such asParti, Muse is more efficient due to the use of par-allel decoding. The use of a pre-trained LLM en-ables fine-grained language understanding, whichtranslates to high-fidelity image generation andthe understanding of visual concepts such as ob-jects, their spatial relationships, pose, cardinalityetc. Our 900M parameter model achieves a newSOTA on CC3M, with an FID score of 6.06. TheMuse 3B parameter model achieves an FID of7.88 on zero-shot COCO evaluation, along with aCLIP score of 0.32. paragraphs: Muse generates images from text by learning to fill in missing image tokens. During training, some discrete tokens representing an image are randomly hidden, and a Transformer predicts them using a text embedding from a pretrained large language model. This combines language understanding with a masked prediction task over the image representation.

The efficiency argument has two parts. Compared with pixel-space diffusion models, Muse uses discrete tokens and needs fewer sampling iterations. Compared with autoregressive models, it can decode tokens in parallel. The authors also connect the pretrained language model to fine-grained understanding of objects, spatial relationships, poses, and quantities, supporting faithful interpretation of text prompts.

The reported results include an FID of 6.06 on CC3M for the 900-million-parameter model, described as a new state of the art. The three-billion-parameter model achieves an FID of 7.88 and a CLIP score of 0.32 on zero-shot COCO evaluation. Muse additionally supports inpainting, outpainting, and mask-free editing without fine-tuning or model inversion, extending the same model beyond initial image generation.
summary.tldr: Muse uses parallel masked-token prediction to generate and edit images efficiently while achieving strong reported text-to-image results.

title: Muse: Text-To-Image Generation via Masked Generative Transformers

abstract: Two main families of node feature augmentation schemes have been explored for enhancing GNNs: random features and spectral positional encoding. Surprisingly, however, there is still no clear understanding of the relation between these two augmentation schemes. Here we propose a novel family of positional encoding schemes which draws a link between the above two approaches and improves over both. The new approach, named Random Feature Propagation (RFP), is inspired by the power iteration method and its generalizations. It concatenates several intermediate steps of an iterative algorithm for computing the dominant eigenvectors of a propagation matrix, starting from random node features. Notably, these propagation steps are based on graph-dependent propagation operators that can be either predefined or learned. We explore the theoretical and empirical benefits of RFP. First, we provide theoretical justifications for using random features, for incorporating early propagation steps, and for using multiple random initializations. Then, we empirically demonstrate that RFP significantly outperforms both spectral PE and random features in multiple node classification and graph classification benchmarks.

The new approach, named Random Feature Propagation (RFP), is inspired by the power iteration method and its generalizations. It concatenates several intermediate steps of an iterative algorithm for computing the dominant eigenvectors of a propagation matrix, starting from random node features. Notably, these propagation steps are based on graph-dependent propagation operators that can be either predefined or learned. We explore the theoretical and empirical benefits of RFP. First, we provide theoretical justifications for using random features, for incorporating early propagation steps, and for using multiple random initializations. Then, we empirically demonstrate that RFP significantly outperforms both spectral PE and random features in multiple node classification and graph classification benchmarks.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can be strengthened by adding information that helps distinguish nodes and describe their structural positions. Two common approaches use random features or spectral positional encodings. This paper connects them through Random Feature Propagation, or RFP, rather than treating them as separate design choices.

RFP begins with random node features and repeatedly propagates them using a graph-dependent operator. Its construction draws on iterative methods for computing dominant eigenvectors. Crucially, it concatenates several intermediate steps, retaining information from the progression of the iteration. The propagation operator can be chosen beforehand or learned.

The authors provide theoretical reasons for using random features, keeping early propagation steps, and combining multiple random initializations. They then show that RFP significantly outperforms both random features and spectral positional encodings on multiple node- and graph-classification benchmarks. The results indicate that the route from random initialization toward spectral structure contains useful information of its own, giving a principled reason to preserve intermediate representations in a positional encoding.
summary.tldr: Random Feature Propagation builds graph positional encodings from intermediate propagation steps, outperforming random-feature and spectral alternatives on multiple benchmarks.

title: Graph Positional Encoding via Random Feature Propagation

abstract: Multi-task learning has the potential to improve generalization by maximizing positive transfer between tasks while reducing task interference. Fully achieving this potential is hindered by manually designed architectures that remain static throughout training. On the contrary, learning in the brain occurs through structural changes that are in tandem with changes in synaptic strength. Thus, we propose Multi-Task Structural Learning (MTSL) that simultaneously learns the multi-task architecture and its parameters. MTSL begins with an identical single-task network for each task and alternates between a task-learning phase and a structural-learning phase. In the task learning phase, each network specializes in the corresponding task. In each of the structural learning phases, starting from the earliest layer, locally similar task layers first transfer their knowledge to a newly created group layer before being removed. MTSL then uses the group layer in place of the corresponding removed task layers and moves on to the next layers. Our empirical results show that MTSL achieves competitive generalization with various baselines and improves robustness to out-of-distribution data.

Thus, we propose Multi-Task Structural Learning (MTSL) that simultaneously learns the multi-task architecture and its parameters. MTSL begins with an identical single-task network for each task and alternates between a task-learning phase and a structural-learning phase. paragraphs: Multi-task learning can benefit when related tasks share useful knowledge, but sharing can also cause interference. A fixed, manually designed architecture decides in advance where that sharing occurs. This paper proposes Multi-Task Structural Learning, or MTSL, which learns the architecture together with its parameters as training proceeds.

MTSL starts with a separate network of the same design for each task. It alternates between task learning, where each network specializes, and structural learning, where locally similar task layers are grouped. Beginning at early layers, those layers transfer knowledge into a newly created shared group layer. The original layers are then removed and replaced by that group layer before the procedure considers subsequent layers.

This process makes sharing depend on similarities found during learning. The reported experiments show generalization competitive with several baselines and improved robustness on out-of-distribution data. The findings support adapting the network’s structure as a way to manage task relationships, while the generalization result is competitive rather than a claim of uniformly superior accuracy.
summary.tldr: MTSL learns which task layers to share during training, achieving competitive generalization and improved out-of-distribution robustness.

title: Multi-Task Structural Learning using Local Task Similarity induced Neuron Creation and Removal

abstract: The goal of offline black-box optimization (BBO) is to optimize an expensive black-box function using a fixed dataset of function evaluations. Prior works consider forward approaches that learn surrogates to the black-box function and inverse approaches that directly map function values to corresponding points in the input domain of the black-box function. These approaches are limited by the quality of the offline dataset and the difficulty in learning one-to-many mappings in high dimensions, respectively. We propose Denoising Diffusion Optimization Models (DDOM), a new inverse approach for offline black-box optimization based on diffusion models. Given an offline dataset, DDOM learns a conditional generative model over the domain of the black-box function conditioned on the function values. We investigate several design choices in DDOM, such as reweighting the dataset to focus on high function values and the use of classifier-free guidance at test-time to enable generalization to function values that can even exceed the dataset maxima. Empirically, we conduct experiments on the Design-Bench benchmark (Trabucco et al., 2022) and show that DDOM achieves results competitive with state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Offline black-box optimization seeks inputs that perform well on an expensive function using only a fixed collection of past evaluations. One approach learns to predict scores from inputs; another learns to generate inputs from desired scores. The latter faces a difficult one-to-many relationship because many different inputs can have the same function value.

The paper introduces Denoising Diffusion Optimization Models, or DDOM, to learn that inverse relationship as a conditional distribution. Given a requested function value, the diffusion model generates candidate inputs associated with it. Representing a distribution lets the method accommodate multiple possible inputs instead of forcing each score to correspond to a single design.

The authors investigate emphasizing high-value examples during training and using classifier-free guidance during generation. These choices are intended to support generalization to requested values that can exceed the dataset’s maximum. On Design-Bench, DDOM achieves results competitive with leading baselines. The empirical finding supports diffusion as an optimization tool, while the ability to condition on higher values is not a guarantee that every generated candidate attains them.
summary.tldr: DDOM uses score-conditioned diffusion to propose inputs for offline black-box optimization, achieving competitive results on Design-Bench.

title: Diffusion Models for Black-Box Optimization

abstract: In many computer vision applications, images are acquired with arbitrary or random rotations and translations, and in such setups, it is desirable to obtain semantic representations disentangled from the image orientation. Examples of such applications include semiconductor wafer defect inspection, plankton microscope images, and inference on single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) micro-graphs. In this work, we propose Invariant Representation Learning with Implicit Neural Representation (IRL-INR), which uses an implicit neural representation (INR) with a hypernetwork to obtain semantic representations disentangled from the orientation of the image. We show that IRL-INR can effectively learn disentangled semantic representations on more complex images compared to those considered in prior works and show that these semantic representations synergize well with SCAN to produce state-of-the-art unsupervised clustering results.

paragraphs: Images can show the same meaningful content at different rotations or positions. In applications such as wafer defect inspection, plankton microscopy, and cryo-electron microscopy, these acquisition differences can be unrelated to the semantic distinctions of interest. This paper aims to learn representations that separate image content from its orientation.

The proposed IRL-INR method combines an implicit neural representation with a hypernetwork. This architecture is used to obtain semantic representations disentangled from image orientation, addressing rotation and translation variation through representation learning. The desired result is a description of image content that is useful even when the way that content is positioned changes.

The authors show effective disentanglement on images more complex than those considered in prior work. They also combine the representations with SCAN and report state-of-the-art unsupervised clustering results. That downstream result gives practical significance to the representation objective: separating orientation from semantics can produce features that work well for grouping images without labels in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: IRL-INR separates semantic image representations from rotation and translation, supporting strong unsupervised clustering when combined with SCAN.

title: Rotation and Translation Invariant Representation Learning with Implicit Neural Representations

abstract: This paper studies the multi-agent performative prediction (Multi-PP) games over multiplex networks. We consider a distributed learning setting where agents partially cooperate on an agent network, while during learning, the data samples drawn depend on the prediction models of the agent itself and neighboring agents on a population network. The dynamics of Multi-PP games is hence affected by the interplay between both networks. This paper concentrates on this Multi-PP game with the following contributions. Firstly, we analyze sufficient conditions for the existence of the performative stable equilibrium (PSE) and Nash equilibrium (NE) of the Multi-PP games. Secondly, we analyze the changes to the equilibrium induced by perturbed data distributions, and derive the closed-form solutions where the network topologies are explicit. Our results connect the existence of PSE/NE with strengths of agents’ cooperation, and the changes of equilibrium solutions across agents with their node centrality, etc. Lastly, we show that a stochastic gradient descent (SGD) based distributed learning procedure finds the PSE under the said sufficient condition. Numerical illustrations on the network effects in Multi-PP games corroborate our findings.

paragraphs: In performative prediction, a model affects the data it later encounters. This paper studies multiple learning agents connected through two networks. An agent network determines partial cooperation, while a population network determines how an agent’s data depends on its own model and neighboring models. Learning therefore depends on both kinds of connection.

The authors derive sufficient conditions for the existence of performatively stable and Nash equilibria. They also analyze how equilibria change when data distributions are perturbed, obtaining closed-form solutions that explicitly involve network topology. The results connect equilibrium existence to cooperation strength and differences in agents’ responses to structural properties such as node centrality.

A distributed procedure based on stochastic gradient descent is shown to find a performatively stable equilibrium under the stated sufficient condition. Numerical illustrations support the network-effect analysis. The contribution is an account of how cooperation and model-induced changes in data interact, with conditional guarantees for stability and learning rather than a claim that every networked prediction system will converge.
summary.tldr: The paper links network structure and cooperation to equilibrium behavior in performative prediction games and proves conditional convergence of distributed SGD.

title: Network Effects in Performative Prediction Games

abstract: In Federated Learning (FL) and many other distributed training frameworks, collaborators can hold their private data locally and only share the network weights trained with the local data after multiple iterations. Gradient inversion is a family of privacy attacks that recovers data from its generated gradients. Seemingly, FL can provide a degree of protection against gradient inversion attacks on weight updates, since the gradient of a single step is concealed by the accumulation of gradients over multiple local iterations. In this work, we propose a principled way to extend gradient inversion attacks to weight updates in FL, thereby better exposing weaknesses in the presumed privacy protection inherent in FL. In particular, we propose a surrogate model method based on the characteristic of two-dimensional gradient flow and low-rank property of local updates. Our method largely boosts the ability of gradient inversion attacks on weight updates containing many iterations and achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance. Additionally, our method runs up to $100\times$ faster than the SOTA baseline in the common FL scenario. Our work re-evaluates and highlights the privacy risk of sharing network weights. Our code is available at https://github.com/JunyiZhu-AI/surrogate_model_extension.

paragraphs: Federated learning keeps training data with individual collaborators while sharing model weights after local training. Sharing an update that combines many training steps may appear to hide the individual gradients needed for data reconstruction. This paper investigates that presumed protection by extending gradient inversion attacks from individual gradients to accumulated weight updates.

The proposed Surrogate Model Extension uses a surrogate model informed by two-dimensional gradient-flow characteristics and the low-rank structure of local updates. These properties provide a principled basis for adapting existing inversion attacks to updates produced over many iterations. The approach therefore addresses the specific obstacle created by combining multiple local training steps.

The authors report substantially stronger reconstruction attacks and state-of-the-art performance. In a common federated learning scenario, the method runs up to one hundred times faster than the leading baseline. That is a reported maximum speedup, not a uniform factor across settings. The findings show that keeping raw data local does not eliminate the privacy risks associated with sharing trained network weights.
summary.tldr: SME strengthens and accelerates data-reconstruction attacks on federated learning updates accumulated over multiple local steps.

title: Surrogate Model Extension (SME): A Fast and Accurate Weight Update Attack on Federated Learning

abstract: Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning (RL) provides a promising paradigm for learning useful behaviors via reward-free per-training. Existing methods for unsupervised RL mainly conduct empowerment-driven skill discovery or entropy-based exploration. However, empowerment often leads to static skills, and pure exploration only maximizes the state coverage rather than learning useful behaviors. In this paper, we propose a novel unsupervised RL framework via an ensemble of skills, where each skill performs partition exploration based on the state prototypes. Thus, each skill can explore the clustered area locally, and the ensemble skills maximize the overall state coverage. We adopt state-distribution constraints for the skill occupancy and the desired cluster for learning distinguishable skills. Theoretical analysis is provided for the state entropy and the resulting skill distributions. Based on extensive experiments on several challenging tasks, we find our method learns well-explored ensemble skills and achieves superior performance in various downstream tasks compared to previous methods.

paragraphs: Unsupervised reinforcement learning aims to acquire behaviors before a task-specific reward is available. The paper identifies a tension in existing approaches: empowerment-based discovery can produce static skills, while maximizing exploration alone emphasizes visiting states without necessarily producing useful behaviors. The proposed framework seeks both broad exploration and distinct skills.

It organizes an ensemble of skills around state prototypes that define clustered regions. Each skill explores its own region locally, while the ensemble collectively expands overall state coverage. Constraints relate each skill’s occupancy distribution—the states it tends to visit—to its intended cluster, encouraging the skills to remain distinguishable.

The authors provide theoretical analysis of state entropy and the resulting skill distributions. Experiments on challenging tasks show well-explored skill ensembles and better performance on various downstream tasks than previous methods. The approach matters because it gives exploration an internal organization: broad coverage is distributed across identifiable behaviors that can later be useful when a concrete task is introduced.
summary.tldr: An ensemble of skills explores separate constrained state regions, combining broad coverage with distinguishable behaviors that improve downstream task performance.

title: Constrained Ensemble Exploration for Unsupervised Skill Discovery

abstract: AI Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) has the potential to improve human decision-making beyond AI predictions alone by providing additional probabilistic information to users. The majority of past research on AI and human decision-making has concentrated on model explainability and interpretability, with little focus on understanding the potential impact of UQ on human decision-making. We evaluated the impact on human decision-making for instance-level UQ, calibrated using a strict scoring rule, in two online behavioral experiments. In the first experiment, our results showed that UQ was beneficial for decision-making performance compared to only AI predictions. In the second experiment, we found UQ had generalizable benefits for decision-making across a variety of representations for probabilistic information. These results indicate that implementing high quality, instance-level UQ for AI may improve decision-making with real systems compared to AI predictions alone.

paragraphs: An AI prediction gives a user an answer, while uncertainty quantification adds probabilistic information about that particular prediction. This paper investigates whether that additional information helps people make better decisions. It focuses on instance-level uncertainty, meaning uncertainty attached to an individual case, rather than only a broad description of model performance.

The researchers conduct two online behavioral experiments using uncertainty estimates calibrated with a strict scoring rule. In the first experiment, participants make better decisions when given uncertainty information alongside predictions than when given predictions alone. This provides direct experimental evidence that the additional probabilities can be useful to human decision-makers.

The second experiment examines several ways of presenting probabilistic information and finds benefits across those representations. The result suggests that the observed usefulness is not confined to a single presentation format. Together, the experiments support further use of high-quality, case-specific uncertainty in AI-assisted decisions. The authors frame the practical implication cautiously: such information may improve decisions in real systems, beyond what predictions alone provide.
summary.tldr: Two online experiments find that calibrated, case-specific AI uncertainty improves human decisions across several probability presentation formats.

title: Using AI Uncertainty Quantification to Improve Human Decision-Making

abstract: Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a widely adopted training paradigm for privacy-preserving machine learning. While the SGD-based FL algorithms have demonstrated considerable success in the past, there is a growing trend towards adopting adaptive federated optimization methods, particularly for the training of large-scale models. However, the conventional synchronous aggregation design poses a significant challenge to the practical deployment of those adaptive federated optimization methods, particularly in the presence of straggler clients. To fill this research gap, this paper introduces federated adaptive asynchronous optimization, named FADAS, a novel method that incorporates asynchronous updates into adaptive federated optimization with provable guarantees. To further enhance the efficiency and resilience of our proposed method in scenarios with significant asynchronous delays, we also extend FADAS with a delay-adaptive learning adjustment strategy. We rigorously establish the convergence rate of the proposed algorithms and empirical results demonstrate the superior performance of FADAS over other asynchronous FL baselines.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines training performed by distributed clients. Adaptive optimization is increasingly used for large models, but its conventional synchronous aggregation creates difficulties when some clients are slow. The paper addresses the challenge of combining adaptive federated optimization with asynchronous updates, so that the training process can accommodate clients progressing at different speeds.

The proposed method, FADAS, introduces asynchronous updates into adaptive federated optimization and supplies theoretical convergence guarantees. The authors also develop a version with a delay-adaptive learning adjustment strategy. This extension is intended to improve efficiency and resilience when asynchronous delays are substantial, directly accounting for a central difficulty of the setting.

The paper establishes convergence rates for the proposed algorithms and reports superior experimental performance relative to other asynchronous federated learning baselines. Its contribution joins an adaptive optimization method, a delay-aware extension, and mathematical analysis in one framework. The stated results support the usefulness of that combination when slow clients make synchronous aggregation difficult to deploy.
summary.tldr: FADAS combines adaptive federated optimization with asynchronous updates and a delay-adaptive extension, supported by convergence guarantees and empirical improvements.

title: FADAS: Towards Federated Adaptive Asynchronous Optimization

abstract: Understanding generalization of overparametrized models remains a fundamental challenge in machine learning. The literature mostly studies generalization from an interpolation point of view, taking convergence towards a global minimum of the training loss for granted. This interpolation paradigm does not seem valid for complex tasks such as in-context learning or diffusion. It has instead been empirically observed that the trained models go from global minima to spurious local minima of the training loss as the number of training samples becomes larger than some level we call optimization threshold. This paper explores theoretically this phenomenon in the context of two-layer ReLU networks. We demonstrate that, despite overparametrization, networks might converge towards simpler solutions rather than interpolating training data, which leads to a drastic improvement on the test loss. Our analysis relies on the so called early alignment phase, during which neurons align toward specific directions. This directional alignment leads to a simplicity bias, wherein the network approximates the ground truth model without converging to the global minimum of the training loss. Our results suggest this bias, resulting in an optimization threshold from which interpolation is not reached anymore, is beneficial and enhances the generalization of trained models.

paragraphs: Accounts of generalization often assume that an overparameterized model reaches a global training-loss minimum. This paper investigates a different possibility in two-layer ReLU networks: increasing the sample count can move training beyond an optimization threshold where interpolation is no longer reached. The resulting solution can nevertheless generalize better.

The analysis centers on an early alignment phase, during which neurons orient toward particular directions. This alignment creates a bias toward simpler solutions. Even with enough parameters to fit the training data, the network may approximate the underlying ground-truth model without attaining the global minimum of training loss.

The authors show that this behavior can produce a drastic reduction in test loss. Their results suggest that the optimization threshold and the associated simplicity bias can be beneficial, linking incomplete fitting to improved generalization in the analyzed setting. The contribution is a theoretical explanation of how the path taken during optimization can favor useful structure, making perfect training fit an insufficient description of why an overparameterized network succeeds.
summary.tldr: Early neuron alignment can steer overparameterized two-layer ReLU networks toward simpler solutions that improve test loss without interpolating training data.

title: Simplicity Bias and Optimization Threshold in Two-Layer ReLU Networks

abstract: Antibodies are widely used as therapeutics, but their development requires costly affinity maturation, involving iterative mutations to enhance binding affinity. This paper explores a sequence-only scenario for affinity maturation, using solely antibody and antigen sequences. Recently AlphaFlow wraps AlphaFold within flow matching to generate diverse protein structures, enabling a sequence-conditioned generative model of structure. Building on this, we propose an alternating optimization framework that (1) fixes the sequence to guide structure generation toward high binding affinity using a structure-based predictor, then (2) applies inverse folding to create sequence mutations, refined by a sequence-based predictor. A key challenge is the lack of labeled data for training both predictors. To address this, we develop a co-teaching module that incorporates valuable information from noisy biophysical energies into predictor refinement. The sequence-based predictor selects consensus samples to teach the structure-based predictor, and vice versa. Our method, AffinityFlow, achieves state-of-the-art performance in proof-of-concept affinity maturation experiments.

paragraphs: AffinityFlow addresses antibody affinity maturation: choosing mutations that improve how strongly an antibody binds its target. The study considers a setting where the available inputs are only the antibody and antigen sequences. Although the inputs are sequences, the method uses generated protein structures internally to help search for promising changes.

The approach alternates between structure and sequence optimization. First, it holds the sequence fixed and guides structure generation toward stronger predicted binding, building on AlphaFlow's sequence-conditioned structure generation. Next, inverse folding proposes sequence mutations from structures, and a sequence-based predictor refines those proposals. This creates a cycle in which structural and sequence information both influence the search.

Training the two predictors is difficult because labeled affinity data are scarce. AffinityFlow addresses this with co-teaching: each predictor selects consensus samples to help refine the other, drawing useful information from noisy biophysical energies. The authors report state-of-the-art results in proof-of-concept maturation experiments. These findings support the alternating approach in the tested setting, while retaining the study's explicit proof-of-concept scope.
summary.tldr: AffinityFlow alternates guided structure generation and sequence mutation, using mutually trained predictors to improve antibody affinity in proof-of-concept experiments.

title: AffinityFlow: Guided Flows for Antibody Affinity Maturation

abstract: Large language models are susceptible to memorizing repeated sequences, posing privacy and copyright concerns. A popular mitigation strategy is to remove memorized information from specific neurons post-hoc. However, such approaches have shown limited success so far. In a controlled setting, we show that the memorization of natural sequences (those that resemble linguistically plausible text) become mechanistically entangled with general language abilities, thereby becoming challenging to remove post-hoc. In this work, we put forward a new paradigm of MemSinks that promotes isolation of memorization by design. We leverage a sequence identifier to activate a unique set of memorization neurons for each sequence across repetitions. By analyzing the dynamics of learning and forgetting, we argue that MemSinks facilitates clean isolation of memorized content, making it easier to remove without compromising general language capabilities. We implement MemSinks at the billion-parameter and billion-token scale, and observe both effective isolation and strong generalization. To our knowledge, this is the first proof-of-concept on real data demonstrating that simultaneous generalization and isolation is achievable. We open-source our code at https://github.com/grghosal/MemSinks.

paragraphs: Repeated text can become memorized by a language model, creating privacy and copyright concerns. Removing that content afterward is difficult if the mechanisms storing it also support ordinary language ability. In a controlled setting, this paper shows such entanglement for natural sequences: text that resembles plausible language can become intertwined with the model’s general capabilities.

MemSinks changes training to encourage memorization to remain isolated. A sequence identifier activates a particular set of memorization neurons consistently across repetitions of that sequence. This gives repeated content a designated place to be learned. Through analysis of learning and forgetting dynamics, the authors argue that this design makes memorized content easier to remove without harming general language capabilities.

The implementation reaches billion-parameter and billion-token scale, where the authors observe effective isolation alongside strong generalization. They present this as a proof of concept on real data. The result supports the possibility of designing training so that generalization and separable memorization coexist, rather than relying entirely on locating memorized information after training.
summary.tldr: MemSinks directs repeated sequences toward dedicated neurons during training, demonstrating separable memorization alongside strong generalization.

title: Memorization Sinks: Isolating Memorization during LLM Training

abstract: We present a novel prompt design for Large Language Models (LLMs) tailored to Asynchronous Time Series. Unlike regular time series, which assume values at evenly spaced time points, asynchronous time series consist of timestamped events occurring at irregular intervals, each described in natural language. Our approach effectively utilizes the rich natural language of event descriptions, allowing LLMs to benefit from their broad world knowledge for reasoning across different domains and tasks. This allows us to extend the scope of asynchronous time series analysis beyond forecasting to include tasks like anomaly detection and data imputation. We further introduce Stochastic Soft Prompting, a novel prompt-tuning mechanism that significantly improves model performance, outperforming existing finetuning methods such as QLORA. Through extensive experiments on real-world datasets, we demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance across different tasks and datasets.

paragraphs: The paper studies asynchronous time series made up of events at irregular times, with each event described in natural language. This differs from a sequence of measurements taken at evenly spaced intervals. The event descriptions provide semantic information that a language model can use together with the temporal structure of the sequence.

The authors introduce a prompt design tailored to these sequences. Its purpose is to make use of the descriptions’ meaning and the model’s broad world knowledge for reasoning across domains and tasks. The resulting approach covers forecasting, anomaly detection, and data imputation, extending the analysis beyond predicting what happens next.

They also introduce Stochastic Soft Prompting, a prompt-tuning mechanism that reports substantial performance improvements and outperforms fine-tuning approaches including QLoRA. Experiments on real-world datasets report state-of-the-art results across different tasks and datasets. The work combines a representation choice—presenting irregular events through their language descriptions—with a tuning method intended to make that information more useful to the model.
summary.tldr: A tailored prompt design and Stochastic Soft Prompting help language models analyze irregularly timed, text-described events across several tasks.

title: LAST SToP for Modeling Asynchronous Time Series

abstract: Visual representations play a crucial role in developing generalist robotic policies. Previous vision encoders, typically pre-trained with single-image reconstruction or two-image contrastive learning, tend to capture static information, often neglecting the dynamic aspects vital for embodied tasks. Recently, video diffusion models (VDMs) demonstrate the ability to predict future frames and showcase a strong understanding of physical world. We hypothesize that VDMs inherently produce visual representations that encompass both current static information and predicted future dynamics, thereby providing valuable guidance for robot action learning. Based on this hypothesis, we propose the Video Prediction Policy (VPP), which learns implicit inverse dynamics model conditioned on predicted future representations inside VDMs. To predict more precise future, we fine-tune pre-trained video foundation model on robot datasets along with internet human manipulation data. In experiments, VPP achieves a 18.6% relative improvement on the Calvin ABC-D generalization benchmark compared to the previous state-of-the-art, and demonstrates a 31.6% increase in success rates for complex real-world dexterous manipulation tasks. For your convenience, videos can be found at https://video-prediction-policy.github.io/
originalAbstract: Visual representations play a crucial role in developing generalist robotic policies. Previous vision encoders, typically pre-trained with single-image reconstruction or two-image contrastive learning, tend to capture static information, often neglecting the dynamic aspects vital for embodied tasks. Recently, video diffusion models (VDMs) demonstrate the ability to predict future frames and showcase a strong understanding of physical world. We hypothesize that VDMs inherently produce visual representations that encompass both current static information and predicted future dynamics, thereby providing valuable guidance for robot action learning. Based on this hypothesis, we propose the Video Prediction Policy (VPP), which learns implicit inverse dynamics model conditioned on predicted future representations inside VDMs. To predict more precise future, we fine-tune pre-trained video foundation model on robot datasets along with internet human manipulation data. In experiments, VPP achieves a 18.6% relative improvement on the Calvin ABC-D generalization benchmark compared to the previous state-of-the-art, and demonstrates a 31.6% increase in success rates for complex real-world dexterous manipulation tasks. For your convenience, videos can be found at https://video-prediction-policy.github.io/

paragraphs: Robot policies need visual information about both the present scene and how it may change after an action. The paper argues that encoders trained with individual images or image pairs tend to emphasize static information. It hypothesizes that video diffusion models contain representations of current appearance alongside predicted future dynamics, making them useful for robot learning.

Video Prediction Policy, or VPP, learns an implicit inverse dynamics model conditioned on predicted future representations inside a video diffusion model. In effect, those future-oriented features help guide action learning. To improve the predictions, the authors fine-tune a pretrained video foundation model using robot datasets together with internet videos of human manipulation.

VPP achieves an 18.6% relative improvement over the previous state of the art on the Calvin ABC-D generalization benchmark. The paper also reports a 31.6% increase in success rates for complex real-world dexterous manipulation tasks. These results support the usefulness of predictive visual representations for the evaluated robot tasks, while the proposed interpretation of what video models internally represent remains the motivating hypothesis.
summary.tldr: VPP uses predicted future representations from video diffusion models to improve robot action learning and manipulation performance.

title: Video Prediction Policy: A Generalist Robot Policy with Predictive Visual Representations

abstract: We consider a spiked random matrix model obtained by applying a function entrywise to a signal-plus-noise symmetric data matrix. We prove that the largest eigenvalue of this model, which we call a transformed spiked Wigner matrix, exhibits Baik-Ben Arous-Péché (BBP) type phase transition. We show that the law of the fluctuation converges to the Gaussian distribution when the effective signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is above the critical number, and to the GOE Tracy-Widom distribution when the effective SNR is below the critical number. We provide precise formulas for the limiting distributions and also concentration estimates for the largest eigenvalues, both in the supercritical and the subcritical regimes.

paragraphs: The paper studies symmetric matrices containing both a signal and random noise, followed by a transformation applied separately to each matrix entry. The authors call the resulting object a transformed spiked Wigner matrix. Their focus is the largest eigenvalue and how its random fluctuations depend on the effective signal-to-noise ratio.

They prove that this eigenvalue exhibits a BBP-type phase transition. Above a critical effective signal-to-noise ratio, its fluctuation law converges to a Gaussian distribution. Below that critical value, it converges to the GOE Tracy-Widom distribution. Thus, changing signal strength across the threshold changes the mathematical form of the limiting randomness, not simply its magnitude.

The paper supplies precise formulas for those limiting distributions and concentration estimates in both the above-threshold and below-threshold regimes. These results characterize both the asymptotic fluctuation pattern and how tightly the largest eigenvalues concentrate. The contribution is a theoretical account of spectral behavior after an entrywise transformation, with distinct conclusions for the two stated signal-strength regimes.
summary.tldr: The largest eigenvalue of a transformed spiked Wigner matrix has different limiting fluctuation laws above and below a critical signal strength.

title: Fluctuations of the largest eigenvalues of transformed spiked Wigner matrices

abstract: Federated Graph Learning (FGL) proposes an effective approach to collaboratively training Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) while maintaining privacy. Nevertheless, communication efficiency becomes a critical bottleneck in environments with limited resources. In this context, one-shot FGL emerges as a promising solution by restricting communication to a single round. However, prevailing FGL methods face two key challenges in the one-shot setting: 1) They heavily rely on gradual personalized optimization over multiple rounds, undermining the capability of the global model to efficiently generalize across diverse graph structures. 2) They are prone to overfitting to local data distributions due to extreme structural bias, leading to catastrophic forgetting. To address these issues, we introduce GHOST, an innovative one-shot FGL framework. In GHOST, we establish a proxy model for each client to leverage diverse local knowledge and integrate it to train the global model. During training, we identify and consolidate parameters essential for capturing topological knowledge, thereby mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Extensive experiments on real-world tasks demonstrate the superiority and generalization capability of GHOST. The code is available at https://github.com/JiaruQian/GHOST.

paragraphs: Federated graph learning trains graph neural networks collaboratively while keeping data local. Restricting communication to one round can help in resource-limited settings, but it removes the repeated exchanges that many methods rely on. A global model must then combine knowledge from diverse graph structures without gradual rounds of personalized refinement.

GHOST creates a proxy model for each client and uses those proxies to integrate local knowledge into global training. It also identifies and consolidates parameters that are important for representing graph topology. This second component addresses a problem caused by strong local structural biases: training can overfit particular client distributions and forget useful structural knowledge.

The framework therefore couples a mechanism for collecting diverse client knowledge with one for retaining it during integration. Experiments on real-world tasks report superior performance and generalization. These findings support proxy-based knowledge integration as an approach to one-shot federated graph learning, where efficient communication must be balanced with the global model's ability to handle graph structures beyond any individual client's local distribution.
summary.tldr: GHOST combines client proxy models and topology-preserving parameter consolidation to improve one-shot federated graph learning.

title: GHOST: Generalizable One-Shot Federated Graph Learning with Proxy-Based Topology Knowledge Retention

abstract: Recent advancements in predictive models have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in predicting the future state of objects and scenes. However, the lack of categorization based on inherent characteristics continues to hinder the progress of predictive model development. Additionally, existing benchmarks are unable to effectively evaluate higher-capability, highly embodied predictive models from an embodied perspective. In this work, we classify the functionalities of predictive models into a hierarchy and take the first step in evaluating World Simulators by proposing a dual evaluation framework called WorldSimBench. WorldSimBench includes Explicit Perceptual Evaluation and Implicit Manipulative Evaluation, encompassing human preference assessments from the visual perspective and action-level evaluations in embodied tasks, covering three representative embodied scenarios: Open-Ended Embodied Environment, Autonomous, Driving, and Robot Manipulation. In the Explicit Perceptual Evaluation, we introduce the HF-Embodied Dataset, a video assessment dataset based on fine-grained human feedback, which we use to train a Human Preference Evaluator that aligns with human perception and explicitly assesses the visual fidelity of World Simulater. In the Implicit Manipulative Evaluation, we assess the video-action consistency of World Simulators by evaluating whether the generated situation-aware video can be accurately translated into the correct control signals in dynamic environments. Our comprehensive evaluation offers key insights that can drive further innovation in video generation models, positioning World Simulators as a pivotal advancement toward embodied artificial intelligence.

paragraphs: A generated video can look convincing while still being unsuitable for guiding an embodied agent. WorldSimBench addresses the need to evaluate predictive video models from both perspectives. The paper first organizes predictive-model capabilities into a hierarchy, then introduces a dual evaluation framework for models intended to function as world simulators.

The perceptual component assesses visual fidelity using human preferences. The authors introduce HF-Embodied, a video-assessment dataset containing fine-grained human feedback, and use it to train a preference evaluator aligned with human perception. This provides an explicit measure of how generated videos appear to human viewers.

The manipulative component evaluates consistency between generated video and actions: it asks whether situation-aware predictions can be translated into correct control signals in dynamic environments. The benchmark covers open-ended embodied environments, autonomous driving, and robot manipulation. Together, the two evaluations examine both visual quality and usefulness for control. The paper presents the benchmark and its evaluation as a foundation for improving world simulators, rather than treating visual fidelity alone as evidence of embodied capability.
summary.tldr: WorldSimBench evaluates video world simulators through both human judgments of visual quality and consistency with embodied control actions.

title: WorldSimBench: Towards Video Generation Models as World Simulators

abstract: Deep neural networks learn structured features from complex, non-Gaussian inputs, but the mechanisms behind this process remain poorly understood. Our work is motivated by the observation that the first-layer filters learnt by deep convolutional neural networks from natural images resemble those learnt by independent component analysis (ICA), a simple unsupervised method that seeks the most non-Gaussian projections of its inputs. This similarity suggests that ICA provides a simple, yet principled model for studying feature learning. Here, we leverage this connection to investigate the interplay between data structure and optimisation in feature learning for the most popular ICA algorithm, FastICA, and stochastic gradient descent (SGD), which is used to train deep networks. We rigorously establish that FastICA requires at least $n\gtrsim d^4$ samples to recover a single non-Gaussian direction from $d$-dimensional inputs on a simple synthetic data model. We show that vanilla online SGD outperforms FastICA, and prove that the optimal sample complexity $n\gtrsim d^2$ can be reached by smoothing the loss, albeit in a data-dependent way. We finally demonstrate the existence of a search phase for FastICA on ImageNet, and discuss how the strong non-Gaussianity of said images compensates for the poor sample complexity of FastICA.

paragraphs: The paper uses independent component analysis, or ICA, as a simplified model of feature learning. Its motivation is that filters learned by ICA resemble first-layer filters learned by deep convolutional networks on natural images. Because ICA searches for strongly non-Gaussian projections, it provides a way to examine how input structure interacts with the optimization algorithm.

On a simple synthetic data model, the authors prove that FastICA needs at least roughly d to the fourth power samples to recover one non-Gaussian direction from d-dimensional inputs. Vanilla online stochastic gradient descent performs better. With data-dependent smoothing of the loss, they prove that the optimal sample complexity of roughly d squared can be reached.

These results show that finding the same underlying feature can require very different amounts of data depending on the optimization procedure. The paper also identifies a search phase for FastICA on ImageNet and discusses how the strong non-Gaussian structure of natural images compensates for its poor sample complexity. The synthetic guarantees and image observations together connect algorithmic difficulty with the strength of structure present in data.
summary.tldr: An ICA analysis shows how optimization choices and non-Gaussian data structure jointly determine the sample requirements of feature learning.

title: Feature learning from non-Gaussian inputs: the case of Independent Component Analysis in high dimensions

abstract: Neural algorithmic reasoning aims to capture computations with neural networks by training models to imitate the execution of classical algorithms. While common architectures are expressive enough to contain the correct model in the weight space, current neural reasoners struggle to generalize well on out-of-distribution data. On the other hand, classical computations are not affected by distributional shifts as they can be described as transitions between discrete computational states. In this work, we propose to force neural reasoners to maintain the execution trajectory as a combination of finite predefined states. To achieve this, we separate discrete and continuous data flows and describe the interaction between them. Trained with supervision on the algorithm’s state transitions, such models are able to perfectly align with the original algorithm. To show this, we evaluate our approach on multiple algorithmic problems and achieve perfect test scores both in single-task and multitask setups. Moreover, the proposed architectural choice allows us to prove the correctness of the learned algorithms for any test data.
