paragraphs: Different hallucination definitions can make it difficult to compare evaluations or discuss remedies consistently. This paper reviews existing definitions and proposes a unified account: hallucination is inaccurate internal modeling of a world that becomes observable to the user. The relevant world may be represented by a knowledge base or by the source material a model is summarizing.

The framework varies two elements: the reference world model and the policy for deciding what counts as a conflict with it. In this way, it brings earlier definitions into a common structure. A factual statement that contradicts a knowledge base and a summary that contradicts its source can be understood through the same underlying relationship.

The authors argue that this approach makes evaluations specify what reference world they assume and helps distinguish hallucinations from errors in planning or reward. They also connect the framework to HalluWorld, a complementary benchmark with fully specified reference world models. The proposed benefit is clearer comparison and diagnosis, providing shared language for evaluation and mitigation rather than a reported solution to hallucination.
summary.tldr: The paper unifies hallucination definitions around observable inaccuracies relative to an explicitly chosen reference world model.

abstract: We propose a generalization of multilabel classification that we refer to as graded multilabel classification. The key idea is that, instead of requesting a yes-no answer to the question of class membership or, say, relevance of a class label for an instance, we allow for a graded membership of an instance, measured on an ordinal scale of membership degrees. This extension is motivated by practical applications in which a graded or partial class membership is natural. Apart from introducing the basic setting, we propose two general strategies for reducing graded multilabel problems to conventional (multilabel) classification problems. Moreover, we address the question of how to extend performance metrics commonly used in multilabel classification to the graded setting, and present first experimental results.

This extension is motivated by practical applications in which a graded or partial class membership is natural. paragraphs: Multilabel classification normally asks whether each label applies to an example. This paper broadens that setting so that a label can apply to different degrees. Those degrees lie on an ordinal scale: their ordering matters. The motivation is that partial or graded membership is a natural description of some practical classification problems.

The authors formalize this graded multilabel setting and propose two general ways to reduce it to conventional classification problems, including ordinary multilabel classification. These reductions connect the richer output format to established learning tasks. They provide routes for handling ordered membership levels through classification machinery designed for more familiar forms of output.

The paper also considers evaluation, asking how common multilabel performance measures should extend when membership is graded. It presents initial experimental results alongside the problem formulation and reduction strategies. The contribution is therefore a framework for both learning and assessing graded predictions, making the desired degree of label membership an explicit part of the task.
summary.tldr: Graded multilabel classification replaces binary label membership with ordered degrees and provides reductions and evaluation measures for the new setting.

title: Graded Multilabel Classification: The Ordinal Case

abstract: The problem of clustering is considered, for the case when each data point is a sample generated by a stationary ergodic process. We propose a very natural asymptotic notion of consistency,and show that simple consistent algorithms exist, under most general non-parametric assumptions. The notion of consistency is as follows: two samples should be put into the same cluster if and only if they we regenerated by the same distribution. With this notion of consistency, clustering generalizes such classical statistical problems as homogeneity testing and process classification. We show that, for the case of a known number of clusters, consistency can be achieved under the only assumption that the joint distribution of the data is stationary ergodic (no parametric or Markovian assumptions, no assumptions of independence, neither between nor within the samples). If the number of clusters is unknown, consistency can be achieved under appropriate assumptions on the mixing rates of the processes (again, no parametric or independence assumptions). In both cases we give examples of simple (at most quadratic in each argument) algorithms which are consistent.

paragraphs: This paper studies clustering when each item is a sample generated by a process. Its target is to group samples exactly according to their generating distributions. The authors formalize an asymptotic notion of consistency: samples belong together if and only if the same distribution generated them. This connects clustering to testing whether samples share a distribution and to process classification.

When the number of clusters is known, consistent algorithms require only that the joint data distribution be stationary and ergodic. The result does not require a parametric model, a Markov assumption, or independence within or between samples. This makes the guarantee applicable to a broad class of dependent data under the stated process assumption.

When the number of clusters is unknown, consistency requires additional conditions on mixing rates, which concern how dependence evolves over separation. The authors provide simple consistent algorithms for both settings, with at most quadratic complexity in each argument. The guarantees are asymptotic, establishing eventual clustering correctness under their respective assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes consistent clustering of process-generated samples under broad dependence assumptions, with stronger conditions needed when the cluster count is unknown.

title: Clustering processes

abstract: We propose a spectral clustering algorithm for the multi-view setting where we have access to multiple views of the data, each of which can be independently used for clustering. Our spectral clustering algorithm has a flavor of co-training, which is already a widely used idea in semi-supervised learning. We work on the assumption that the true underlying clustering would assign a point to the same cluster irrespective of the view. Hence, we constrain our approach to only search for the clusterings that agree across the views. Our algorithm does not have any hyperparameters to set, which is a major advantage in unsupervised learning. We empirically compare with a number of baseline methods on synthetic and real-world datasets to show the efficacy of the proposed algorithm.

Hence, we constrain our approach to only search for the clusterings that agree across the views. Our algorithm does not have any hyperparameters to set, which is a major advantage in unsupervised learning. We empirically compare with a number of baseline methods on synthetic and real-world datasets to show the efficacy of the proposed algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper studies clustering when each data point has several different views, each sufficient to support clustering on its own. Instead of treating those views as unrelated tasks, it proposes a spectral clustering algorithm that lets them inform a shared grouping. The approach draws on co-training, an idea usually associated with semi-supervised learning.

Its central assumption is that the underlying cluster membership should remain the same whichever view is used. The algorithm therefore restricts its search to clusterings that agree across views. This agreement requirement gives the multiple representations a concrete role: a proposed grouping must be compatible with more than one account of the data. Its justification depends on the stated shared-clustering assumption.

The authors also emphasize that their algorithm introduces no hyperparameters to set, making it attractive in an unsupervised setting where tuning can be difficult. Comparisons with baseline methods on synthetic and real-world datasets support its effectiveness. These results provide empirical evidence for using cross-view agreement to guide spectral clustering.
summary.tldr: A hyperparameter-free spectral clustering method combines multiple views by searching for clusterings that agree across them.

title: A Co-training Approach for Multi-view Spectral Clustering

abstract: Regularization is a powerful technique for extracting useful information from noisy data. Typically, it is implemented by adding some sort of norm constraint to an objective function and then exactly optimizing the modified objective function. This procedure often leads to optimization problems that are computationally more expensive than the original problem, a fact that is clearly problematic if one is interested in large-scale applications. On the other hand, a large body of empirical work has demonstrated that heuristics, and in some cases approximation algorithms, developed to speed up computations sometimes have the side-effect of performing regularization implicitly. Thus, we consider the question: What is the regularized optimization objective that an approximation algorithm is exactly optimizing? We address this question in the context of computing approximations to the smallest nontrivial eigenvector of a graph Laplacian; and we consider three random-walk-based procedures: one based on the heat kernel of the graph, one based on computing the the PageRank vector associated with the graph, and one based on a truncated lazy random walk. In each case, we provide a precise characterization of the manner in which the approximation method can be viewed as implicitly computing the exact solution to a regularized problem. Interestingly, the regularization is not on the usual vector form of the optimization problem, but instead it is on a related semidefinite program.

This paper investigates a different possibility: computational shortcuts may already impose a form of regularization, even when no explicit regularization term appears in the original calculation.

The authors study approximations to the smallest nontrivial eigenvector of a graph Laplacian. They analyze three procedures based on random walks: a graph heat-kernel method, a PageRank-based method, and a truncated lazy random walk. For each procedure, they ask which regularized optimization problem its output can be understood as solving exactly.

The contribution is a precise characterization of that implicit regularization for all three procedures. A crucial distinction is that the corresponding regularization acts on a related semidefinite program, rather than on the usual vector formulation of the eigenvector problem. This gives a mathematical interpretation to the shortcuts: their approximations can also be viewed as exact solutions to particular regularized problems.
summary.tldr: Three random-walk methods for approximate eigenvector computation are characterized as exactly solving related regularized semidefinite problems.

title: Implementing regularization implicitly via approximate eigenvector computation
